docs.text: SupplyNetPy Documentation SupplyNetPy is a Python library specifically designed and developed to model and simulate different supply chain problems with ease. It provides configurable components such as raw-material suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, retailers and customer demands for creating arbitrary supply chain networks, along with configurable replenishment policies and supplier-selection policies. With SupplyNetPy, we can quickly assemble a supply chain, specify demand and supply behaviors, and run simulations to evaluate performance metrics such as orders fulfilled, shortages, costs and profit, for each site, each link and the whole network. Estimating Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) System Description As Best Buy sells through its current inventory of HP computers, the purchasing manager places a replenishment order for Q more computers (the lot size ). Each order carries a fixed cost of S dollars. This is an overhead for each order, covering paperwork, transport, receiving and similar costs that do not grow with the size of the order. The purchasing manager has to decide how many computers to put in each order. The decision uses the following inputs. D is the annual demand for the product (how many units are sold per year). S is the fixed cost of each order (whatever its size). C is the cost per unit (what HP charges Best Buy for one computer). h is the holding cost per year, as a fraction of the cost per unit. For example, h = 0.2 means it costs 20% of the unit price to keep one unit in inventory for a year, covering storage, the money tied up in inventory and so on. Assume that HP does not offer any discounts, and each unit costs $C no matter how large an order is. The holding cost per unit per year is then H = hC. The model rests on the following basic assumptions. Demand is steady at D units per time unit. No shortages are allowed, that is, all demand must be met from inventory. The lead time is fixed (at first assumed to be zero). The purchasing manager chooses the lot size to keep the store's total cost as low as possible. The manager must consider three costs when deciding on the lot size. Annual material cost Annual ordering cost Annual holding cost Because the price per unit does not depend on the lot size, we have Annual material cost = \(CD\) The number of orders must be enough to meet the annual demand D. Given a lot size of Q, we thus have Number of orders per year = \(\frac{D}{Q}\) Because an order cost of S is paid for each order placed, we find that Annual ordering cost = \((\frac{D}{Q}){S}\) Given a lot size of Q, we have an average inventory of Q/2. The annual holding cost is thus the cost of holding Q/2 units in inventory for one year, which is Annual holding cost = \((\frac{Q}{2})H = (\frac{Q}{2})hC\) The total annual cost, TC, is the sum of all three costs, which is Total annual cost, \(TC = CD + (\frac{D}{Q})S + (\frac{Q}{2})hC\) Image source, the textbook Supply Chain Management: Strategy, Planning, and Operation (Chopra and Meindl). The figure above shows how the different costs change with the lot size. Observe that the annual holding cost increases with an increase in lot size. In contrast, the annual ordering cost declines with an increase in lot size. The material cost is independent of lot size because we have assumed the price to be fixed. The total annual cost thus first declines and then increases with an increase in lot size. From the point of view of the manager at Best Buy, the optimal lot size is the one that keeps Best Buy's total cost as low as possible. It is found by taking the first derivative of the total cost with respect to Q and setting it equal to 0. The optimal lot size is called the economic order quantity (EOQ). It is written Q* and is given by the equation below. Optimal lot size, \(Q* = \sqrt{\frac{2DS}{hC}}\) Numerical Example Demand for the Deskpro computer at Best Buy is 1,000 units per month. Best Buy incurs a fixed order placement, transportation, and receiving cost of $4,000 each time an order is placed. Each computer costs Best Buy $500 and the retailer has a holding cost of 20 percent. Work out the number of computers the store manager should order in each replenishment order. Analysis. In this case, the store manager has the following inputs. Annual demand, \(D = 1,000 * 12 = 12,000\) units Order cost per lot, \(S = 4,000\) Unit cost per computer, \(C = 500\) Holding cost per year as a fraction of the unit cost, \(h = 0.2\) Using the EOQ formula, the optimal lot size is Optimal order size = Q* = \(\sqrt{\frac{2 * 12,000 * 4,000}{0.2 * 500}} = 980\) To keep the total cost at Best Buy as low as possible, the store manager orders a lot size of 980 computers in each replenishment order. The cycle inventory is the resulting average inventory, which is Cycle inventory = \(\frac{Q*}{2} = 490\) For a lot size of Q* = 980, the store manager works out Number of orders per year = \(\frac{D} {Q*} = \frac{12,000} {980} = 12.24\) Annual ordering and holding cost = \(\frac{D} {Q*} S + (\frac{Q*} {2}) hC = 97,980\) Average flow time = \(\frac{Q*} {2D} = \frac{490} {12,000} = 0.041\) year \(= 0.49\) month Each computer thus spends 0.49 month, on average, at Best Buy before it is sold because it was purchased in a batch of 980. constant) """ D = 12000 # annual demand d = 34 # daily demand order_cost = 4000 # order cost unit_cost = 500 # unit cost holding_cost = 0.273 # holding cost per day lead_time = 0 # lead time simlen = name="Best Buy", node_type="distributor", capacity=lot_size, initial_level=lot_size, inventory_holding_cost=holding_cost, replenishment_policy=scm.PeriodicReplenishment, product_buy_price=450, policy_param={'T':order_interval,'Q':lot_size}, product_sell_price=unit_cost) link1 = scm.Link(env=env,ID="l1", source=hp_supplier, sink=bestbuy, cost=order_cost, lead_time=lambda: lead_time) demand1 = scm.Demand(env=env,ID="d1", name="demand_d1", order_arrival_model=lambda: 1, order_quantity_model=lambda: d, demand_node=bestbuy, consume_available=True) scm.global_logger.disable_logging() # disable logging for all components env.run(until=simlen) bb_invlevels = np.array(bestbuy.inventory.instantaneous_levels) hp_sup_transportation_cost = bestbuy.stats.transportation_cost total_cost = bestbuy.stats.inventory_carry_cost + bestbuy.stats.transportation_cost total_cost_arr.append([lot_size, total_cost/simlen]) unsat_demand = demand1.stats.demand_placed[1]-demand1.stats.fulfillment_received[1] unsat_arr.append([lot_size,unsat_demand]) print(f"{lot_size} \t\t docs.text: About SupplyNetPy SupplyNetPy is an open source Python library for building, running, and analyzing supply chain simulations. You describe a supply chain, with its raw-material suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, warehouses, retailers, customer demands and the links between them. SupplyNetPy then plays out the events in that chain (orders being placed, orders arriving, customers ordering, disruptions starting) and reports how the system behaves, such as the inventory level at each site, where shortages appear, what each part costs, and how profitable the chain is overall. It is built on SimPy , a Python framework for event-driven simulation . Instead of advancing the clock one fixed step at a time, the simulator jumps directly from one event to the next (the next customer order, the next delivery, the next disruption), so long runs stay fast when events are few. SupplyNetPy is intended for researchers, students, and practitioners working in operations, logistics, and supply chain management. The words used in these pages are explained in the Glossary , and the User Guide explains common tasks step by step. Purpose Build detailed supply chain models, with raw-material suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, retailers and customer demands. Simulate how inventories change over time, with replenishment orders, lead times, supplier selection, perishable products, costs and disruptions. Test and compare replenishment policies and supplier-selection policies. Analyze performance through the simulation log and the results for each node, each link and the whole network, such as orders fulfilled, revenue, shortages, lost sales, costs and profit. Run experiments with many replications, and compare settings fairly. Features Modular design. Build supply chain networks of any size and with as many levels as you need (for example raw-material suppliers, manufacturers, distributors and retailers) by assembling the built in components. Customer demand. Customer orders can arrive at fixed or random times, for fixed or random numbers of units, or follow recorded data. When a site is short of units, its customers can leave, take the units that are there, or wait for the rest, with partial deliveries if they accept them. See Customer Demand . Replenishment policies. Several built in replenishment policies , the rules that decide when to place a replenishment order and how many units to order. You can also write your own. See Replenishment Policies . (s, S). When the inventory position falls to s or below, order enough to bring it back up to S . (s, S) with safety stock. The same rule, with the safety stock added to both s and S , so a sudden rise in demand does not immediately cause a shortage. (R, Q). When the inventory position falls to R or below, order a fixed Q units. Periodic (T, Q). Every T time units, order Q units, whatever the inventory position. Periodic (T, Q) with safety stock. The same rule, and if the inventory level is below the safety stock, the order also includes the units needed to bring it back up. Supplier selection. A site with several suppliers chooses one for each replenishment order with a supplier-selection policy . The built in policies choose the first supplier, the first that can fill the whole order, the cheapest or the fastest, or choose at random with a probability for each supplier, and you can write your own. In fixed mode the site keeps its first choice, and in dynamic mode it chooses again for every order. See Supplier Selection . Lead times and costs. Each link has its own lead time, fixed or random, and its own transportation cost. Perishable products. Units can have a shelf life. Each batch keeps its manufacturing date from site to site, orders take the oldest units first, and expired units are thrown away and counted. See Perishable Products . Disruptions. Both sites and links can be disrupted, either at scheduled times or at random with a given probability. While a site is disrupted it takes no new orders, from other sites or from customers, and the customers it turns away are counted apart from its shortage. The disruption_impact setting describes what happens to the units at a site when a disruption starts. With "destroy_all" , all units are lost (for example in a fire or flood at a warehouse). With "destroy_fraction" and a loss fraction, part of the units is lost. The fraction can be a fixed number or drawn at random for each disruption (useful, say, for a power cut that destroys part of the units kept cold). A custom function can describe any other effect you want to capture (contamination, theft, partial damage and so on). The units lost and their value are recorded for each site, and the value is part of its costs, so the financial impact of disruptions shows up in the profit without extra bookkeeping. See Disruptions . * Statistics and results. Every node and every link keeps its own statistics, such as orders placed and fulfilled, shortages, lost sales, waiting times, lead times, the fill rate, the average inventory level, availability and costs. The results for the whole network are added up from them. A warm-up can leave the first stretch of a run out of the statistics. See Statistics and Results . * Reproducible experiments. Seeded random numbers make every run repeatable, so settings can be compared over many replications with confidence intervals. See Running Experiments . * Simple API. Build and simulate supply chain models with clear Python code, either from plain Python dictionaries or by creating each part as an object. Architecture SupplyNetPy provides these core components for supply chain modeling. The API Reference describes each of them. Node classes. Supplier (a raw-material supplier), Manufacturer , InventoryNode (a distributor, warehouse or retailer), Demand (a customer demand), and their base class Node . Link. The connection between a site and one of its suppliers, with its own transportation cost and lead time. Inventory. Keeps the inventory level and the related records at each site, including the batches of a perishable product. Product and RawMaterial. The product a manufacturer makes, and the raw materials it uses. InventoryReplenishment. The base class for replenishment policies. SSReplenishment. The (s, S) policy. RQReplenishment. The (R, Q) policy. PeriodicReplenishment. The periodic policy, which places a replenishment order at fixed intervals. SupplierSelectionPolicy. The base class for supplier-selection policies, each used in fixed or dynamic mode. All built in policies skip suppliers whose site or link is disrupted. If no supplier can take a replenishment order, the order is not placed, and the replenishment policy checks again as soon as a supplier or a link recovers. SelectFirst. Chooses the first supplier. SelectAvailable. Chooses the first supplier whose inventory level can fill the whole order. SelectCheapest. Chooses the supplier with the lowest transportation cost. SelectFastest. Chooses the supplier with the shortest lead time. SelectProbabilistic. Chooses the supplier of each order at random, with a probability for each supplier. Statistics and LinkStatistics. The statistics of each node and of each link. Network and the utility functions. create_sc_net builds a network, simulate_sc_net runs it and works out the results for the whole network, reset_stats starts the statistics again after a warm-up, and further functions print, return or draw the results. The Network class holds a network and its results. Why SupplyNetPy? Made for supply chains. Sites, links, replenishment and supplier-selection policies, disruptions and perishable products come ready to use, so a model takes a few lines of Python instead of a simulation written from scratch. Open source and extensible. Every part can be configured, and policies and disruption effects can be replaced by your own. Validated. SupplyNetPy was validated in four ways. Automated tests. Tests check each part of the library, and run on every change to it. Textbook results. The examples reproduce analytical results, such as the economic order quantity , the safety stock and the newsvendor order quantity. A commercial tool. In eight models, all 19 performance metrics agree exactly with those of anyLogistix . The models and results are in the validation folder . A published study. The pharmacy case study reproduces the results of a published paper. Authors Tushar Lone Neha Karanjkar Lekshmi P License License

docs.text: SupplyNetPy is an open source Python library for building, running, and analyzing supply chain simulations. You describe a supply chain, with its raw-material suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, warehouses, retailers, customer demands and the links between them. SupplyNetPy then plays out the events in that chain (orders being placed, orders arriving, customers ordering, disruptions starting) and reports how the system behaves, such as the inventory level at each site, where shortages appear, what each part costs, and how profitable the chain is overall. It is built on SimPy , a Python framework for event-driven simulation . Instead of advancing the clock one fixed step at a time, the simulator jumps directly from one event to the next (the next customer order, the next delivery, the next disruption), so long runs stay fast when events are few. SupplyNetPy is intended for researchers, students, and practitioners working in operations, logistics, and supply chain management. The words used in these pages are explained in the Glossary , and the User Guide explains common tasks step by step.

docs.text: Find the Google Colab notebook for this example here . Pharmacy Supply Chain This study comes from the publication 'Improving Simulation Optimization Run Time When Solving For Periodic Review Inventory Policies in A Pharmacy' , which you can read here . It uses simulation based optimization (SBO) to find the values of the (s, S) policy parameters that keep the total cost of the pharmacy supply chain as low as possible. In this example, we aim to understand the supply chain network described by the authors, implement it with SupplyNetPy, and replicate their results. This shows how much effort it takes to rebuild a specific system with SupplyNetPy, and helps to validate the library. System Description The system is a supply chain with a single level between the source and the customers. A hospital pharmacy (modeled as a distributor) is supplied directly by a pharmaceutical manufacturer (modeled as an infinite supplier). The pharmacy faces random demand, and is supplied by a supplier that never runs out. On any given day, a disruption of the supplier (when it cannot ship) starts with probability 0.01. The pharmacy follows an (s, S) replenishment policy. When its inventory position falls below s , it orders enough to bring the inventory position back up to S . The product is perishable, with a shelf life of 90 days. The authors model and simulate this system to find the values of s and S that minimize the expected total cost per day. The inventory is perishable. The inventory position is what the pharmacy can count on today, the units it holds now plus the units already ordered that have not arrived yet (in transit from the supplier). The next replenishment order is decided from it.   Inventory position = inventory level + inventory in transit The replenishment policy is (s, S). When the inventory position falls below s , the pharmacy orders ( S − inventory position) units, which brings the inventory position back up to S . Review period = 1 day (the pharmacy checks its inventory every day). The flowchart below uses this shorthand.   H = inventory level (the units the pharmacy holds)   H′ = the part of H that will expire at the end of day t   P = inventory position = H + inventory in transit This flowchart shows the order of the events that take place at the pharmacy each day. ( Image source ) Daily Process for the Perishable Inventory Begin day t 1. Order arrive at the Pharmacy 2. Update Inventory Levels (H) 3. Satisfy demand based on Inventory Levels 3.1. If (d>H): - demand Satisfied = H - Shortage = d-H - Waste = 0 3.2. Else: - demand Satisfied = d - Shortage = 0 - Waste = max{0,H'-d} 4. Discard Expired Drugs 5. Update Inventory Levels (H) 5.1. Is (s>P) and (Supplier not Disrupted): - Place order for (S-P) 5.2. Else: - Do not place order 6. End of the day t The optimization objective is to minimize the expected cost per day. The costs of interest are the shortage, waste, holding and ordering costs. Assumptions All drugs that arrive in the same month come from the same production batch, and expire at the end of the same month. So drugs are only thrown away at the end of a month. The inventory level is known each day. The number of days until the inventory expires is known each day. The lead time is fixed and positive. An order placed at the end of day ( t − 1) arrives at the beginning of day t . Demand is random. Supply is uncertain because of disruptions. Demand and disruptions are independent of each other. All demand that is not met is lost. Orders are served with the oldest units first (first in, first out). System Configuration T = number of days (360) Costs are counted from day 31 to day 360, after a warm up of 30 days, as in the paper. A SupplyNetPy run stops just before its end time, so the warm up runs to time 31 and the main run to time T + 1. l = lead time (6 days) e = shelf life of the drugs (3 months, that is 90 days) R = number of simulation runs, or replications (5000) b = shortage cost (5, relative to the buy price) z = waste cost (1, relative to the buy price) h = holding cost (0.001, relative to the buy price) o = ordering cost (0.5, relative to the buy price) d t = demand on day t (random, Poisson with a mean of 25 a day) y t = whether the supply is disrupted on day t (y t = 0 disrupted, y t = 1 available) Time until the next disruption, geometric with p = 0.01 Time to recover from a disruption, geometric with p = 1/30 Implementation import simpy import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from matplotlib.pyplot import figure import SupplyNetPy.Components as scm class Distributions: """ Class to generate random numbers for demand (order quantity) and order arrival arrival times. Parameters: mu (float): Mean of the exponential distribution for order arrival times. lam (float): Lambda parameter of the Poisson distribution for demand (order quantity). """ def __init__(self,mu=1,lam=1,p=0.01): self.mu = mu self.lam = lam self.p = p def poisson_demand(self): return np.random.poisson(self.lam) def expo_arrival(self): return np.random.exponential(self.mu) def geometric(self): return np.random.geometric(self.p,1)[0] def manufacturer_date_cal(time_now): """Calculate manufacturing date rounded down to the nearest month.""" return time_now - (time_now % 30) # Global parameters T = 360 #number of days (360 days) l = 6 #deterministic lead time (6 days) e = 90 #shelf life of the drugs (months) (3 months) R = 5000 #number of simulation replication (5000) b = 5 #shortage cost (5 units) z = 1 #waste cost (1 units) h = 0.001 #holding cost (0.001 units) o = 0.5 #ordering cost (0.5 units) dt = 25 #demand on day t (stochastic) (Poisson 25/day) # yt = binary variable for supply disruption status on day t (yt=0 disrupted, yt=1 available) (stochastic) (p=0.01) yt_p = 0.01 # ~ Geometric(p=0.01), sampled from Geometric distribution with probability p = 0.01 yt_r = 1/30 # node recovery time ~ Geometric(p=1/30), sampled from Geometric distribution with probability p = 1/30 = 0.033 price = 7 # unit cost of drug def setup_simulation(env, s, S, ini_level, st, disrupt_time, recovery_time): """Setup environment, supplier, distributor, link, and demand process.""" supplier = scm.Supplier(env=env, ID="S1", name="Supplier 1", node_type="infinite_supplier", node_disrupt_time=disrupt_time.geometric, node_recovery_time=recovery_time.geometric) distributor = scm.InventoryNode(env=env, ID="D1", name="Distributor 1", node_type="distributor", capacity=float('inf'), initial_level=ini_level, inventory_holding_cost=h, inventory_type="perishable", manufacture_date=manufacturer_date_cal, shelf_life=e, replenishment_policy=scm.SSReplenishment, policy_param={'s': s, 'S': S, 'period': 1}, product_buy_price=0, product_sell_price=price) link = scm.Link(env=env, ID="l1", source=supplier, sink=distributor, cost=o, lead_time=lambda: l) demand = scm.Demand(env=env, ID="d1", name="demand 1", order_arrival_model=lambda: 1, consume_available=True, order_quantity_model=st.poisson_demand, demand_node=distributor) return supplier, distributor, demand, link def single_sim_run(S, s, ini_level, logging=True): """Run a single simulation instance and return expected cost.""" env = simpy.Environment() st = Distributions(mu=1, lam=dt) disrupt_time = Distributions(p=yt_p) recovery_time = Distributions(p=yt_r) supplier, distributor, demand, link = setup_simulation(env, s, S, ini_level, st, disrupt_time, recovery_time) pharma_chain = scm.create_sc_net(env=env, nodes=[supplier, distributor], links=[link], demands=[demand]) # warm-up: days 1 to 30 (a run stops just before sim_time, so 31 includes day 30) pharma_chain = scm.simulate_sc_net(pharma_chain,sim_time=31,logging=logging) supplier.stats.reset() distributor.stats.reset() demand.stats.reset() # days 31 to T, as in the paper (T + 1 includes day T) pharma_chain = scm.simulate_sc_net(pharma_chain,sim_time=T + 1,logging=logging) shortage = distributor.stats.shortage[1] waste = distributor.stats.inventory_waste holding = distributor.stats.inventory_carry_cost transport = distributor.stats.transportation_cost total_cost = (shortage * b + waste * z + holding + transport) cost_per_day = total_cost / (T - 30) * price if logging: print("Shortage cost:", shortage * b) print("Waste cost:", waste * z) print("Holding cost:", holding) print("Transportation cost:", transport) return cost_per_day def run_for_s(s_low, s_high, s_step, capacity, ini_level, num_replications): """Run simulations across reorder point values and report results.""" results = [] st = Distributions(mu=1, lam=dt) disrupt_time = Distributions(p=yt_p) recovery_time = Distributions(p=yt_r) #print("reorder_point, exp_cost_per_day, std, std_err") for s in range(s_low, s_high, s_step): costs = [] for _ in range(num_replications): env = simpy.Environment() supplier, distributor, demand, link = setup_simulation(env, s, capacity, ini_level, st, disrupt_time, recovery_time) pharma_chain = scm.create_sc_net(env=env, nodes=[supplier, distributor], links=[link], demands=[demand]) # warm-up: days 1 to 30 (a run stops just before sim_time, so 31 includes day 30) pharma_chain = scm.simulate_sc_net(pharma_chain,sim_time=31,logging=False) supplier.stats.reset() distributor.stats.reset() demand.stats.reset() # days 31 to T, as in the paper (T + 1 includes day T) pharma_chain = scm.simulate_sc_net(pharma_chain,sim_time=T + 1,logging=False) shortage = distributor.stats.shortage[1] waste = distributor.stats.inventory_waste holding = distributor.stats.inventory_carry_cost transport = distributor.stats.transportation_cost total_cost = (shortage * b + waste * z + holding + transport) cost_per_day = total_cost / (T - 30) * price costs.append(cost_per_day) mean_cost = np.mean(costs) std_dev = np.std(costs) std_err = std_dev / np.sqrt(num_replications) #print(f"[{s}, {mean_cost}, {std_dev}, {std_err}]") results.append((s, mean_cost, std_dev, std_err)) return results # Parameters for the simulation s_low = 100 s_high = 5000 s_step = 100 capacity = 5000 ini_level = 5000 num_rep = 1000 Assessing Time Complexity First, let's evaluate the time complexity in relation to the number of simulation runs (replications) (R) in order to estimate the expected costs. The code estimates the execution time for R simulations, where R takes on the values of 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, and 5000. import time stats = [] scm.global_logger.disable_logging() # enable logging for replications in [1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000]: exp_cost_arr = [] start_time = time.time() for rep in range(0, replications): exp_cost_arr.append(single_sim_run(s=2000,S=5000,ini_level=5000,logging=False)) exp_cost_arr = np.array(exp_cost_arr) exe_time = time.time() - start_time print(f"R ={replications}, exe_time:{exe_time} sec, mean:{np.mean(exp_cost_arr)}, std:{np.std(exp_cost_arr)}, std_err:{np.std(exp_cost_arr)/np.sqrt(replications)}") stats.append((replications, exe_time, np.mean(exp_cost_arr), np.std(exp_cost_arr), np.std(exp_cost_arr)/np.sqrt(replications))) R =1000, exe_time:51.769 sec, mean:50.048060053, std:7.4660307713637595, std_err:0.2360966231841331 R =2000, exe_time:101.864 sec, mean:49.9624304385, std:7.811992134196132, std_err:0.1746814545175621 R =3000, exe_time:149.301 sec, mean:50.108267019, std:7.6860393971748335, std_err:0.14032723852353549 R =4000, exe_time:209.294 sec, mean:49.780505389750004, std:7.452137829370824, std_err:0.11782864489157517 R =5000, exe_time:308.672 sec, mean:49.6810310832, std:7.299895652439416, std_err:0.10323611435588215 Estimating Confidence Interval To ensure the estimation error is reasonable, we estimate the expected costs for the replenishment policy setting \(S = 5000\) and variable \(s\) with \(R = 1000\) simulation runs and plot the confidence intervals. exp_cost_per_day = run_for_s(s_low=s_low,s_high=s_high,s_step=s_step,capacity=capacity,ini_level=ini_level,num_replications=num_rep) exp_cost_per_day = np.array(exp_cost_per_day) figure(figsize=(25, 10), dpi=60) plt.plot(exp_cost_per_day[:,0], exp_cost_per_day[:,1],marker='o', linestyle='-', color='b', label='S=5000') plt.fill_between(exp_cost_per_day[:,0], exp_cost_per_day[:,1]-2*exp_cost_per_day[:,3], exp_cost_per_day[:,1]+2*exp_cost_per_day[:,3],alpha=0.2, color='b', label='95% CI') plt.xlabel('Reorder Point (s)', fontsize=20) plt.ylabel('Expected Cost per Day', fontsize=20) plt.xticks(np.arange(s_low, s_high, 200), rotation=90) plt.tick_params(labelsize=18) plt.title('Expected Cost per Day vs Reorder Point (s)', fontsize=22) plt.legend(fontsize=18) plt.grid() plt.show() Running the Model with Varying (S, s) To determine the optimal values of the parameters \(S\) and \(s\) , we run the model with different settings for both parameters. The parameter \(S\) takes on values of 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, and 5000. For each value of \(S\) , the parameter \(s\) is set to values ranging from 100 up to \(S\) . The results obtained from these runs are then plotted and compared with the findings reported by the authors. Below, we present both sets of plots for comparison. exp_cost_per_day = run_for_s(s_low=s_low, s_high=5000, s_step=s_step, capacity=5000, ini_level=5000, num_replications=num_rep) exp_cost_per_day = np.array(exp_cost_per_day) exp_cost_per_day2 = run_for_s(s_low=s_low,s_high=4000,s_step=s_step,capacity=4000,ini_level=4000,num_replications=num_rep) exp_cost_per_day2 = np.array(exp_cost_per_day2) exp_cost_per_day3 = run_for_s(s_low=s_low,s_high=3000,s_step=s_step,capacity=3000,ini_level=3000,num_replications=num_rep) exp_cost_per_day3 = np.array(exp_cost_per_day3) exp_cost_per_day4 = run_for_s(s_low=s_low,s_high=2000,s_step=s_step,capacity=2000,ini_level=2000,num_replications=num_rep) exp_cost_per_day4 = np.array(exp_cost_per_day4) exp_cost_per_day5 = run_for_s(s_low=s_low,s_high=1000,s_step=s_step,capacity=1000,ini_level=1000,num_replications=num_rep) exp_cost_per_day5 = np.array(exp_cost_per_day5) figure(figsize=(25, 10), dpi=60) plt.plot(exp_cost_per_day[:,0], exp_cost_per_day[:,1],marker='o', linestyle='-', color='m', label='S=5000') plt.plot(exp_cost_per_day2[:,0], exp_cost_per_day2[:,1],marker='o', linestyle='-', color='b', label='S=4000') plt.plot(exp_cost_per_day3[:,0], exp_cost_per_day3[:,1],marker='o', linestyle='-', color='g', label='S=3000') plt.plot(exp_cost_per_day4[:,0], exp_cost_per_day4[:,1],marker='o', linestyle='-', color='c', label='S=2000') plt.plot(exp_cost_per_day5[:,0], exp_cost_per_day5[:,1],marker='o', linestyle='-', color='r', label='S=1000') plt.xticks(np.arange(s_low, s_high, 200), rotation=90) plt.tick_params(labelsize=18) plt.xlabel('Reorder Point (s)', fontsize=20) plt.ylabel('Expected Cost per Day', fontsize=20) plt.title('Expected Cost per Day vs Reorder Point (s)', fontsize=22) plt.legend(fontsize=18) plt.grid() plt.show() The following plot displays the results obtained by the authors. docs.title: Pharmacy Supply Chain

docs.text: This study comes from the publication 'Improving Simulation Optimization Run Time When Solving For Periodic Review Inventory Policies in A Pharmacy' , which you can read here . It uses simulation based optimization (SBO) to find the values of the (s, S) policy parameters that keep the total cost of the pharmacy supply chain as low as possible. In this example, we aim to understand the supply chain network described by the authors, implement it with SupplyNetPy, and replicate their results. This shows how much effort it takes to rebuild a specific system with SupplyNetPy, and helps to validate the library.
docs.title: Pharmacy Supply Chain

docs.text: The system is a supply chain with a single level between the source and the customers. A hospital pharmacy (modeled as a distributor) is supplied directly by a pharmaceutical manufacturer (modeled as an infinite supplier). The pharmacy faces random demand, and is supplied by a supplier that never runs out. On any given day, a disruption of the supplier (when it cannot ship) starts with probability 0.01. The pharmacy follows an (s, S) replenishment policy. When its inventory position falls below s , it orders enough to bring the inventory position back up to S . The product is perishable, with a shelf life of 90 days. The authors model and simulate this system to find the values of s and S that minimize the expected total cost per day. The inventory is perishable. The inventory position is what the pharmacy can count on today, the units it holds now plus the units already ordered that have not arrived yet (in transit from the supplier). The next replenishment order is decided from it.   Inventory position = inventory level + inventory in transit The replenishment policy is (s, S). When the inventory position falls below s , the pharmacy orders ( S − inventory position) units, which brings the inventory position back up to S . Review period = 1 day (the pharmacy checks its inventory every day). The flowchart below uses this shorthand.   H = inventory level (the units the pharmacy holds)   H′ = the part of H that will expire at the end of day t   P = inventory position = H + inventory in transit This flowchart shows the order of the events that take place at the pharmacy each day. ( Image source )
docs.title: System Description

docs.text: Begin day t 1. Order arrive at the Pharmacy 2. Update Inventory Levels (H) 3. Satisfy demand based on Inventory Levels 3.1. If (d>H): - demand Satisfied = H - Shortage = d-H - Waste = 0 3.2. Else: - demand Satisfied = d - Shortage = 0 - Waste = max{0,H'-d} 4. Discard Expired Drugs 5. Update Inventory Levels (H) 5.1. Is (s>P) and (Supplier not Disrupted): - Place order for (S-P) 5.2. Else: - Do not place order 6. End of the day t The optimization objective is to minimize the expected cost per day. The costs of interest are the shortage, waste, holding and ordering costs.
docs.title: Daily Process for the Perishable Inventory

docs.text: All drugs that arrive in the same month come from the same production batch, and expire at the end of the same month. So drugs are only thrown away at the end of a month. The inventory level is known each day. The number of days until the inventory expires is known each day. The lead time is fixed and positive. An order placed at the end of day ( t − 1) arrives at the beginning of day t . Demand is random. Supply is uncertain because of disruptions. Demand and disruptions are independent of each other. All demand that is not met is lost. Orders are served with the oldest units first (first in, first out).
docs.title: Assumptions

docs.text: T = number of days (360) Costs are counted from day 31 to day 360, after a warm up of 30 days, as in the paper. A SupplyNetPy run stops just before its end time, so the warm up runs to time 31 and the main run to time T + 1. l = lead time (6 days) e = shelf life of the drugs (3 months, that is 90 days) R = number of simulation runs, or replications (5000) b = shortage cost (5, relative to the buy price) z = waste cost (1, relative to the buy price) h = holding cost (0.001, relative to the buy price) o = ordering cost (0.5, relative to the buy price) d t = demand on day t (random, Poisson with a mean of 25 a day) y t = whether the supply is disrupted on day t (y t = 0 disrupted, y t = 1 available) Time until the next disruption, geometric with p = 0.01 Time to recover from a disruption, geometric with p = 1/30
docs.title: System Configuration

docs.text: import simpy import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from matplotlib.pyplot import figure import SupplyNetPy.Components as scm class Distributions: """ Class to generate random numbers for demand (order quantity) and order arrival arrival times. Parameters: mu (float): Mean of the exponential distribution for order arrival times. lam (float): Lambda parameter of the Poisson distribution for demand (order quantity). """ def __init__(self,mu=1,lam=1,p=0.01): self.mu = mu self.lam = lam self.p = p def poisson_demand(self): return np.random.poisson(self.lam) def expo_arrival(self): return np.random.exponential(self.mu) def geometric(self): return np.random.geometric(self.p,1)[0] def manufacturer_date_cal(time_now): """Calculate manufacturing date rounded down to the nearest month.""" return time_now - (time_now % 30) # Global parameters T = 360 #number of days (360 days) l = 6 #deterministic lead time (6 days) e = 90 #shelf life of the drugs (months) (3 months) R = 5000 #number of simulation replication (5000) b = 5 #shortage cost (5 units) z = 1 #waste cost (1 units) h = 0.001 #holding cost (0.001 units) o = 0.5 #ordering cost (0.5 units) dt = 25 #demand on day t (stochastic) (Poisson 25/day) # yt = binary variable for supply disruption status on day t (yt=0 disrupted, yt=1 available) (stochastic) (p=0.01) yt_p = 0.01 # ~ Geometric(p=0.01), sampled from Geometric distribution with probability p = 0.01 yt_r = 1/30 # node recovery time ~ Geometric(p=1/30), sampled from Geometric distribution with probability p = 1/30 = 0.033 price = 7 # unit cost of drug def setup_simulation(env, s, S, ini_level, st, disrupt_time, recovery_time): """Setup environment, supplier, distributor, link, and demand process.""" supplier = scm.Supplier(env=env, ID="S1", name="Supplier 1", node_type="infinite_supplier", node_disrupt_time=disrupt_time.geometric, node_recovery_time=recovery_time.geometric) distributor = scm.InventoryNode(env=env, ID="D1", name="Distributor 1", node_type="distributor", capacity=float('inf'), initial_level=ini_level, inventory_holding_cost=h, inventory_type="perishable", manufacture_date=manufacturer_date_cal, shelf_life=e, replenishment_policy=scm.SSReplenishment, policy_param={'s': s, 'S': S, 'period': 1}, product_buy_price=0, product_sell_price=price) link = scm.Link(env=env, ID="l1", source=supplier, sink=distributor, cost=o, lead_time=lambda: l) demand = scm.Demand(env=env, ID="d1", name="demand 1", order_arrival_model=lambda: 1, consume_available=True, order_quantity_model=st.poisson_demand, demand_node=distributor) return supplier, distributor, demand, link def single_sim_run(S, s, ini_level, logging=True): """Run a single simulation instance and return expected cost.""" env = simpy.Environment() st = Distributions(mu=1, lam=dt) disrupt_time = Distributions(p=yt_p) recovery_time = Distributions(p=yt_r) supplier, distributor, demand, link = setup_simulation(env, s, S, ini_level, st, disrupt_time, recovery_time) pharma_chain = scm.create_sc_net(env=env, nodes=[supplier, distributor], links=[link], demands=[demand]) # warm-up: days 1 to 30 (a run stops just before sim_time, so 31 includes day 30) pharma_chain = scm.simulate_sc_net(pharma_chain,sim_time=31,logging=logging) supplier.stats.reset() distributor.stats.reset() demand.stats.reset() # days 31 to T, as in the paper (T + 1 includes day T) pharma_chain = scm.simulate_sc_net(pharma_chain,sim_time=T + 1,logging=logging) shortage = distributor.stats.shortage[1] waste = distributor.stats.inventory_waste holding = distributor.stats.inventory_carry_cost transport = distributor.stats.transportation_cost total_cost = (shortage * b + waste * z + holding + transport) cost_per_day = total_cost / (T - 30) * price if logging: print("Shortage cost:", shortage * b) print("Waste cost:", waste * z) print("Holding cost:", holding) print("Transportation cost:", transport) return cost_per_day def run_for_s(s_low, s_high, s_step, capacity, ini_level, num_replications): """Run simulations across reorder point values and report results.""" results = [] st = Distributions(mu=1, lam=dt) disrupt_time = Distributions(p=yt_p) recovery_time = Distributions(p=yt_r) #print("reorder_point, exp_cost_per_day, std, std_err") for s in range(s_low, s_high, s_step): costs = [] for _ in range(num_replications): env = simpy.Environment() supplier, distributor, demand, link = setup_simulation(env, s, capacity, ini_level, st, disrupt_time, recovery_time) pharma_chain = scm.create_sc_net(env=env, nodes=[supplier, distributor], links=[link], demands=[demand]) # warm-up: days 1 to 30 (a run stops just before sim_time, so 31 includes day 30) pharma_chain = scm.simulate_sc_net(pharma_chain,sim_time=31,logging=False) supplier.stats.reset() distributor.stats.reset() demand.stats.reset() # days 31 to T, as in the paper (T + 1 includes day T) pharma_chain = scm.simulate_sc_net(pharma_chain,sim_time=T + 1,logging=False) shortage = distributor.stats.shortage[1] waste = distributor.stats.inventory_waste holding = distributor.stats.inventory_carry_cost transport = distributor.stats.transportation_cost total_cost = (shortage * b + waste * z + holding + transport) cost_per_day = total_cost / (T - 30) * price costs.append(cost_per_day) mean_cost = np.mean(costs) std_dev = np.std(costs) std_err = std_dev / np.sqrt(num_replications) #print(f"[{s}, {mean_cost}, {std_dev}, {std_err}]") results.append((s, mean_cost, std_dev, std_err)) return results # Parameters for the simulation s_low = 100 s_high = 5000 s_step = 100 capacity = 5000 ini_level = 5000 num_rep = 1000
docs.title: Implementation

docs.text: First, let's evaluate the time complexity in relation to the number of simulation runs (replications) (R) in order to estimate the expected costs. The code estimates the execution time for R simulations, where R takes on the values of 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, and 5000. import time stats = [] scm.global_logger.disable_logging() # enable logging for replications in [1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000]: exp_cost_arr = [] start_time = time.time() for rep in range(0, replications): exp_cost_arr.append(single_sim_run(s=2000,S=5000,ini_level=5000,logging=False)) exp_cost_arr = np.array(exp_cost_arr) exe_time = time.time() - start_time print(f"R ={replications}, exe_time:{exe_time} sec, mean:{np.mean(exp_cost_arr)}, std:{np.std(exp_cost_arr)}, std_err:{np.std(exp_cost_arr)/np.sqrt(replications)}") stats.append((replications, exe_time, np.mean(exp_cost_arr), np.std(exp_cost_arr), np.std(exp_cost_arr)/np.sqrt(replications))) R =1000, exe_time:51.769 sec, mean:50.048060053, std:7.4660307713637595, std_err:0.2360966231841331 R =2000, exe_time:101.864 sec, mean:49.9624304385, std:7.811992134196132, std_err:0.1746814545175621 R =3000, exe_time:149.301 sec, mean:50.108267019, std:7.6860393971748335, std_err:0.14032723852353549 R =4000, exe_time:209.294 sec, mean:49.780505389750004, std:7.452137829370824, std_err:0.11782864489157517 R =5000, exe_time:308.672 sec, mean:49.6810310832, std:7.299895652439416, std_err:0.10323611435588215

docs.text: To ensure the estimation error is reasonable, we estimate the expected costs for the replenishment policy setting \(S = 5000\) and variable \(s\) with \(R = 1000\) simulation runs and plot the confidence intervals. exp_cost_per_day = run_for_s(s_low=s_low,s_high=s_high,s_step=s_step,capacity=capacity,ini_level=ini_level,num_replications=num_rep) exp_cost_per_day = np.array(exp_cost_per_day) figure(figsize=(25, 10), dpi=60) plt.plot(exp_cost_per_day[:,0], exp_cost_per_day[:,1],marker='o', linestyle='-', color='b', label='S=5000') plt.fill_between(exp_cost_per_day[:,0], exp_cost_per_day[:,1]-2*exp_cost_per_day[:,3], exp_cost_per_day[:,1]+2*exp_cost_per_day[:,3],alpha=0.2, color='b', label='95% CI') plt.xlabel('Reorder Point (s)', fontsize=20) plt.ylabel('Expected Cost per Day', fontsize=20) plt.xticks(np.arange(s_low, s_high, 200), rotation=90) plt.tick_params(labelsize=18) plt.title('Expected Cost per Day vs Reorder Point (s)', fontsize=22) plt.legend(fontsize=18) plt.grid() plt.show()

The results obtained from these runs are then plotted and compared with the findings reported by the authors. Below, we present both sets of plots for comparison. exp_cost_per_day = run_for_s(s_low=s_low, s_high=5000, s_step=s_step, capacity=5000, ini_level=5000, num_replications=num_rep) exp_cost_per_day = np.array(exp_cost_per_day) exp_cost_per_day2 = run_for_s(s_low=s_low,s_high=4000,s_step=s_step,capacity=4000,ini_level=4000,num_replications=num_rep) exp_cost_per_day2 = np.array(exp_cost_per_day2) exp_cost_per_day3 = run_for_s(s_low=s_low,s_high=3000,s_step=s_step,capacity=3000,ini_level=3000,num_replications=num_rep) exp_cost_per_day3 = np.array(exp_cost_per_day3) exp_cost_per_day4 = run_for_s(s_low=s_low,s_high=2000,s_step=s_step,capacity=2000,ini_level=2000,num_replications=num_rep) exp_cost_per_day4 = np.array(exp_cost_per_day4) exp_cost_per_day5 = run_for_s(s_low=s_low,s_high=1000,s_step=s_step,capacity=1000,ini_level=1000,num_replications=num_rep) exp_cost_per_day5 = np.array(exp_cost_per_day5) figure(figsize=(25, 10), dpi=60) plt.plot(exp_cost_per_day[:,0], exp_cost_per_day[:,1],marker='o', linestyle='-', color='m', label='S=5000') plt.plot(exp_cost_per_day2[:,0], exp_cost_per_day2[:,1],marker='o', linestyle='-', color='b', label='S=4000') plt.plot(exp_cost_per_day3[:,0], exp_cost_per_day3[:,1],marker='o', linestyle='-', color='g', label='S=3000') plt.plot(exp_cost_per_day4[:,0], exp_cost_per_day4[:,1],marker='o', linestyle='-', color='c', label='S=2000') plt.plot(exp_cost_per_day5[:,0], exp_cost_per_day5[:,1],marker='o', linestyle='-', color='r', label='S=1000') plt.xticks(np.arange(s_low, s_high, 200), rotation=90) plt.tick_params(labelsize=18) plt.xlabel('Reorder Point (s)', fontsize=20) plt.ylabel('Expected Cost per Day', fontsize=20) plt.title('Expected Cost per Day vs Reorder Point (s)', fontsize=22) plt.legend(fontsize=18) plt.grid() plt.show() The following plot displays the results obtained by the authors. docs.text: /* Release history only: undo the grey h3 banner from css/extra.css */ h3 { padding: 0; margin: 1em 0 0.4em; border: none; border-radius: 0; background: none; } Release history Changes to SupplyNetPy, newest first. The library was first published on PyPI on 2025-08-21 (version 0.1.0). Each entry is tagged: [NEW] a new feature, [FIX] a bug fix, [CHANGE] a change in behavior, [BREAKING] a change that may need action from you, and [DOCS] documentation only. 0.5.1 (2026-10-27) Simulation results are the same as in 0.5.0, except for models in which a disruption destroys units at a site whose replenishment policy has no period . This release makes such a site order again when it recovers. [FIX] A site whose units were destroyed by a disruption ( disruption_impact ) now orders again when it recovers. Before, its replenishment policy was not woken, so a site with no units left waited until a buyer ordered from it or a customer waited for units. A site whose buyers had moved to other suppliers could stay empty for the rest of the run. A site now checks its inventory position whenever it recovers. Results change only for models where a disruption destroys units and the replenishment policy has no period . [DOCS] The Disruptions and Replenishment Policies guides say that a site checks its inventory position when it recovers, and why destroying units does not wake its replenishment policy. The Disruptions guide also lists the two cases in which a disrupted site can still order. 0.5.0 (2026-10-17) Simulation results are the same as in 0.4.0. This release adds probability-based supplier selection, and supplier-selection policies can now take settings. [NEW] SelectProbabilistic , a supplier-selection policy that chooses the supplier of each replenishment order at random, with a probability for each supplier. The probabilities are given in the new site setting supplier_selection_param , keyed by supplier ID, and must sum to 1. When a supplier is disrupted, the others share its orders in their ratios ( on_disruption="rescale" , the default), or the order is blocked ( "block" ). The policy draws one random number per order from its own random number generator ( seed or rng ), so its choices change no other random numbers. create_sc_net checks that every link to the site has a probability. See the Supplier Selection guide. [CHANGE] A site gives its supplier-selection policy a mode only when supplier_selection_mode is given, so each policy keeps its own default: "fixed" for the four existing policies, as before, and "dynamic" for SelectProbabilistic . Results are the same as in 0.4.0. [BREAKING] A custom supplier-selection policy whose own __init__ takes mode without a default value now fails when the site is given no mode. Give mode a default, such as mode="fixed" . Policies that do not override __init__ are not affected. [CHANGE] A built in supplier-selection policy given settings it does not use in supplier_selection_param warns about them, as replenishment policies do for policy_param . A manufacturer given a supplier-selection policy, a mode or settings warns that they are not used, since it does not use its policy yet. [CHANGE] get_sc_net_info shows the settings of each site's replenishment policy and supplier-selection policy, not only their names, for example (s: 100, S: 150, first_review_delay: 0, period: 0) or the probabilities of SelectProbabilistic . A distributor or retailer now reports its replenishment policy in get_info() , as a manufacturer already did. [DOCS] The Supplier Selection guide has two new sections. One shows how to choose suppliers at random with SelectProbabilistic , and the other how to give settings to a supplier-selection policy you write yourself ( self.params , _param_keys and check_links ). New glossary entries for probability-based supplier selection and selection probability. The Known Issues page says that a manufacturer does not use its supplier-selection policy yet. [DOCS] Level 3 headings in the guides and other pages are shown as plain headings. The grey box is kept for the classes and functions of the API reference. [DOCS] The source code shown in the API reference keeps its line breaks and indentation again. 0.4.0 (2026-10-16) Simulation results are the same as in 0.3.0. This release adds statistics for each link, and a User Guide with seven guides to common tasks. [NEW] Every link now keeps statistics, in link.stats . They count the replenishment orders the buyer placed over the link, what arrived, the shortage and backorders at the supplier, how long orders waited at the supplier, the lead time, the costs, and the disruptions of the link. From these they work out the average waiting time, lead time and order cycle time, the fill rate (the share of units the supplier sent without the order having to wait), the availability of the link, and two spreads of order sizes, one per order and one per time unit, for studying the bullwhip effect. Read them with link.stats.get_statistics() . [NEW] get_link_wise_performance , format_link_wise_performance and print_link_wise_performance give the statistics of several links as data, as text or printed, like the node versions. Pass node.suppliers to see what a site ordered and from whom, or node.buyers to see who ordered from it. [NEW] reset_stats(supplychainnet) and Network.reset_stats() start the statistics of every node, customer demand and link again in one call, for a warm-up. [FIX] A raw-material supplier given a perishable inventory ( inventory_type="perishable" ) now raises a clear error when it is created. SupplyNetPy does not model perishable raw materials yet. Before, the setting was accepted, and the run failed at the first mining with a message about a missing manufacturing date. [CHANGE] SelectAvailable , SelectCheapest and SelectFastest (and the base class SupplierSelectionPolicy ) now default to fixed mode, as SelectFirst and every site already did. A site always passes its own supplier_selection_mode , so networks give the same results as before. Only a policy created directly, without a mode, behaves differently. [DOCS] A new User Guide with seven guides, on customer demand, replenishment policies, supplier selection, disruptions, perishable products, statistics and results (including link statistics and warm-ups), and running experiments. The longer sections of the API introduction moved into them, and the introduction is now a short overview of the modules. [DOCS] New glossary entries for order cycle time, fill rate, bullwhip effect, standard deviation, fixed and dynamic mode, and, in a new Experiments section, replication, seed, confidence interval and common random numbers. Also a new example, examples/py/link_statistics.py . [DOCS] The About page describes the newer features (customer demand options, supplier selection modes, perishable products, link statistics and reproducible experiments), links to the guides, and mentions the validation against anyLogistix. The home page lists the case studies, the User Guide, the known issues and the release history. [DOCS] The planned work on the known issues page is split into next updates (probability-based supplier selection, orders in smaller parts, checking the whole network, and the new entry for perishable raw materials) and long-term goals. 0.3.0 (2026-10-16) This release adds new node statistics, fixes how statistics are reset for a warm-up, and adds warnings for two mistakes in how a network is built. Results stay the same for networks that are not reset during a run and have no disrupted site with customers, such as the quickstart example. The three fixes below say which results change. [FIX] Customers can no longer order from a disrupted site. Before, they were served from its inventory as usual, although a disrupted site takes no new replenishment orders. A customer who arrives while the site is disrupted now goes away, and the order is recorded in the new statistic disruption_lost_sales . It is kept apart from shortage , because a shortage is units the site did not have, and a disruption lost sale is an order the site could not take. Customers already waiting when the disruption starts are still served. Results change for networks in which a site with customers can be disrupted. [FIX] stats.reset() , used for a warm-up, now starts the counting again without changing the present. Before, it also set backorder and inventory_level to zero. A site with orders waiting at the reset then ordered too little, and its backorders went below zero once those orders were served. The holding cost is now brought up to date before the reset, so afterwards it covers only the time since the reset, also when the run was advanced with env.run() . The record of inventory levels ( inventory.instantaneous_levels ) also starts again. Results after a warm-up change when orders are waiting at the reset, or when the run was advanced with env.run() . [FIX] A manufacturer's raw-material order now counts in its demand_placed and transportation_cost when it is placed, as for every other site. Before, it counted only once the supplier served it. Totals at the end of a run change only for raw-material orders still waiting then. [NEW] Statistics about disruptions. disruptions and disrupted_time (including a disruption still going on when read), availability (the share of time the node was not disrupted), and blocked (replenishment orders a site could not place because every supplier it has, or the link to it, was disrupted). [NEW] Statistics about inventory over time. avg_inventory_level and inventory_level_time (inventory level times time), worked out exactly and apart from the holding cost, and zero_inventory_time and zero_inventory_share (how long the inventory level was zero). [NEW] Statistics about orders that end badly or wait. lost_sales (the customer units a site never delivered), dropped_qty (delivered units that did not fit in the inventory), and waited , waiting_time and avg_waiting_time , for customers and for orders from other sites. [NEW] Each node's statistics keep a clock. start_time is when counting began, and elapsed_time is the time since then. A reset moves start_time , so averages after a warm-up cover only the measured period. Averages are worked out when they are read and are None when there is nothing to divide by. [NEW] simulate_sc_net and Network.results add up lost_sales and disruption_lost_sales for the whole network. [NEW] Node.has_suppliers() tells whether a site has any supplier at all. For a manufacturer it checks that every raw material has one. [CHANGE] get_statistics() and the performance tables show the new statistics, so they have more rows. [CHANGE] Two new warnings for mistakes in how a network is built. A site with no supplier at all that tries to order is warned about once, and is not counted as blocked . To include them, run to a slightly later time, such as sim_time + 1 . 0.2.1 (2026-10-12) Results change for networks with disruptions. Networks without disruptions, such as the quickstart example, give the same results as before. [FIX] A site whose replenishment order was blocked by a disruption now orders as soon as its supplier, or the link to it, recovers. Before, a replenishment policy without a review period could stop ordering for good. If the site had no units left, nothing woke the policy again, even after the supplier recovered. [FIX] Supplier-selection policies now skip a supplier whose site is disrupted, not only one whose link is disrupted. Before, a site with two suppliers could send its order to the disrupted one and lose it, while the other supplier was working. [CHANGE] place_order now checks that some supplier can take the order before choosing one. If none can, no order is placed. New methods Link.can_take_order , Node.can_place_order , Node.wake_replenishment and Node.add_buyer_link , and a new list Node.buyers of the links to a node's buyers. [FIX] The performance table ( get_node_wise_performance , format_node_wise_performance , print_node_wise_performance ) now shows every metric that any node has. Before, it showed only the metrics of the first node in the list, so a raw-material supplier's mining figures were left out when another node came first. Two nodes with the same name now each get a column; the second is told apart by its ID. [FIX] disable_logging and set_log_file now close the log file they stop writing to. Before, the file stayed open until the program ended, which caused a ResourceWarning and, on Windows, kept the file locked. 0.2.0 (2026-10-11) Most of these fixes come from issue #1 , reported by @ashwingaikwadiby . Results change for networks with manufacturers, raw-material suppliers with finite inventory, perishable goods, customers who wait, or replenishment orders that have to wait at a supplier. Simple networks, such as the quickstart example, give the same results as before. [FIX] A replenishment order that has to wait at its supplier is now a backorder there only while it waits, and is no longer counted twice in the supplier's inventory position. Before, the supplier ordered too much, kept the extra units for the rest of the run, and its backorders were never cleared. [FIX] A manufacturer now keeps making production batches until every planned unit is made, orders raw material for every planned unit, and carries on when units leave its full inventory. Before, it could stop producing for good, with raw material left unused or with orders waiting forever. [FIX] A raw-material supplier with finite inventory starts mining again as soon as its inventory drops. Before, once its inventory had been full it never mined again, and manufacturers buying from it waited forever. [FIX] Perishable goods. An order now gets the batches that are really in inventory when it is filled, oldest first. Expired units are thrown away at once and are no longer shipped to an order that was waiting, and destroyed units are removed at once too. Before, an order that had to wait could lose units, and expired units could be shipped. [FIX] Customers who wait ( tolerance above 0) now leave as soon as their tolerance runs out, and their backorders are cleared when they leave. All waiting customers are woken when units arrive, two waiting customers can no longer take the same units, and a partial delivery of 0 units no longer crashes. [FIX] A waiting customer's shortage is recorded once, when the order arrives. Before, it was recorded again at every check, so shortage figures were too high. [FIX] A supplier whose site is disrupted is no longer counted as short for orders it never receives. [FIX] Inventory.destroy() now wakes a raw-material supplier (to mine again) and a manufacturer (to make more). It still does not wake a replenishment policy. [NEW] Inventory.get() takes a site_order argument, and Inventory.waiting_orders() and Inventory.waiting_site_orders() report the units asked for by orders still waiting at an inventory. [DOCS] The (R, Q) policy ( RQReplenishment ) never used safety_stock , so passing it had no effect. The documentation no longer says that it does. [DOCS] A new Glossary page defines one word for each idea, and the documentation, docstrings and code comments now use those words. The API reference now lists every result of simulate_sc_net , and no longer shows raw markup from the docstrings. [DOCS] Several documentation pages described their examples wrongly, and are corrected. The complex network example now has the links shown in its picture, lead times that differ as intended, and a fixed seed. 0.1.12 (2026-05-31) [FIX] Replenishment orders that were bigger than the free space on the shelf no longer throw away the extra units. Previously, a node with waiting customers could order enough to refill the shelf and also cover them, and any units that did not fit were silently lost even though they had been paid for. In some cases this also pushed the node's inventory position below zero. [CHANGE] When arriving units are dropped because the shelf is full, a warning is now logged suggesting that the node's capacity may be too small. [CHANGE] A customer order that is bigger than the node's whole shelf, with no partial delivery accepted, is now recorded as lost demand right away. Before, it triggered a replenishment order that could never be served. [DOCS] Code comments and docstrings were rewritten in plainer language. 0.1.11 (2026-05-09) [FIX] Random node and link disruptions set with failure_p no longer happen almost immediately at time 0. The failure chance is now applied once per time unit, as documented. 0.1.10 (2026-05-06) [NEW] Inventory.destroy() removes stock (all of it, a fraction, or a custom amount) when a node is disrupted. Nodes accept a matching disruption_impact option. Destroyed units and their value appear in the node's statistics and count towards its cost. [FIX] Expiry of perishable stock ( Inventory.remove_expired ) now works correctly. [DOCS] Documentation wording was simplified throughout. 0.1.9 (2026-04-28) [NEW] Network wrapper around the supply-chain dictionary, with named access to nodes and results. The dictionary-based way of working still works. [NEW] NodeType , a list of the valid node types. Node types can be given either as text ( "retailer" ) or as a NodeType member. [NEW] log_window=(start, stop) option on simulate_sc_net to log only part of a run. [BREAKING] Python 3.9 or newer is now required. networkx and matplotlib are now declared as dependencies. [CHANGE] Logging is now opt-in. Creating nodes no longer opens (or overwrites) the trace file. simulate_sc_net(logging=True) turns it on for you. [CHANGE] The shortage statistic is now called shortage . The old name, orders_shortage , still works as an alias. [CHANGE] Expiry of perishable stock is now driven by the batches' expiry times instead of repeated checks, which makes large simulations faster. [CHANGE] The remaining items from the code review (see REVIEW.md ) were resolved, and the test suite was expanded. 0.1.8 (2026-04-24) [NEW] set_seed() makes random disruptions repeatable. [BREAKING] SupplyNetPy.Components now exposes a fixed, documented list of names. Modules that used to be reachable by accident (such as scm.simpy ) are no longer available through it. [FIX] A full code review fixed a set of correctness problems, including: Expired perishable stock was not always removed correctly, so holding cost could keep being charged on stock that no longer existed. A manufacturer could place duplicate orders for the same raw materials. A customer's "demand fulfilled" figure was inflated when an order arrived in several partial shipments. Cost totals could pick up unrelated values whose names happened to contain the word "cost". Disrupted links were still used for new shipments, and supplier-selection policies did not take link status into account. Adding stock to a full shelf could leave the inventory records out of step. [CHANGE] Misspelled node parameters (for example shelf_live ) are now reported as an error instead of being silently ignored. [CHANGE] A much larger test suite was added. 0.1.7 (2026-03-13) [NEW] record_inv_levels option on Inventory to switch recording of inventory levels over time on or off (off by default). [FIX] Adding stock to an inventory that is already full is now handled safely. 0.1.6 (2025-11-19) [FIX] When adding stock would go over capacity, only the amount that fits is now added, instead of failing. 0.1.5 (2025-11-08) [NEW] name is now included in node statistics. [CHANGE] The minimum required Python version was relaxed. 0.1.2 to 0.1.4 (2025-09-15) [FIX] The wheel build target was added so the package builds correctly. [CHANGE] Package metadata (classifiers and author details) was corrected. 0.1.1 (2025-09-02) [CHANGE] Parameters that expect a "callable" (lead times, arrival intervals, and so on) now also accept a plain number such as 2 or 1.5 . 0.1.0 (2025-08-21) First public release on PyPI. It included: Supply-chain building blocks: suppliers, manufacturers, inventory nodes (distributors and retailers), demand nodes, and links. Replenishment policies: (s, S), (R, Q), and periodic review (with or without safety stock). Supplier-selection policies: first, available, cheapest, and fastest. Perishable inventory, disruptions of nodes and links, and backorders with partial fulfilment. Node-level and network-level results (cost, revenue, profit, shortage), plus create_sc_net and simulate_sc_net . A documentation site, worked examples, and a unit-test suite. Before the first release Development began in May 2024; the repository was moved from its earlier home in July 2024. Internal versions 0.0.11 to 0.0.69 were used during development and were never published on PyPI.
docs.title: Release History

docs.text: Changes to SupplyNetPy, newest first. The library was first published on PyPI on 2025-08-21 (version 0.1.0). Each entry is tagged: [NEW] a new feature, [FIX] a bug fix, [CHANGE] a change in behavior, [BREAKING] a change that may need action from you, and [DOCS] documentation only.
docs.title: Release history

docs.text: Simulation results are the same as in 0.5.0, except for models in which a disruption destroys units at a site whose replenishment policy has no period . This release makes such a site order again when it recovers. [FIX] A site whose units were destroyed by a disruption ( disruption_impact ) now orders again when it recovers. Before, its replenishment policy was not woken, so a site with no units left waited until a buyer ordered from it or a customer waited for units. A site whose buyers had moved to other suppliers could stay empty for the rest of the run. A site now checks its inventory position whenever it recovers. Results change only for models where a disruption destroys units and the replenishment policy has no period . [DOCS] The Disruptions and Replenishment Policies guides say that a site checks its inventory position when it recovers, and why destroying units does not wake its replenishment policy. The Disruptions guide also lists the two cases in which a disrupted site can still order.

Simulation results are the same as in 0.4.0. This release adds probability-based supplier selection, and supplier-selection policies can now take settings. [NEW] SelectProbabilistic , a supplier-selection policy that chooses the supplier of each replenishment order at random, with a probability for each supplier. The probabilities are given in the new site setting supplier_selection_param , keyed by supplier ID, and must sum to 1. When a supplier is disrupted, the others share its orders in their ratios ( on_disruption="rescale" , the default), or the order is blocked ( "block" ). The policy draws one random number per order from its own random number generator ( seed or rng ), so its choices change no other random numbers. create_sc_net checks that every link to the site has a probability. See the Supplier Selection guide. [CHANGE] A site gives its supplier-selection policy a mode only when supplier_selection_mode is given, so each policy keeps its own default: "fixed" for the four existing policies, as before, and "dynamic" for SelectProbabilistic . Results are the same as in 0.4.0. [BREAKING] A custom supplier-selection policy whose own __init__ takes mode without a default value now fails when the site is given no mode. Give mode a default, such as mode="fixed" . Policies that do not override __init__ are not affected. [CHANGE] A built in supplier-selection policy given settings it does not use in supplier_selection_param warns about them, as replenishment policies do for policy_param . A manufacturer given a supplier-selection policy, a mode or settings warns that they are not used, since it does not use its policy yet. [CHANGE] get_sc_net_info shows the settings of each site's replenishment policy and supplier-selection policy, not only their names, for example (s: 100, S: 150, first_review_delay: 0, period: 0) or the probabilities of SelectProbabilistic . A distributor or retailer now reports its replenishment policy in get_info() , as a manufacturer already did. [DOCS] The Supplier Selection guide has two new sections. One shows how to choose suppliers at random with SelectProbabilistic , and the other how to give settings to a supplier-selection policy you write yourself ( self.params , _param_keys and check_links ). New glossary entries for probability-based supplier selection and selection probability. The Known Issues page says that a manufacturer does not use its supplier-selection policy yet. [DOCS] Level 3 headings in the guides and other pages are shown as plain headings. The grey box is kept for the classes and functions of the API reference. [DOCS] The source code shown in the API reference keeps its line breaks and indentation again.

Simulation results are the same as in 0.3.0. This release adds statistics for each link, and a User Guide with seven guides to common tasks. [NEW] Every link now keeps statistics, in link.stats . They count the replenishment orders the buyer placed over the link, what arrived, the shortage and backorders at the supplier, how long orders waited at the supplier, the lead time, the costs, and the disruptions of the link. From these they work out the average waiting time, lead time and order cycle time, the fill rate (the share of units the supplier sent without the order having to wait), the availability of the link, and two spreads of order sizes, one per order and one per time unit, for studying the bullwhip effect. Read them with link.stats.get_statistics() . [NEW] get_link_wise_performance , format_link_wise_performance and print_link_wise_performance give the statistics of several links as data, as text or printed, like the node versions. Pass node.suppliers to see what a site ordered and from whom, or node.buyers to see who ordered from it. [NEW] reset_stats(supplychainnet) and Network.reset_stats() start the statistics of every node, customer demand and link again in one call, for a warm-up. [FIX] A raw-material supplier given a perishable inventory ( inventory_type="perishable" ) now raises a clear error when it is created. SupplyNetPy does not model perishable raw materials yet. Before, the setting was accepted, and the run failed at the first mining with a message about a missing manufacturing date. [CHANGE] SelectAvailable , SelectCheapest and SelectFastest (and the base class SupplierSelectionPolicy ) now default to fixed mode, as SelectFirst and every site already did. A site always passes its own supplier_selection_mode , so networks give the same results as before. Only a policy created directly, without a mode, behaves differently. [DOCS] A new User Guide with seven guides, on customer demand, replenishment policies, supplier selection, disruptions, perishable products, statistics and results (including link statistics and warm-ups), and running experiments. The longer sections of the API introduction moved into them, and the introduction is now a short overview of the modules. [DOCS] New glossary entries for order cycle time, fill rate, bullwhip effect, standard deviation, fixed and dynamic mode, and, in a new Experiments section, replication, seed, confidence interval and common random numbers. Also a new example, examples/py/link_statistics.py . [DOCS] The About page describes the newer features (customer demand options, supplier selection modes, perishable products, link statistics and reproducible experiments), links to the guides, and mentions the validation against anyLogistix. The home page lists the case studies, the User Guide, the known issues and the release history. [DOCS] The planned work on the known issues page is split into next updates (probability-based supplier selection, orders in smaller parts, checking the whole network, and the new entry for perishable raw materials) and long-term goals.

docs.title: 0.1.2 to 0.1.4 (2025-09-15)

docs.text: [CHANGE] Parameters that expect a "callable" (lead times, arrival intervals, and so on) now also accept a plain number such as 2 or 1.5 .

First public release on PyPI. It included: Supply-chain building blocks: suppliers, manufacturers, inventory nodes (distributors and retailers), demand nodes, and links. Replenishment policies: (s, S), (R, Q), and periodic review (with or without safety stock). Supplier-selection policies: first, available, cheapest, and fastest. Perishable inventory, disruptions of nodes and links, and backorders with partial fulfilment. Node-level and network-level results (cost, revenue, profit, shortage), plus create_sc_net and simulate_sc_net . A documentation site, worked examples, and a unit-test suite.
Development began in May 2024; the repository was moved from its earlier home in July 2024. Internal versions 0.0.11 to 0.0.69 were used during development and were never published on PyPI.
