Complex Supply Chain Network This example shows how to build and simulate a larger supply chain in SupplyNetPy , with several levels and with retailers that can order from more than one distributor, using a mix of replenishment policies. Three raw-material suppliers (a flour mill, a yeast factory and a sugar factory) supply a manufacturer (a bakery), the bakery supplies two distributors, and the distributors supply five retailers (cake shops). In the picture, cake shops 2 and 4 can order from either distributor. Goals Create a network with several raw materials, three raw-material suppliers, a manufacturer, two distributors and five retailers. Mix replenishment policies ((s, S), (R, Q) and periodic). Let some retailers order from either of two distributors. Key Concepts Used Products and raw materials. The class Product creates the product, bread. RawMaterial creates the raw materials (flour, sugar and yeast). Nodes. The classes Supplier , Manufacturer and InventoryNode create the raw-material suppliers (infinite suppliers here), the bakery (a manufacturer), the distributors and the retailers (cake shops). Links. The class Link connects the sites. Replenishment policies. SSReplenishment . When the inventory position falls to s or below, order enough to bring it back up to S . RQReplenishment . When the inventory position falls to the reorder point R or below, order a fixed Q units. PeriodicReplenishment . Every T time units, order Q units. Supplier selection. Each cake shop chooses between its suppliers with SelectFirst or SelectAvailable . Perishable goods. Every site that holds bread has inventory_type set to perishable , with a shelf_life of 5 time units. Full Example This script builds the network with two distributors and five retailers, then simulates it for 365 time units. import SupplyNetPy.Components as scm import simpy import numpy as np # Same random numbers on every run np.random.seed(42) class Distributions: def __init__(self, lam=5, mu=5, low=1, high=10): self.lam = lam self.mu = mu self.low = low self.high = high def poisson_arrival(self): return np.random.exponential(scale=1/self.lam) def uniform_quantity(self): return int(np.random.uniform(low=self.low, high=self.high)) env = simpy.Environment() # ------------------- Raw Materials ------------------- flour = scm.RawMaterial(ID='flourk11', name='Flour', extraction_quantity=50, extraction_time=1, mining_cost=10, cost=2.5) sugar = scm.RawMaterial(ID='sugark21', name='Sugar', extraction_quantity=30, extraction_time=1, mining_cost=8, cost=1.4) yeast = scm.RawMaterial(ID='yeast31', name='Yeast', extraction_quantity=20, extraction_time=1, mining_cost=3, cost=0.2) # ------------------- Suppliers ------------------- flour_mill = scm.Supplier(env=env, ID='fmill', name='Flour Mill', node_type='infinite_supplier', raw_material=flour, logging=False) sugar_factory = scm.Supplier(env=env, ID='sfact', name='Sugar Factory', node_type='infinite_supplier', raw_material=sugar, logging=False) yeast_factory = scm.Supplier(env=env, ID='yfact', name='Yeast Factory', node_type='infinite_supplier', raw_material=yeast, logging=False) # ------------------- Manufacturer ------------------- bread = scm.Product(ID='soft_regular11', name='Bread', manufacturing_cost=10, manufacturing_time=1, sell_price=40, raw_materials=[(flour, 30), (sugar, 15), (yeast, 15)], batch_size=300) bakery = scm.Manufacturer(env=env, ID='bakery', name='Bakery', product=bread, shelf_life=5, inventory_type='perishable', capacity=500, initial_level=100, inventory_holding_cost=0.5, replenishment_policy=scm.SSReplenishment, policy_param={'s':300,'S':400}, product_sell_price=35, logging=False) # ------------------- Distributors ------------------- distributor1 = scm.InventoryNode(env=env, ID='dist1', name='Distributor 1', node_type='distributor', product=bread, inventory_type='perishable', shelf_life=5, capacity=float('inf'), initial_level=50, inventory_holding_cost=0.2, replenishment_policy=scm.RQReplenishment, policy_param={'R':150,'Q':50}, product_buy_price=0, product_sell_price=36, logging=False) distributor2 = scm.InventoryNode(env=env, ID='dist2', name='Distributor 2', node_type='distributor', product=bread, inventory_type='perishable', shelf_life=5, capacity=float('inf'), initial_level=40, inventory_holding_cost=0.25, replenishment_policy=scm.SSReplenishment, policy_param={'s':150,'S':200}, product_buy_price=0, product_sell_price=37, logging=False) # ------------------- Retailers ------------------- cake_shops = [] capacities = [40,60,80,60,100] ini_levels = [30,20,30,20,50] policies = [scm.RQReplenishment, scm.PeriodicReplenishment, scm.SSReplenishment, scm.RQReplenishment, scm.PeriodicReplenishment] policy_params = [{'R':20,'Q':40}, {'T':3,'Q':50}, {'s':20,'S':50}, {'R':20,'Q':40}, {'T':3,'Q':100}] supplier_selection = [scm.SelectFirst,scm.SelectAvailable,scm.SelectFirst,scm.SelectAvailable,scm.SelectFirst] for i in range(0,5): shop = scm.InventoryNode(env=env, ID=f'cake_shop{i+1}', name=f'Cake Shop {i+1}', node_type='retailer', product=bread, inventory_type='perishable', shelf_life=5, capacity=capacities[i], initial_level=ini_levels[i], inventory_holding_cost=0.1, replenishment_policy=policies[i], policy_param=policy_params[i], supplier_selection_policy=supplier_selection[i], product_buy_price=25, product_sell_price=40, logging=False) cake_shops.append(shop) # ------------------- Links ------------------- links = [] # Raw material links, suppliers to bakery suppliers = [flour_mill, sugar_factory, yeast_factory] costs = [5, 6, 5] for i in range(3): links.append(scm.Link(env=env, ID=f'l{i+1}', source=suppliers[i], sink=bakery, cost=costs[i], lead_time=lambda: 0.3)) # Bakery → Distributors links.append(scm.Link(env=env, ID='l4', source=bakery, sink=distributor1, cost=6, lead_time=lambda: 1)) links.append(scm.Link(env=env, ID='l5', source=bakery, sink=distributor2, cost=7, lead_time=lambda: 1.2)) # Distributor 1 → Shops 1, 2, 3 for i in range(0,3): link = scm.Link(env=env, ID=f'l{i+6}', source=distributor1, sink=cake_shops[i], cost=4, lead_time=lambda i=i: 0.4 + i*0.1) links.append(link) # Distributor 2 → Shops 4, 5 for i in range(3,5): link = scm.Link(env=env, ID=f'l{i+6}', source=distributor2, sink=cake_shops[i], cost=5, lead_time=lambda: 0.5) links.append(link) # Distributor 1 → Shop 4, Distributor 2 → Shop 2 links.append(scm.Link(env=env, ID='l11', source=distributor1, sink=cake_shops[3], cost=8, lead_time=lambda: 0.5)) links.append(scm.Link(env=env, ID='l12', source=distributor2, sink=cake_shops[1], cost=6, lead_time=lambda: 0.8)) # ------------------- Demands ------------------- arrival = Distributions(lam=5) quantity = Distributions(low=1, high=5) demands = [] for i in range(5): demands.append(scm.Demand(env=env, ID=f'd{i+1}', name=f'Demand Shop {i+1}', order_arrival_model=arrival.poisson_arrival, order_quantity_model=quantity.uniform_quantity, demand_node=cake_shops[i], logging=False)) # ------------------- Network ------------------- bread_chain = scm.create_sc_net( env=env, nodes=[flour_mill, sugar_factory, yeast_factory, bakery, distributor1, distributor2, *cake_shops], links=links, demands=demands ) scm.simulate_sc_net(bread_chain, sim_time=365, logging=True) print("---- Node-wise performance ----
---- ---- Suppliers and Bakery---- ----") scm.print_node_wise_performance([flour_mill, sugar_factory, yeast_factory, bakery]) print("
---- ---- Distributors ---- ----") scm.print_node_wise_performance([distributor1, distributor2]) print("
---- ---- Retail Shops ---- ----") scm.print_node_wise_performance(cake_shops) Sample Output INFO sim_trace - Supply chain info: INFO sim_trace - available_inv : 505 INFO sim_trace - avg_available_inv docs.text: img{ width:70%; } News Vendor Problem Imagine a newspaper vendor who buys copies wholesale every morning and sells them through the day. Demand is uncertain, as some days are busy and some quiet. If the vendor buys too few copies, they miss out on sales (and on the profit those sales would have brought in). If they buy too many, the leftover papers are wasted at the end of the day, since yesterday's news doesn't sell tomorrow. How many copies should the vendor buy? That is the newsvendor problem , finding the order quantity that, on average, gives the highest profit when you weigh the cost of running out against the cost of leftovers. The same balance shows up for any perishable product with unpredictable demand, such as fresh produce, baked goods, daily prepared meals, magazines and flowers. Problem Definition The newsvendor orders Q units every day. Each unit costs c, and the sell price is p. The newsvendor faces normally distributed demand with mean μ and standard deviation σ. If, on a certain day, the actual demand is k, then the net profit after selling k units is Profit = Revenue − Order Cost = k × p − Q × c However, any units left unsold at the end of the day are wasted, since they cannot be sold the next day. The newsvendor can sell these unsold units back to the supplier at a lower price, called the salvage value s. If the actual demand that day is less than the order size Q, then the net profit is Profit = Revenue + Salvage − Order Cost = k × p + ( Q − k ) × s − Q × c When the actual demand k is more than the newsvendor's order quantity Q , the profit is Profit = Q × p − Q × c     (In this case, all available units are sold, and the profit is the revenue from selling Q units minus the total ordering cost.) So, the newsvendor problem is defined by the following parameters. Ordering cost (c). Cost per unit ordered. Sell price (p). Price per unit sold. Salvage value (s). Value per unsold unit at the end of the period. Mean demand (μ). Average demand during the period. Standard deviation of demand (σ). How much the demand varies. Number of samples (n). Number of demand samples for the simulation. Order quantity (Q). Units ordered for the period. The objective is to find the order quantity Q * that maximizes the expected profit. Analytical Solution The optimal order quantity is Q * = μ + σ · Φ −1 ( C u / (C u + C o ) ) where C u = p − c is the underage cost (profit lost per unit of demand that could not be met), C o = c − s is the overage cost (cost per unsold unit), Φ −1 is the inverse of the standard normal distribution, and C u /(C u + C o ) is the critical ratio (the share of demand to satisfy). Example Parameters The parameters in this example are c = 2 p = 5 s = 1 μ = 100 σ = 15 n = 1000 Q = 100 (example order quantity) Putting in the values C u = 5 − 2 = 3 C o = 2 − 1 = 1 Critical ratio = 3/(3 + 1) = 0.75 Q = 100 + 15 · Φ −1 (0.75) Q ≈ 100 + 15 · 0.6745 = 110.12 So, the optimal order quantity is about 110 units . Modeling and Simulating the Newsvendor Problem It is a simple supply chain with three nodes, an infinite supplier, the newsvendor (a retailer), and a customer demand at the newsvendor with normally distributed order sizes. One time unit is read as one day. Simulation Setup An infinite_supplier gives the newsvendor an unlimited supply. The simulation focuses on the newsvendor, newsvendor1 , which keeps a perishable inventory with a shelf life of 1 day, and uses a periodic replenishment policy, placing a replenishment order every day. The link between the supplier and the newsvendor has a lead time of 0, so each day's order arrives at once. The customer demand places one customer order a day, with an order size drawn from a normal distribution by the normal_quantity() function. With consume_available set to True, a customer whose order cannot be filled in full takes the units that are there. This is needed because the simulation represents the whole day's demand as a single customer order, while in reality many customers each buy a newspaper. After the run, the profit is worked out from the units sold, the expired units (sold back at the salvage value) and the ordering cost. import simpy import random import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import SupplyNetPy.Components as scm random.seed(42) # fixed seed for repeatable results mean = 100 std_dev = 15 num_samples = 1000 def normal_quantity(): """Generates a random order quantity based on a normal distribution.""" sample = random.gauss(mean, std_dev) while(sample<0): sample = random.gauss(mean, std_dev) return int(sample) cost = 2 # newspaper buy price sell_price = 5 # newspaper sell price salvage = 1 # newspaper salvage price order_quantity = 100 # initial order quantity cost_arr = [] # to store cost for each order quantity profit_arr = [] # to store profit for each order quantity for order_quantity in range(10, 200, 10): env = simpy.Environment() # create an infinite supplier supplier1 = scm.Supplier(env=env, ID="S1", name="Supplier1", node_type="infinite_supplier") #create the distributor newsvendor1 = scm.InventoryNode(env=env, ID="D1", name="News Vendor", node_type="distributor", capacity=float('inf'), initial_level=order_quantity, inventory_holding_cost=0.1, inventory_type="perishable", shelf_life=1, replenishment_policy=scm.PeriodicReplenishment, policy_param={"T": 1, "Q": order_quantity}, product_sell_price=sell_price, product_buy_price=cost) link1 = scm.Link(env=env,ID="l1", source=supplier1, sink=newsvendor1, cost=10, lead_time=lambda: 0) demand1 = scm.Demand(env=env,ID="d1", name="demand_d1", order_arrival_model=lambda: 1, consume_available=True, order_quantity_model=normal_quantity, demand_node=newsvendor1) scm.global_logger.disable_logging() env.run(until=num_samples) # Calculate the cost and profit # total demand fulfilled by newsvendor is available in variable demand_fulfilled # list element 0 is number of orders, element 1 is total quantity daily_sales = newsvendor1.stats.demand_fulfilled[1] wasted_inventory = newsvendor1.inventory.waste everyday_profit = (daily_sales*sell_price + wasted_inventory*salvage - order_quantity*num_samples*cost)/num_samples profit_arr.append([order_quantity,everyday_profit]) profit_arr = np.array(profit_arr) # convert to numpy array for easier manipulation Q = np.argmax(profit_arr[:,1]) # index of maximum profit plt.plot(profit_arr[:,0], profit_arr[:,1], marker='.', linestyle='-', color='b') plt.plot(profit_arr[Q,0], profit_arr[Q,1], marker='o', linestyle='-', color='r', label=f'Q={profit_arr[Q,0]}') plt.xlabel('Order Quantity') plt.ylabel('Profit') plt.title('Profit vs Order Quantity') plt.legend() plt.grid() plt.show() The following plot shows how the profit changes with the order quantity (Q). The highest profit is reached when Q is about 110, which confirms the analytical solution for the optimal order quantity. Takeaway This example showed how to solve the newsvendor problem by simulation with the SupplyNetPy library. By simulating different order quantities and comparing the resulting profits, we can see and confirm the order quantity that maximizes the expected profit. This approach can be extended to more complex inventory scenarios and demand distributions, giving useful insights for inventory decisions.

docs.text: Supply Chain With a Manufacturer This example shows how to create a complete supply chain with a raw-material supplier, a manufacturer, a distributor and a customer demand. Creating Nodes In this scenario, we create a raw-material supplier with finite inventory. A raw-material supplier with finite inventory needs a raw material, which is created first. The raw material is defined by its ID, its name, how many units are mined in each round of mining ( extraction_quantity ), how long each round takes ( extraction_time ), the mining cost per unit, and the sell price per unit ( cost ). The raw-material supplier mines a single raw material. It mines whenever its inventory is not full, and starts again as soon as its inventory drops. import SupplyNetPy.Components as scm raw_mat1 = scm.RawMaterial(ID='rm1', name='raw_mat1', extraction_quantity=1000, extraction_time=1, mining_cost=0.5, cost=0.8) supplier1 = {'ID':'S1', 'name':'supplier1', 'node_type':'supplier', 'capacity':5000, 'initial_level':5000, 'inventory_holding_cost':0.01, 'raw_material':raw_mat1} Creating a manufacturer requires a product. The product, the manufacturer and the distributor are created below. In the code, the manufacturer has the node type "factory" , which means the same as "manufacturer" . product1 = scm.Product(ID='p1', name='product1', manufacturing_cost=20, manufacturing_time=1, batch_size=1000, raw_materials=[(raw_mat1, 2)], sell_price=30) factory1 = {'ID':'F1', 'name':'factory1', 'node_type':'factory', 'capacity':2500, 'initial_level':2500, 'inventory_holding_cost':0.02, 'replenishment_policy':scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s':1000,'S':2500}, 'product':product1, 'product_sell_price':30} distributor1 = {'ID': 'D1', 'name': 'Distributor1', 'node_type': 'distributor', 'capacity': 1000, 'initial_level': 1000, 'inventory_holding_cost': 0.2, 'replenishment_policy': scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s':300,'S':1000}, 'product_buy_price':30,'product_sell_price': 35} The manufacturer plans its production with a replenishment policy, here an (s, S) policy. When the inventory position of its product falls to s (1000) or below, it plans enough production to bring the inventory position back up to S (2500), and orders the raw materials needed. Each unit of the product needs 2 units of the raw material. The manufacturer makes the planned units in production batches of at most 1000 units, each taking 1 time unit. The distributor also follows an (s, S) policy, with s = 300 and S = 1000. Defining Links Links carry units from one site to another, each with its own transportation cost and lead time. links1f1 = {'ID': 'L1', 'source': 'S1', 'sink': 'F1', 'cost': 100, 'lead_time': lambda: 2} linkf1d1 = {'ID': 'L2', 'source': 'F1', 'sink': 'D1', 'cost': 120, 'lead_time': lambda: 3} Modeling Demand The customer demand is at the distributor, with a customer order of 30 units every 0.4 time units (fixed, with no randomness). demand1 = {'ID': 'd1', 'name': 'Demand1', 'order_arrival_model': lambda: 0.4, 'order_quantity_model': lambda: 30, 'demand_node': 'D1'} Running the Simulation Create the supply chain network and simulate it. supplychainnet = scm.create_sc_net(nodes=[supplier1, factory1, distributor1], links=[links1f1, linkf1d1], demands=[demand1]) supplychainnet = scm.simulate_sc_net(supplychainnet, sim_time=20, logging=True) Review Results Here is the simulation log produced by the network. docs.title: Supply Chain With a Manufacturer

docs.text: This example shows how to create a complete supply chain with a raw-material supplier, a manufacturer, a distributor and a customer demand.
docs.title: Supply Chain With a Manufacturer

docs.text: In this scenario, we create a raw-material supplier with finite inventory. A raw-material supplier with finite inventory needs a raw material, which is created first. The raw material is defined by its ID, its name, how many units are mined in each round of mining ( extraction_quantity ), how long each round takes ( extraction_time ), the mining cost per unit, and the sell price per unit ( cost ). The raw-material supplier mines a single raw material. It mines whenever its inventory is not full, and starts again as soon as its inventory drops. import SupplyNetPy.Components as scm raw_mat1 = scm.RawMaterial(ID='rm1', name='raw_mat1', extraction_quantity=1000, extraction_time=1, mining_cost=0.5, cost=0.8) supplier1 = {'ID':'S1', 'name':'supplier1', 'node_type':'supplier', 'capacity':5000, 'initial_level':5000, 'inventory_holding_cost':0.01, 'raw_material':raw_mat1} Creating a manufacturer requires a product. The product, the manufacturer and the distributor are created below. In the code, the manufacturer has the node type "factory" , which means the same as "manufacturer" . product1 = scm.Product(ID='p1', name='product1', manufacturing_cost=20, manufacturing_time=1, batch_size=1000, raw_materials=[(raw_mat1, 2)], sell_price=30) factory1 = {'ID':'F1', 'name':'factory1', 'node_type':'factory', 'capacity':2500, 'initial_level':2500, 'inventory_holding_cost':0.02, 'replenishment_policy':scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s':1000,'S':2500}, 'product':product1, 'product_sell_price':30} distributor1 = {'ID': 'D1', 'name': 'Distributor1', 'node_type': 'distributor', 'capacity': 1000, 'initial_level': 1000, 'inventory_holding_cost': 0.2, 'replenishment_policy': scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s':300,'S':1000}, 'product_buy_price':30,'product_sell_price': 35} The manufacturer plans its production with a replenishment policy, here an (s, S) policy. When the inventory position of its product falls to s (1000) or below, it plans enough production to bring the inventory position back up to S (2500), and orders the raw materials needed. Each unit of the product needs 2 units of the raw material. The manufacturer makes the planned units in production batches of at most 1000 units, each taking 1 time unit. The distributor also follows an (s, S) policy, with s = 300 and S = 1000.
docs.title: Creating Nodes

docs.text: Links carry units from one site to another, each with its own transportation cost and lead time. links1f1 = {'ID': 'L1', 'source': 'S1', 'sink': 'F1', 'cost': 100, 'lead_time': lambda: 2} linkf1d1 = {'ID': 'L2', 'source': 'F1', 'sink': 'D1', 'cost': 120, 'lead_time': lambda: 3}
docs.title: Defining Links

docs.text: The customer demand is at the distributor, with a customer order of 30 units every 0.4 time units (fixed, with no randomness). demand1 = {'ID': 'd1', 'name': 'Demand1', 'order_arrival_model': lambda: 0.4, 'order_quantity_model': lambda: 30, 'demand_node': 'D1'}
docs.title: Modeling Demand

docs.text: Create the supply chain network and simulate it. supplychainnet = scm.create_sc_net(nodes=[supplier1, factory1, distributor1], links=[links1f1, linkf1d1], demands=[demand1]) supplychainnet = scm.simulate_sc_net(supplychainnet, sim_time=20, logging=True)
docs.title: Running the Simulation

docs.text: Glossary SupplyNetPy uses one word for each idea . This page lists those words, says what each one means, and gives the name it has in the code. The same words are used in this documentation, in the code's comments and docstrings, and in the API reference, so that two words never stand for the same thing. A few names in the code use a different word from the one chosen here (for example inventory.on_hand ). They are kept so that existing programs keep working; the entry explains what they really hold. The network Term Meaning In the code Supply chain network The whole model: the sites, the links between them, and the customers. create_sc_net returns it as a dictionary (often named supplychainnet ); Network wraps the same dictionary. Node Any point in the network: a raw-material supplier, a manufacturer, a warehouse, distributor or retailer, and a customer demand. Node (all of these classes are nodes, including Demand ). Site A node that holds inventory: every node except a customer demand. Use "node" when customers are included, and "site" when they are not. site_order , waiting_site_orders() , and the results demand_by_site , fulfillment_received_by_site . Link The transport connection that carries goods from one site to another. It has a cost per order and a lead time. Link . Its statistics (the replenishment orders its buyer placed over it, what arrived, and its disruptions) are in link.stats . Supplier (of a site) The site at the sending end of a link, seen from the site that orders over it. A warehouse is the supplier of the retailers it serves. link.source ; chosen by a supplier-selection policy. Note: in process_order(supplier, ...) and process_order_raw(..., supplier, ...) , the parameter named supplier is the link to the supplier, not the supplier itself (the supplier is supplier.source ). Buyer A site that buys from another site: the site at the receiving end of a link, which places orders over it. A buyer is always a site; someone who buys and takes the units out of the network is a customer. link.sink Kinds of node Term Meaning In the code Raw-material supplier A site at the start of the network that mines a raw material. It has no supplier of its own. Supplier , node_type="supplier" Infinite supplier A raw-material supplier that never runs out. Supplier , node_type="infinite_supplier" Manufacturer A site that turns raw materials into a product. Manufacturer , node_type="manufacturer" (or "factory" , which means the same) Distributor, warehouse, retailer Sites that buy a product, hold it, and sell it on. They behave the same; the name only describes their place in the network. InventoryNode , node_type="distributor" , "warehouse" , "retailer" , "store" or "shop" Customer Someone who orders units from a site and takes them out of the network (the end customer). One order from a Demand . Customer demand A stream of customer orders arriving at one site, with a given time between orders and order size. Demand , node_type="demand" Inventory Term Meaning In the code Inventory The units a site holds, together with its records about them (costs, dated batches, and so on). Inventory , reached as node.inventory . The units themselves sit in a SimPy container, node.inventory.inventory . Inventory level The number of units physically at the site right now. node.inventory.level Average inventory level The inventory level averaged over time, so that each level counts for as long as it lasted. Holding 10 units for 3 time units and then 4 units for 2 time units gives (10 × 3 + 4 × 2) / 5 = 7.6. stats.avg_inventory_level , worked out from stats.inventory_level_time (the sum of inventory level × time) Capacity The largest inventory level a site can hold. capacity In transit Units that have been sent to a site but have not arrived yet. (counted inside inventory.on_hand ) Inventory position What a site can count on: inventory level, plus units in transit to it, minus units it still owes (to other sites and to waiting customers). Replenishment policies decide using this number. node.position() on_hand Despite its name, not the units physically at the site. It holds the inventory position before units owed to waiting customers are taken off: inventory level, plus units in transit, minus units promised to other sites. Use node.position() for the inventory position. node.inventory.on_hand Units The way quantities are counted. Product The thing a manufacturer makes and the other sites sell. Product Raw material What a raw-material supplier mines and a manufacturer uses up. RawMaterial ; a product lists them in raw_materials as (raw material, quantity per unit) Perishable goods Term Meaning In the code Perishable Goods that can only be sold for a limited time after they are made. inventory_type="perishable" Shelf life How long a perishable unit can be sold after it is made. "Shelf life" is the standard industry term, so it is kept even though "shelf" is otherwise avoided. shelf_life Manufacturing date When a unit was made. manufacturing_date Batch Units of a perishable good that share a manufacturing date. Every order takes units from the oldest batch first, then from the next oldest, and so on. entries (manufacturing date, quantity) in inventory.perish_queue Expired units Perishable units that reached the end of their shelf life and were thrown away. inventory.waste ; reported as inventory_waste Destroyed units Units lost in a disruption (fire, flood, theft, and so on). Inventory.destroy ; recorded as destroyed_qty and destroyed_value Orders Term Meaning In the code Order A request for a number of units. There are two kinds: replenishment orders and customer orders. Replenishment order An order a site places with its supplier, to refill its inventory (or, for a manufacturer, to get raw material). Seen from the supplier, it is an order from a site rather than from a customer, which is why the code labels it a "site order". Placed by place_order / process_order (and process_order_raw for raw material). At the supplier it is marked site_order=True , and waiting_site_orders() counts the ones still waiting. In the results it is counted under demand_by_site . Customer order An order placed by a customer. Created by Demand ; counted under demand_by_customers in the results. Request Only in the code's internals: the SimPy object that waits at an inventory until enough units are there to fill an order. inventory.get(...) returns one Demand In the statistics, the orders a node placed or received, counted as [number of orders, number of units] . Includes both customer orders and site orders. demand_placed , demand_received Fulfilled An order the supplier has sent out in full. demand_fulfilled (at the supplier) Received An order that has arrived at the site that placed it. fulfillment_received (at the buyer) Lead time How long an order takes to arrive after it is sent: over a link, or from a site to a customer. Link.lead_time , Demand.lead_time . Over a link, the total and the average are link.stats.lead_time and link.stats.avg_lead_time . Backorder An order, or part of one, that a site owes right now: it has been accepted but is still waiting for units. It is removed once it is filled, or when a waiting customer gives up. stats.backorder , as [orders, units] Shortage How many units a site was missing when an order arrived. It is a running total, never reduced, whether the order is later filled or not. Customers turned away by a disruption are not part of it (see disruption lost sales). stats.shortage , as [orders, units] Disruption lost sales Customer orders a site lost because it was disrupted when they arrived. A disrupted site takes no new orders, so the customer goes away. Kept apart from shortage, which counts units the site did not have, because the cause and the remedy differ. stats.disruption_lost_sales , as [orders, units] Lost sales Customer units a site never delivered, for any reason other than a disruption. A customer with no tolerance who finds too few units, the rest of an order when the customer takes only what is there, an order too big for the site ever to hold, and what a waiting customer was still owed when they gave up. Unlike shortage, it counts only units that were never delivered. Everything a site lost is lost sales plus disruption lost sales. stats.lost_sales , as [orders, units] Blocked order A replenishment order a site could not place, because the supplier chosen for it (or the link to it) was disrupted, or every supplier it has was. It is not lost. The site orders again when a supplier or a link recovers. A site with no supplier at all has no blocked orders, because no recovery would ever let its orders through. That is a mistake in how the network is built, and a warning says so. stats.blocked , as [orders, units] Waiting time How long an order waited at a site before its units left the inventory, for orders that could not be served at once. Orders served at once wait 0. stats.waited , stats.waiting_time , stats.avg_waiting_time . For the replenishment orders a buyer placed over a link, the same names in link.stats . Order cycle time How long a replenishment order takes from the moment the buyer places it until it arrives. It is the waiting time at the supplier plus the lead time. link.stats.avg_order_cycle_time Fill rate The share of the units ordered that the supplier sent at once, without the order having to wait. An order that had to wait counts as not sent at once, even if part of it was there. The order fill rate is the same share counted in orders instead of units. A fill rate of 1 means no order ever waited. link.stats.fill_rate , link.stats.order_fill_rate Bullwhip effect Orders becoming more and more uneven as they pass from the customers towards the raw-material suppliers. Customers may buy about the same amount every day, while their retailer orders in large irregular amounts, and its supplier in even larger swings. It is measured per time unit. Compare the standard deviation of the units ordered over a link in each time unit with that of the customer demand in each time unit. link.stats.units_per_time_unit_std Dropped units Units of a delivery that did not fit in the inventory of the site that ordered them, when no waiting customer could take them either. The site does not pay for them, and they are not stored. stats.dropped_qty Tolerance How long a customer is willing to wait for units that are not there. A customer with no tolerance leaves at once. tolerance Partial delivery Sending a customer part of an order now and the rest later. order_min_split_ratio Deadlock Two parts of a model each waiting for the other, so neither ever moves again. For example, a buyer waits for an order larger than its supplier's capacity, and the supplier can never hold enough units to send it. SupplyNetPy warns about this when the link between them is created. Replenishment policies Term Meaning In the code Replenishment policy The rule a site follows to decide when to place a replenishment order and how many units to order. InventoryReplenishment and its subclasses, passed as replenishment_policy (s, S) policy When the inventory position falls to s or below, order enough to bring it back up to S . SSReplenishment (R, Q) policy When the inventory position falls to R or below, order a fixed Q units. RQReplenishment Periodic policy Every T time units, order a fixed Q units. PeriodicReplenishment Reorder point The inventory position at which a policy places an order ( s or R ). Safety stock Extra units a policy keeps as a buffer against uncertain demand or lead times. A standard industry term, so "stock" is kept here. safety_stock Supplier-selection policy The rule a site follows to choose which of its suppliers receives an order. SupplierSelectionPolicy , SelectFirst , SelectAvailable , SelectCheapest , SelectFastest , SelectProbabilistic Probability-based supplier selection A supplier-selection policy that chooses the supplier of each replenishment order at random, with a selection probability for each supplier. SelectProbabilistic Selection probability The share of a site's replenishment orders that goes to one supplier, while every supplier can take orders. The probabilities of a site's suppliers sum to 1. With disruptions, the shares at the end of a run differ from them. supplier_selection_param["probabilities"] , keyed by supplier ID Fixed mode , dynamic mode How often a supplier-selection policy chooses. In dynamic mode it chooses again for every replenishment order. docs.text: SupplyNetPy uses one word for each idea . This page lists those words, says what each one means, and gives the name it has in the code. The same words are used in this documentation, in the code's comments and docstrings, and in the API reference, so that two words never stand for the same thing. A few names in the code use a different word from the one chosen here (for example inventory.on_hand ). They are kept so that existing programs keep working; the entry explains what they really hold.
docs.title: Glossary

docs.text: Term Meaning In the code Supply chain network The whole model: the sites, the links between them, and the customers. create_sc_net returns it as a dictionary (often named supplychainnet ); Network wraps the same dictionary. Node Any point in the network: a raw-material supplier, a manufacturer, a warehouse, distributor or retailer, and a customer demand. Node (all of these classes are nodes, including Demand ). Site A node that holds inventory: every node except a customer demand. Use "node" when customers are included, and "site" when they are not. site_order , waiting_site_orders() , and the results demand_by_site , fulfillment_received_by_site . Link The transport connection that carries goods from one site to another. It has a cost per order and a lead time. Link . Its statistics (the replenishment orders its buyer placed over it, what arrived, and its disruptions) are in link.stats . Supplier (of a site) The site at the sending end of a link, seen from the site that orders over it. A warehouse is the supplier of the retailers it serves. link.source ; chosen by a supplier-selection policy. Note: in process_order(supplier, ...) and process_order_raw(..., supplier, ...) , the parameter named supplier is the link to the supplier, not the supplier itself (the supplier is supplier.source ). Buyer A site that buys from another site: the site at the receiving end of a link, which places orders over it. A buyer is always a site; someone who buys and takes the units out of the network is a customer. link.sink
docs.title: The network

docs.text: Term Meaning In the code Raw-material supplier A site at the start of the network that mines a raw material. It has no supplier of its own. Supplier , node_type="supplier" Infinite supplier A raw-material supplier that never runs out. Supplier , node_type="infinite_supplier" Manufacturer A site that turns raw materials into a product. Manufacturer , node_type="manufacturer" (or "factory" , which means the same) Distributor, warehouse, retailer Sites that buy a product, hold it, and sell it on. They behave the same; the name only describes their place in the network. InventoryNode , node_type="distributor" , "warehouse" , "retailer" , "store" or "shop" Customer Someone who orders units from a site and takes them out of the network (the end customer). One order from a Demand . Customer demand A stream of customer orders arriving at one site, with a given time between orders and order size. Demand , node_type="demand"
docs.title: Kinds of node

docs.text: Term Meaning In the code Inventory The units a site holds, together with its records about them (costs, dated batches, and so on). Inventory , reached as node.inventory . The units themselves sit in a SimPy container, node.inventory.inventory . Inventory level The number of units physically at the site right now. node.inventory.level Average inventory level The inventory level averaged over time, so that each level counts for as long as it lasted. Holding 10 units for 3 time units and then 4 units for 2 time units gives (10 × 3 + 4 × 2) / 5 = 7.6. stats.avg_inventory_level , worked out from stats.inventory_level_time (the sum of inventory level × time) Capacity The largest inventory level a site can hold. capacity In transit Units that have been sent to a site but have not arrived yet. (counted inside inventory.on_hand ) Inventory position What a site can count on: inventory level, plus units in transit to it, minus units it still owes (to other sites and to waiting customers). Replenishment policies decide using this number. node.position() on_hand Despite its name, not the units physically at the site. It holds the inventory position before units owed to waiting customers are taken off: inventory level, plus units in transit, minus units promised to other sites. Use node.position() for the inventory position. node.inventory.on_hand Units The way quantities are counted. Product The thing a manufacturer makes and the other sites sell. Product Raw material What a raw-material supplier mines and a manufacturer uses up. RawMaterial ; a product lists them in raw_materials as (raw material, quantity per unit)
docs.title: Inventory

docs.text: Term Meaning In the code Perishable Goods that can only be sold for a limited time after they are made. inventory_type="perishable" Shelf life How long a perishable unit can be sold after it is made. "Shelf life" is the standard industry term, so it is kept even though "shelf" is otherwise avoided. shelf_life Manufacturing date When a unit was made. manufacturing_date Batch Units of a perishable good that share a manufacturing date. Every order takes units from the oldest batch first, then from the next oldest, and so on. entries (manufacturing date, quantity) in inventory.perish_queue Expired units Perishable units that reached the end of their shelf life and were thrown away. inventory.waste ; reported as inventory_waste Destroyed units Units lost in a disruption (fire, flood, theft, and so on). Inventory.destroy ; recorded as destroyed_qty and destroyed_value
docs.title: Perishable goods

docs.text: Term Meaning In the code Order A request for a number of units. There are two kinds: replenishment orders and customer orders. Replenishment order An order a site places with its supplier, to refill its inventory (or, for a manufacturer, to get raw material). Seen from the supplier, it is an order from a site rather than from a customer, which is why the code labels it a "site order". Placed by place_order / process_order (and process_order_raw for raw material). At the supplier it is marked site_order=True , and waiting_site_orders() counts the ones still waiting. In the results it is counted under demand_by_site . Customer order An order placed by a customer. Created by Demand ; counted under demand_by_customers in the results. Request Only in the code's internals: the SimPy object that waits at an inventory until enough units are there to fill an order. inventory.get(...) returns one Demand In the statistics, the orders a node placed or received, counted as [number of orders, number of units] . Includes both customer orders and site orders. demand_placed , demand_received Fulfilled An order the supplier has sent out in full. demand_fulfilled (at the supplier) Received An order that has arrived at the site that placed it. fulfillment_received (at the buyer) Lead time How long an order takes to arrive after it is sent: over a link, or from a site to a customer. Link.lead_time , Demand.lead_time . Over a link, the total and the average are link.stats.lead_time and link.stats.avg_lead_time . Backorder An order, or part of one, that a site owes right now: it has been accepted but is still waiting for units. It is removed once it is filled, or when a waiting customer gives up. stats.backorder , as [orders, units] Shortage How many units a site was missing when an order arrived. It is a running total, never reduced, whether the order is later filled or not. Customers turned away by a disruption are not part of it (see disruption lost sales). stats.shortage , as [orders, units] Disruption lost sales Customer orders a site lost because it was disrupted when they arrived. A disrupted site takes no new orders, so the customer goes away. Kept apart from shortage, which counts units the site did not have, because the cause and the remedy differ. stats.disruption_lost_sales , as [orders, units] Lost sales Customer units a site never delivered, for any reason other than a disruption. A customer with no tolerance who finds too few units, the rest of an order when the customer takes only what is there, an order too big for the site ever to hold, and what a waiting customer was still owed when they gave up. Unlike shortage, it counts only units that were never delivered. Everything a site lost is lost sales plus disruption lost sales. stats.lost_sales , as [orders, units] Blocked order A replenishment order a site could not place, because the supplier chosen for it (or the link to it) was disrupted, or every supplier it has was. It is not lost. The site orders again when a supplier or a link recovers. A site with no supplier at all has no blocked orders, because no recovery would ever let its orders through. That is a mistake in how the network is built, and a warning says so. stats.blocked , as [orders, units] Waiting time How long an order waited at a site before its units left the inventory, for orders that could not be served at once. Orders served at once wait 0. stats.waited , stats.waiting_time , stats.avg_waiting_time . For the replenishment orders a buyer placed over a link, the same names in link.stats . Order cycle time How long a replenishment order takes from the moment the buyer places it until it arrives. It is the waiting time at the supplier plus the lead time. link.stats.avg_order_cycle_time Fill rate The share of the units ordered that the supplier sent at once, without the order having to wait. An order that had to wait counts as not sent at once, even if part of it was there. The order fill rate is the same share counted in orders instead of units. A fill rate of 1 means no order ever waited. link.stats.fill_rate , link.stats.order_fill_rate Bullwhip effect Orders becoming more and more uneven as they pass from the customers towards the raw-material suppliers. Customers may buy about the same amount every day, while their retailer orders in large irregular amounts, and its supplier in even larger swings. It is measured per time unit. Compare the standard deviation of the units ordered over a link in each time unit with that of the customer demand in each time unit. link.stats.units_per_time_unit_std Dropped units Units of a delivery that did not fit in the inventory of the site that ordered them, when no waiting customer could take them either. The site does not pay for them, and they are not stored. stats.dropped_qty Tolerance How long a customer is willing to wait for units that are not there. A customer with no tolerance leaves at once. tolerance Partial delivery Sending a customer part of an order now and the rest later. order_min_split_ratio Deadlock Two parts of a model each waiting for the other, so neither ever moves again. For example, a buyer waits for an order larger than its supplier's capacity, and the supplier can never hold enough units to send it. SupplyNetPy warns about this when the link between them is created.
docs.title: Orders

docs.text: Term Meaning In the code Replenishment policy The rule a site follows to decide when to place a replenishment order and how many units to order. InventoryReplenishment and its subclasses, passed as replenishment_policy (s, S) policy When the inventory position falls to s or below, order enough to bring it back up to S . SSReplenishment (R, Q) policy When the inventory position falls to R or below, order a fixed Q units. RQReplenishment Periodic policy Every T time units, order a fixed Q units. PeriodicReplenishment Reorder point The inventory position at which a policy places an order ( s or R ). Safety stock Extra units a policy keeps as a buffer against uncertain demand or lead times. A standard industry term, so "stock" is kept here. safety_stock Supplier-selection policy The rule a site follows to choose which of its suppliers receives an order. SupplierSelectionPolicy , SelectFirst , SelectAvailable , SelectCheapest , SelectFastest , SelectProbabilistic Probability-based supplier selection A supplier-selection policy that chooses the supplier of each replenishment order at random, with a selection probability for each supplier. SelectProbabilistic Selection probability The share of a site's replenishment orders that goes to one supplier, while every supplier can take orders. The probabilities of a site's suppliers sum to 1. With disruptions, the shares at the end of a run differ from them. supplier_selection_param["probabilities"] , keyed by supplier ID Fixed mode , dynamic mode How often a supplier-selection policy chooses. In dynamic mode it chooses again for every replenishment order. In fixed mode it keeps the first supplier it chose, and uses another only while that supplier or the link to it is disrupted. supplier_selection_mode , "fixed" (the default of every built in policy except SelectProbabilistic , which always works in dynamic mode) or "dynamic"

docs.text: /* Known issues only: undo the grey h3 banner from css/extra.css, as on the release history page */ h3 { padding: 0; margin: 1em 0 0.4em; border: none; border-radius: 0; background: none; } Known Issues and Planned Work This page lists known issues, current limitations, and planned improvements for upcoming versions of SupplyNetPy . Known Issues ⚠️ Loops in a supply chain. The library does not check for loops in the network. It is possible to create a supply chain with loops, for example when two distributors are linked to each other to cover shortages. ⚠️ Simultaneous events. When several events are due at the same time (for example at time 10), they are carried out one after another. SupplyNetPy is built on SimPy and carries out such events in SimPy's order, by event ID. For simulations without randomness, every run gives the same output. ⚠️ A run stops just before its end time. A run with simulate_sc_net(..., sim_time=T) or env.run(until=T) carries out every event due before time T, but not the events due at exactly time T. For example, a run with sim_time=360 does not see a customer order or an expiry due at time 360. To include the events at time T, run to a slightly later time, such as T + 1. This is how SimPy works. The pharmacy case study runs to T + 1 for this reason, so that it counts the same days as the paper it reproduces. ⚠️ Simulation parallelization. SupplyNetPy does not currently run a simulation in parallel. ⚠️ Simulating in real time. Running a simulation in step with the real clock is not supported. ⚠️ A link disruption only blocks new orders. When a Link is disrupted, orders already in transit over it still arrive. SupplyNetPy does not currently stop orders in transit on a disrupted link. Only new replenishment orders are not sent until the link recovers. The supplier-selection policies ( SelectFirst , SelectAvailable , SelectCheapest , SelectFastest ) skip suppliers whose site or link is disrupted, so they choose a supplier that can take the order when there is one. If no supplier can take it, the order is not placed, and the replenishment policy checks its inventory position again as soon as a supplier or a link recovers. In "fixed" mode, while the remembered supplier or the link to it is disrupted, the policy uses another supplier, and goes back to the remembered supplier once it recovers. ⚠️ A manufacturer does not use its supplier-selection policy. For each raw material, a manufacturer orders from the first raw-material supplier of that raw material that can take the order, whatever supplier-selection policy it is given. It warns when it is given one. Choosing among raw-material suppliers with a policy, one choice for each raw material, is planned. ⚠️ An order larger than the supplier can hold is never filled. A supplier sends a replenishment order only when it has all of it, in one shipment. So if a buyer orders more units than its supplier's capacity, the supplier can never hold enough to send the order. The buyer waits for it for ever, and the two are stuck (a deadlock). For example, a distributor that holds at most 100 units can never fill an order of 150 units from a retailer that holds 200. For a manufacturer, count the raw material it needs. A manufacturer that holds 150 units of a product made from 2 units of raw material each can order up to 300 units of that raw material. SupplyNetPy warns about such a pair when the link between them is created, and again if such an order is placed. Until this changes, give each supplier a capacity at least as large as what its buyers can order. Planned Work Next updates Features and fixes planned for the coming versions of the library. Orders in smaller parts. A buyer will be able to receive a replenishment order in smaller parts as the supplier gets units, or to take only what the supplier has, so that an order larger than the supplier's capacity can still be filled. Checking the whole network. A check, run before a simulation, that every node is connected, that the settings fit together, and that units flow towards the customers. Perishable raw materials. Raw materials with manufacturing dates and a shelf life, as many have in reality. For now, SupplyNetPy assumes that raw materials are not perishable, so the inventory of a raw-material supplier and the raw materials a manufacturer holds are always non-perishable. Long-term goals Larger directions for SupplyNetPy, beyond the next few versions. More case studies. Models of real supply chains. Logistics operations. Geographic map locations, CO₂ calculations, and fleet management. Simulation parallelization. Faster runs of the model, and support for simulating in real time. Simulation based optimization (SBO). Optimization methods from Python's SciPy library, to support SBO.
docs.title: Known Issues and Planned Work

img{ width:75%; } This example is from the textbook Supply Chain Management: Strategy, Planning, and Operation, (Chopra and Meindl) Find the Google Colab notebook for this example here . Estimating Safety Stock Level Safety inventory (the textbook's name for safety stock, the extra units kept as a buffer) can help a supply chain make its product more available when supply and demand vary. Image source, the textbook Supply Chain Management: Strategy, Planning, and Operation (Chopra and Meindl). System Description Bloomingdale sells Gucci purses. Demand is 100 per week. Gucci takes 3 weeks to deliver purses to Bloomingdale after an order. So Bloomingdale could place an order when exactly 300 purses are left in its inventory. Because demand varies, the demand over three weeks may be more or less than 300. If it is more, Bloomingdale will lose sales. The store manager decides to place an order when 400 purses are left (so the safety inventory is 100). Goal. To work out the right level of safety inventory. Replenishment policies. Continuous review. The inventory is tracked all the time, and an order for a fixed lot size Q is placed the moment the inventory falls to a set level called the reorder point (ROP) . For example, consider the store manager at B&M who tracks the inventory of phones all the time. She orders 600 phones the moment the inventory drops below the reorder point of 400. In this case, the size of each order is fixed (always 600), and only the time between orders varies, depending on how fast customers buy the phones. In SupplyNetPy, this is the (R, Q) policy. Periodic review. The inventory is checked at regular intervals, and an order is placed to raise the inventory to a set level. For example, consider the purchase of film at B&M. The store manager does not track film inventory all the time. Every Thursday, employees check the film inventory, and the manager orders enough so that the available inventory plus the order adds up to 1,000 films. In this case, the time between orders is fixed, but the size of each order can vary with demand. Numerical Example Evaluating Safety Inventory, Given an Inventory Policy Assume that weekly demand for phones at B&M Office Supplies is normally distributed, with a mean of 2,500 and a standard deviation of 500. The manufacturer takes two weeks to fill an order placed by the B&M manager. The store manager currently orders 10,000 phones when the inventory drops to 6,000. Evaluate the safety inventory and the average inventory carried by B&M. Also evaluate the average time a phone spends at B&M. Analytical solution. Under this replenishment policy, we have Average demand per week, \(D = 2500\) Standard deviation of weekly demand, \(\sigma_D = 500\) Average lead time, \(L = 2\) weeks Reorder point, \(ROP = 6000\) Average lot size, \(Q = 10000\) Using equation 12.3 in the textbook, Safety inventory, \(ss = ROP - D^*L = 6000-5000 = 1000\) B&M thus carries a safety inventory of 1,000 phones. Cycle inventory = \( rac{Q}{2} =  rac{10000}{2} = 5000\) Average inventory = cycle inventory + safety inventory \(= 5000 + 1000 = 6000\) Average flow time = average inventory/throughput \(=  rac{6000}{2500} = 2.4\) weeks The network. The cost per unit and the transportation cost are not given, so any values can be used. We want to find the following. Safety inventory level (the average number of phones in inventory when a replenishment order arrives). Cycle inventory (the average inventory level). Average flow time (the average time a unit spends in the inventory). Implementation import simpy import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import SupplyNetPy.Components as scm np.random.seed(42) # fixed seed for repeatable results daily_demand_mean = 2500/7 daily_demand_std = 500/(7**0.5) simlen = 3650 # simulation length in days def normal_quantity(): global daily_demand_mean, daily_demand_std sample = -1 while sample < 0: sample = np.random.normal(daily_demand_mean, daily_demand_std, 1)[0] return sample env = simpy.Environment() # create an infinite supplier supplier1 = scm.Supplier(env=env, ID="S1", name="Supplier1", node_type="infinite_supplier") #create the distributor distributor1 = scm.InventoryNode(env=env, ID="D1", name="Distributor1", node_type="distributor", capacity=float('inf'), initial_level=6000, inventory_holding_cost=0.1, product_buy_price=0, replenishment_policy=scm.RQReplenishment, policy_param={'R':6000,'Q':10000}, product_sell_price=399, record_inv_levels=True) link1 = scm.Link(env=env,ID="l1", source=supplier1, sink=distributor1, cost=100, lead_time=lambda: 14) demand1 = scm.Demand(env=env,ID="d1", name="demand_d1", order_arrival_model=lambda: 1, order_quantity_model=normal_quantity, demand_node=distributor1) scm.global_logger.disable_logging() # disable logging env.run(until=simlen) # calculate performance metrics safety_stock = [] replenish_cycles = [0] inv_levels = np.array(distributor1.inventory.instantaneous_levels) # instantaneous inventory levels # lets calculate safety stock level for i in range(len(inv_levels)-1): if(inv_levels[i,1]<inv_levels[i+1,1]): # inventory level is increasing that means a replenishment order is received safety_stock.append(inv_levels[i,1]) replenish_cycles.append(inv_levels[i,0]) # time of replenishment order # calculate average flow time (amount of time an item is stored in inventory) flow_time = [] for i in range(len(replenish_cycles)-1): flow_time.append(replenish_cycles[i+1]-replenish_cycles[i]) print("
	***
Safety Stock Level: ", np.mean(safety_stock)) print("Average Inventory Level:", np.mean(inv_levels[:,1])) print("Average Flow Time: ", np.mean(flow_time)/2, "days","
") # plot the inventory level over time plt.plot(inv_levels[:,0], inv_levels[:,1], marker='.', label="Inventory Level", color='green', linestyle='') plt.axhline(y=6000, color='r', linestyle='--', label="ROP") plt.xlabel("Time (days)") plt.ylabel("Inventory Level") plt.title("Inventory Level over Time") plt.legend() plt.grid() plt.show() *** Safety Stock Level: 1260.7957571939298 Average Inventory Level: 6115.0800971596045 Average Flow Time: 13.371323529411764 days Since the demand at the B&M office is unpredictable, we will estimate the safety inventory by conducting multiple simulations. First, we will define a function to simulate the B&M office sales. We will then use this function to run several simulations. np.random.seed(42) # fixed seed for repeatable results def bnmoffice(): env = simpy.Environment() # create an infinite supplier supplier1 = scm.Supplier(env=env, ID="S1", name="Supplier1", node_type="infinite_supplier") #create the distributor distributor1 = scm.InventoryNode(env=env, ID="D1", name="Distributor1", node_type="distributor", capacity=16000, initial_level=6000, inventory_holding_cost=0.1, product_buy_price=0, replenishment_policy=scm.SSReplenishment, policy_param={'s':6000,'S':16000}, product_sell_price=399, record_inv_levels=True) link1 = scm.Link(env=env,ID="l1", source=supplier1, sink=distributor1, cost=100, lead_time=lambda: 14) demand1 = scm.Demand(env=env,ID="d1", name="demand_d1", order_arrival_model=lambda: 1, order_quantity_model=normal_quantity, demand_node=distributor1) scm.global_logger.disable_logging() # disable logging env.run(until=simlen) # calculate performance metrics safety_stock = [] replenish_cycles = [0] inv_levels = np.array(distributor1.inventory.instantaneous_levels) # instantaneous inventory levels # lets calculate safety stock level for i in range(len(inv_levels)-1): if(inv_levels[i,1]<inv_levels[i+1,1]): # inventory level is increasing that means a replenishment order is received safety_stock.append(inv_levels[i,1]) replenish_cycles.append(inv_levels[i,0]) # time of replenishment order # calculate average flow time (amount of time an item is stored in inventory) flow_time = [] for i in range(len(replenish_cycles)-1): flow_time.append(replenish_cycles[i+1]-replenish_cycles[i]) return np.mean(safety_stock), np.mean(inv_levels[:,1]), np.mean(flow_time)/2 num_simulations = 100 ana_arr = [] # let us gather all stats in this variable for i in range(0,num_simulations): ana_arr.append([]) safety_stock, avg_inv, flow_t = bnmoffice() ana_arr[-1].extend([safety_stock, avg_inv, flow_t]) ana_arr = np.array(ana_arr) # convert to array for convenience #Final Stats print("
	***
Safety Stock Level: Mean: ", np.mean(ana_arr[:,0]), " Std:", np.std(ana_arr[:,0])) print("Average Inventory Level:", np.mean(ana_arr[:,1]), " Std:", np.std(ana_arr[:,1])) print("Average Flow Time: ", np.mean(ana_arr[:,2]), "days","
", " Std:", np.std(ana_arr[:,2])) Results *** Safety Stock Level: Mean: 1339.5033048247421 Std: 49.96583138717028 Average Inventory Level: 6310.421891038721 Std: 40.27311395206424 Average Flow Time: 13.806400122912272 days Std: 0.10341730434846103 We obtain a slightly higher safety level, and average inventory levels from the simulation because sampling from a normal distribution can yield a few values less than zero. In our method, normal_quantity() , we resample in such cases to ensure that we only get numbers that are greater than or equal to zero, as negative demand is not possible. This resampling increases the probability of obtaining positive values. We will demonstrate this further below. def normal_quantity(): """ Normal Distribution with given mean, and std A new sample is generated for every negative sample """ global daily_demand_mean, daily_demand_std sample = -1 while sample < 0: sample = np.random.normal(daily_demand_mean, daily_demand_std, 1)[0] return sample def normal_quantity_mean(): """ Normal Distribution with given mean, and std The mean value replaces a negative sample """ global daily_demand_mean, daily_demand_std sample = np.random.normal(daily_demand_mean, daily_demand_std, 1)[0] if sample < 0: sample = daily_demand_mean return sample def normal_quantity_wn(): """ Normal Distribution with given mean, and std including negatives """ global daily_demand_mean, daily_demand_std sample = np.random.normal(daily_demand_mean, daily_demand_std, 1)[0] return sample np.random.seed(42) # fixed seed for repeatable results samples = [] samples_wn = [] samples_mean = [] for r in range(5000): samples.append(normal_quantity()) samples_wn.append(normal_quantity_wn()) samples_mean.append(normal_quantity_mean()) plt.figure(figsize=(5, 3)) plt.hist(samples, bins=50, density=True, alpha=0.5, color='blue', label='Normal without negatives') plt.title('Normal') plt.xlabel('Quantity') plt.ylabel('Density') plt.grid() plt.legend() plt.figure(figsize=(5, 3)) plt.hist(samples_wn, bins=50, density=True, alpha=0.5, color='green', label='Normal with negatives') #plt.title('Normal without negative quantities') plt.xlabel('Quantity') plt.ylabel('Density') plt.grid() plt.legend() plt.figure(figsize=(5, 3)) plt.hist(samples_mean, bins=50, density=True, alpha=0.5, color='red', label='Normal: replace mean for negatives') #plt.title('Normal with mean for negative quantities') plt.xlabel('Quantity') plt.ylabel('Density') plt.grid() plt.legend()

docs.text: SupplyNetPy in 10 Minutes Installation SupplyNetPy can be installed using pip. pip install supplynetpy Quick Start, Building a Simple Supply Chain with Three Nodes Follow these steps to create and simulate a basic supply chain with an infinite supplier, a distributor and a customer demand. Import the Library import SupplyNetPy.Components as scm The Components module gives you the building blocks of a supply chain. These are the nodes (raw-material suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, warehouses and retailers), products and inventories, customer demands, and the links that connect them. You assemble them into a model that fits your scenario. The words used on this page are explained in the Glossary . Create Nodes Let us create an infinite supplier, a supplier that never runs out and so can supply any number of units to its buyers. It needs an ID, a name and a node type. To make it an infinite supplier, set the node type to infinite_supplier . supplier1 = {'ID': 'S1', 'name': 'Supplier1', 'node_type': 'infinite_supplier'} Next, a distributor that buys units from the supplier. Its settings include the ID, the name, the capacity, the replenishment policy and its parameters, and the buy and sell prices. distributor1 = {'ID': 'D1', 'name': 'Distributor1', 'node_type': 'distributor', 'capacity': 150, 'initial_level': 50, 'inventory_holding_cost': 0.2, 'replenishment_policy': scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s':100,'S':150}, 'product_buy_price': 100,'product_sell_price': 105} For a manufacturer, distributor, warehouse or retailer, we give its replenishment policy (the rule it follows to decide when to place a replenishment order and how many units to order) and the policy's parameters. The policies are subclasses of the InventoryReplenishment class, which you can also subclass to define your own. SupplyNetPy has the following replenishment policies. The (s, S) policy . When the inventory position falls to s or below, order enough units to bring it back up to S. Parameters {s, S}, class SSReplenishment . The (s, S) policy with a safety stock . The same, with the safety stock added to both s and S. Parameters {s, S, safety_stock}, class SSReplenishment . The (R, Q) policy . When the inventory position falls to R or below, order a fixed Q units. Parameters {R, Q}, class RQReplenishment . The periodic policy . Every T time units, order Q units. Parameters {T, Q}, class PeriodicReplenishment . The periodic policy with a safety stock . The same, but if the inventory level is below the safety stock, the order also includes the units needed to bring it back up to the safety stock. Parameters {T, Q, safety_stock}, class PeriodicReplenishment . The inventory position is the inventory level, plus the units in transit, minus the units still owed. By default, the (s, S) and (R, Q) policies check it each time the inventory drops. Create a Link A link is created as shown below. Its settings include the transportation cost and the lead time. The lead time can be a number, or a function with no arguments that returns one lead time each time it is called, for example a random one drawn from a distribution of your choice. For a constant lead time, a Python lambda such as lambda: 2 is enough. link1 = {'ID': 'L1', 'source': 'S1', 'sink': 'D1', 'cost': 5, 'lead_time': lambda: 2} Specify Demand A customer demand is created by giving an ID, a name, the site the customers order from, how often orders arrive, and how many units each order is for. The "how often" and "how many" values are each given as a small function with no arguments that returns a number. If you want randomness, for example customer orders arriving at times drawn from an exponential distribution, write a function that samples from that distribution and returns one number per call. If you want a fixed value, just use a lambda such as lambda: 1 . A customer demand can be at any site except a raw-material supplier, usually a retailer or a distributor. The example below sets up a steady demand of 10 units every time unit (read here as a day) at distributor D1. demand1 = {'ID': 'd1', 'name': 'Demand1', 'order_arrival_model': lambda: 1, 'order_quantity_model': lambda: 10, 'demand_node': 'D1'} Assemble and Simulate the Network To create and simulate the supply chain, use the create_sc_net function to create the nodes and assemble them into a network. This function also records information about the network, such as the number of nodes, and returns a Python dictionary that holds all the parts of the network. The simulate_sc_net function then simulates the network up to a given time and writes a log of the run. It also calculates results for the whole network, such as the total cost, the revenue and the profit. Let's use these functions to build and simulate our supply chain. # create a supply chain network supplychainnet = scm.create_sc_net(nodes=[supplier1, distributor1], links=[link1], demands=[demand1]) # simulate for 20 days supplychainnet = scm.simulate_sc_net(supplychainnet, sim_time=20, logging=True) Review Results After the simulation, look at supplychainnet to see the results. When simulate_sc_net runs with logging=True (the default), the simulation log is shown in the console and saved to a file named simulation_trace.log in the folder you run the script from. Each node has its own logger, and you can switch it on or off with logging=True or logging=False when you create the node. To switch all simulation logs on or off at once, call scm.global_logger.enable_logging() or scm.global_logger.disable_logging() . Repeating the same run. Some parts of the simulation can be random, for example disruptions that start at random ( failure_p on a node, and the similar settings on a Link ). By default, every run draws different random numbers, so two runs in a row may give slightly different results. If you want to repeat exactly the same run , for instance to compare two policies under the same sequence of disruptions, call scm.set_seed(n) once before you build the network. For even finer control, you can also create your own random number generator with random.Random() and pass it as the rng argument when you create a node or a link. That node or link then uses its own random numbers, independent of the rest. Below is an example of a simulation log from this program. At the end of the log, the results for the whole network are printed. They are added up from every node and include the following. Holding cost ( inventory_carry_cost ) What the sites paid for the units they received ( inventory_spend_cost ) Transportation cost Total cost Revenue Profit What each result means is listed under simulate_sc_net in the API reference . INFO D1 - 0.0000:D1: Inventory levels:50, on hand:50 INFO D1 - 0.0000:D1:Replenishing inventory from supplier:Supplier1, order placed for 100 units. INFO D1 - 0.0000:D1:shipment in transit from supplier:Supplier1. INFO d1 - 0.0000:d1:Customer1:Order quantity:10, available. INFO D1 - 0.0000:D1: Inventory levels:40, on hand:140 INFO d1 - 1.0000:d1:Customer2:Order quantity:10, available. INFO D1 - 1.0000:D1: Inventory levels:30, on hand:130 INFO D1 - 2.0000:D1:Inventory replenished. reorder_quantity=100, Inventory levels:130 INFO d1 - 2.0000:d1:Customer3:Order quantity:10, available. INFO D1 - 2.0000:D1: Inventory levels:120, on hand:120 INFO d1 - 3.0000:d1:Customer4:Order quantity:10, available. docs.title: SupplyNetPy in 10 Minutes

docs.text: SupplyNetPy can be installed using pip. pip install supplynetpy
docs.title: Installation

docs.text: Follow these steps to create and simulate a basic supply chain with an infinite supplier, a distributor and a customer demand.
docs.title: Quick Start, Building a Simple Supply Chain with Three Nodes

docs.text: import SupplyNetPy.Components as scm The Components module gives you the building blocks of a supply chain. These are the nodes (raw-material suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, warehouses and retailers), products and inventories, customer demands, and the links that connect them. You assemble them into a model that fits your scenario. The words used on this page are explained in the Glossary .
docs.title: Import the Library

docs.text: Let us create an infinite supplier, a supplier that never runs out and so can supply any number of units to its buyers. It needs an ID, a name and a node type. To make it an infinite supplier, set the node type to infinite_supplier . supplier1 = {'ID': 'S1', 'name': 'Supplier1', 'node_type': 'infinite_supplier'} Next, a distributor that buys units from the supplier. Its settings include the ID, the name, the capacity, the replenishment policy and its parameters, and the buy and sell prices. distributor1 = {'ID': 'D1', 'name': 'Distributor1', 'node_type': 'distributor', 'capacity': 150, 'initial_level': 50, 'inventory_holding_cost': 0.2, 'replenishment_policy': scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s':100,'S':150}, 'product_buy_price': 100,'product_sell_price': 105} For a manufacturer, distributor, warehouse or retailer, we give its replenishment policy (the rule it follows to decide when to place a replenishment order and how many units to order) and the policy's parameters. The policies are subclasses of the InventoryReplenishment class, which you can also subclass to define your own. SupplyNetPy has the following replenishment policies. The (s, S) policy . When the inventory position falls to s or below, order enough units to bring it back up to S. Parameters {s, S}, class SSReplenishment . The (s, S) policy with a safety stock . The same, with the safety stock added to both s and S. Parameters {s, S, safety_stock}, class SSReplenishment . The (R, Q) policy . When the inventory position falls to R or below, order a fixed Q units. Parameters {R, Q}, class RQReplenishment . The periodic policy . Every T time units, order Q units. Parameters {T, Q}, class PeriodicReplenishment . The periodic policy with a safety stock . The same, but if the inventory level is below the safety stock, the order also includes the units needed to bring it back up to the safety stock. Parameters {T, Q, safety_stock}, class PeriodicReplenishment . The inventory position is the inventory level, plus the units in transit, minus the units still owed. By default, the (s, S) and (R, Q) policies check it each time the inventory drops.
docs.title: Create Nodes

docs.text: A link is created as shown below. Its settings include the transportation cost and the lead time. The lead time can be a number, or a function with no arguments that returns one lead time each time it is called, for example a random one drawn from a distribution of your choice. For a constant lead time, a Python lambda such as lambda: 2 is enough. link1 = {'ID': 'L1', 'source': 'S1', 'sink': 'D1', 'cost': 5, 'lead_time': lambda: 2}
docs.title: Create a Link

docs.text: A customer demand is created by giving an ID, a name, the site the customers order from, how often orders arrive, and how many units each order is for. The "how often" and "how many" values are each given as a small function with no arguments that returns a number. If you want randomness, for example customer orders arriving at times drawn from an exponential distribution, write a function that samples from that distribution and returns one number per call. If you want a fixed value, just use a lambda such as lambda: 1 . A customer demand can be at any site except a raw-material supplier, usually a retailer or a distributor. The example below sets up a steady demand of 10 units every time unit (read here as a day) at distributor D1. demand1 = {'ID': 'd1', 'name': 'Demand1', 'order_arrival_model': lambda: 1, 'order_quantity_model': lambda: 10, 'demand_node': 'D1'}
docs.title: Specify Demand

docs.text: To create and simulate the supply chain, use the create_sc_net function to create the nodes and assemble them into a network. This function also records information about the network, such as the number of nodes, and returns a Python dictionary that holds all the parts of the network. The simulate_sc_net function then simulates the network up to a given time and writes a log of the run. It also calculates results for the whole network, such as the total cost, the revenue and the profit. Let's use these functions to build and simulate our supply chain. # create a supply chain network supplychainnet = scm.create_sc_net(nodes=[supplier1, distributor1], links=[link1], demands=[demand1]) # simulate for 20 days supplychainnet = scm.simulate_sc_net(supplychainnet, sim_time=20, logging=True)
docs.title: Assemble and Simulate the Network

docs.text: After the simulation, look at supplychainnet to see the results. When simulate_sc_net runs with logging=True (the default), the simulation log is shown in the console and saved to a file named simulation_trace.log in the folder you run the script from. Each node has its own logger, and you can switch it on or off with logging=True or logging=False when you create the node. To switch all simulation logs on or off at once, call scm.global_logger.enable_logging() or scm.global_logger.disable_logging() . Repeating the same run. Some parts of the simulation can be random, for example disruptions that start at random ( failure_p on a node, and the similar settings on a Link ). By default, every run draws different random numbers, so two runs in a row may give slightly different results. If you want to repeat exactly the same run , for instance to compare two policies under the same sequence of disruptions, call scm.set_seed(n) once before you build the network. For even finer control, you can also create your own random number generator with random.Random() and pass it as the rng argument when you create a node or a link. That node or link then uses its own random numbers, independent of the rest. Below is an example of a simulation log from this program. At the end of the log, the results for the whole network are printed. They are added up from every node and include the following.
