docs.title: Another Approach, Creating the Objects Yourself

docs.text: SupplyNetPy API Reference SupplyNetPy includes a submodule called Components , which helps you create supply chain networks by providing their parts, such as nodes, links and customer demands, and assembling them into a network. The Components module contains three submodules, core , logger and utilities . The pages that follow describe each of them, module by module and class by class. The words used on these pages are explained in the Glossary . The core module creates the parts of a supply chain. It includes the classes RawMaterial , Product , Inventory , Node , Link , Supplier , Manufacturer , InventoryNode and Demand , the statistics of a node ( Statistics ) and of a link ( LinkStatistics ), the replenishment policies ( SSReplenishment , RQReplenishment , PeriodicReplenishment ), and the supplier-selection policies ( SelectFirst , SelectAvailable , SelectCheapest , SelectFastest , SelectProbabilistic ). Every node created with these classes runs in a SimPy environment. The Inventory class keeps the inventory of a site, one product per inventory, in a SimPy Container , and can also record how the inventory level changes. For a different kind of inventory with custom behavior, extend Inventory or SimPy Container . The node_type of a node is checked against the NodeType enum, and can be given as a string in any letter case or as an enum member such as scm.NodeType.SUPPLIER . The core module also exports set_seed(seed) , which seeds the random numbers the whole library uses, so runs can be repeated exactly. The logger module keeps the simulation logs. It includes the GlobalLogger class, a common logger for all the parts of the simulation. You can set it up to save logs to a file or to print them to the console. A global_logger instance for the whole package is also exported, so you can call scm.global_logger.disable_logging() or scm.global_logger.enable_logging() to switch all simulation logs off or on at once. The utilities module provides useful Python functions that save manual work. It contains functions for creating supply chains ( create_sc_net ), running simulations ( simulate_sc_net ), starting the statistics again after a warm-up ( reset_stats ), and inspecting or drawing the resulting network ( get_sc_net_info , print_node_wise_performance , print_link_wise_performance , visualize_sc_net ). It also contains the Network class, which holds a network and its results. create_sc_net builds a network either from plain dict descriptions or from ready made Node , Link and Demand objects, but each of its lists must use only one of the two. Each submodule lists its public names in __all__ , and SupplyNetPy.Components exports exactly these names. Guides For tasks that use several parts together, the User Guide explains how to do them step by step. Customer Demand . How often customers order and how many units, demand from recorded data, what customers do when the site is short, and delivering their orders. Replenishment Policies . Choosing a built in policy, when it checks, safety stock, and writing your own policy. Supplier Selection . Choosing a supplier-selection policy, fixed and dynamic mode, choosing suppliers at random, and writing your own policy. Disruptions . Scheduled and random disruptions of sites and links, what happens to orders, and units lost in a disruption. Perishable Products . Shelf life, batches and their manufacturing dates, when units expire, and expired units in the statistics. Statistics and Results . Results for the whole network, statistics of nodes and links, and warm-ups. Running Experiments . Replications, seeds, comparing settings fairly, confidence intervals, and running replications in parallel. SupplyNetPy Library Hierarchy SupplyNetPy ├── Components │ ├── core.py │ ├── logger.py │ ├── utilities.py

The node_type of a node is checked against the NodeType enum, and can be given as a string in any letter case or as an enum member such as scm.NodeType.SUPPLIER . The core module also exports set_seed(seed) , which seeds the random numbers the whole library uses, so runs can be repeated exactly. The logger module keeps the simulation logs. It includes the GlobalLogger class, a common logger for all the parts of the simulation. You can set it up to save logs to a file or to print them to the console. A global_logger instance for the whole package is also exported, so you can call scm.global_logger.disable_logging() or scm.global_logger.enable_logging() to switch all simulation logs off or on at once. The utilities module provides useful Python functions that save manual work. It contains functions for creating supply chains ( create_sc_net ), running simulations ( simulate_sc_net ), starting the statistics again after a warm-up ( reset_stats ), and inspecting or drawing the resulting network ( get_sc_net_info , print_node_wise_performance , print_link_wise_performance , visualize_sc_net ). It also contains the Network class, which holds a network and its results. create_sc_net builds a network either from plain dict descriptions or from ready made Node , Link and Demand objects, but each of its lists must use only one of the two. Each submodule lists its public names in __all__ , and SupplyNetPy.Components exports exactly these names.

Choosing a built in policy, when it checks, safety stock, and writing your own policy. Supplier Selection . Choosing a supplier-selection policy, fixed and dynamic mode, choosing suppliers at random, and writing your own policy. Disruptions . Scheduled and random disruptions of sites and links, what happens to orders, and units lost in a disruption. Perishable Products . Shelf life, batches and their manufacturing dates, when units expire, and expired units in the statistics. Statistics and Results . Results for the whole network, statistics of nodes and links, and warm-ups. Running Experiments . Replications, seeds, comparing settings fairly, confidence intervals, and running replications in parallel.

docs.text: SupplyNetPy Components.core Module The Components.core module provides the foundational building blocks for modeling and simulating supply chain networks in SupplyNetPy. It defines key classes representing entities and their interactions within a supply chain. SupplyNetPy.Components.core NodeType Bases: str , Enum Canonical node types accepted by Node and create_sc_net . NodeType is a str subclass, so every existing comparison against a literal string ( node.node_type == "demand" , "supplier" in node.node_type , node.node_type.lower() ) continues to work unchanged. Users can pass either a plain string (case-insensitive, via _missing_ ) or a NodeType member: scm.Supplier(env=env, ID="S1", name="S1", node_type="supplier") scm.Supplier(env=env, ID="S1", name="S1", node_type=scm.NodeType.SUPPLIER) Some types are different names for the same kind of node: "manufacturer" and "factory" both create a manufacturer, and "warehouse" , "distributor" , "retailer" , "store" and "shop" all create an InventoryNode . "supplier" creates a raw-material supplier and "infinite_supplier" an infinite supplier. create_sc_net looks up which class to create for each type in a table ( _NODE_DISPATCH in utilities.py ). To add a new node type, add it to this enum and add an entry to that table. NamedEntity The NamedEntity class provides a standardized way to display names of the objects in the supply chain model. When printed or displayed, the object will show its name (if defined), otherwise its ID , or the class name as a fallback. This improves the readability and interpretability of simulation outputs by ensuring objects are easily identifiable. Every link has one, as link.stats , created with the link. Node statistics say how much a site ordered and received in total, but not from whom. A buyer with two suppliers has a link to each, and each link counts only the orders sent over it. A site finds the links it orders over in node.suppliers , and the links its buyers order over in node.buyers . The same events are counted in the node statistics too, so the totals over a buyer's links add up to the buyer's own figures. Customers do not order over links, so customer orders are not in any link (each Demand has its own statistics). Running totals are kept, not a record of each order. Values worked out when read are properties, and are None when there is nothing to divide by (a fill rate of 0 would look like a very bad link). Two spreads of order sizes. Both are sample standard deviations (how far values usually are from their average, dividing by one less than the number of values), and both are None with fewer than two values. order_size_std takes one value per order: the size of each order. units_per_time_unit_std takes one value per time unit: the units ordered in that time unit, with time units in which nothing was ordered counting as 0. The two can disagree completely. A distributor that orders 60 units at time 3 and 60 units at time 7, and nothing in between, has an order_size_std of 0 (every order is the same size) but a large units_per_time_unit_std (the orders come in bursts). The bullwhip effect (orders becoming more uneven as they pass from the customers towards the raw-material suppliers) is measured per time unit: compare a link's units_per_time_unit_std with the spread of customer demand per time unit. A policy usually checks the node's inventory position each time the node's inventory drops (the inventory_drop event), or at fixed intervals. How a custom policy should talk to its node. A policy should use these four helper methods instead of reaching into the node's internal attributes: self.node.position() — the inventory position: inventory level plus units in transit, minus units the node still owes (to other sites and to waiting customers). self.node.place_order(quantity) — picks a supplier using the node's supplier-selection policy and places the replenishment order. Link.available_quantity() — lets a supplier-selection policy check a supplier's inventory level without reading link.source.inventory.level directly. Sticking to these helpers keeps a policy from depending on how a particular node is built, so it works with any future Node type that offers the same methods. Each policy is a subclass that overrides the select method with its own rule. A site gives its policy the mode and the settings ( supplier_selection_param ) only when the user gives them, so each policy keeps its own default mode. For example, a retailer that sends half of its orders to distributor D1, 30% to D2 and 20% to D3 is given supplier_selection_param={"probabilities": {"D1": 0.5, "D2": 0.3, "D3": 0.2}} . The probabilities are keyed by supplier ID ( link.source.ID ), so they can be given before the links exist, and they must sum to 1. A supplier with probability 0 is never chosen. For every order the policy draws exactly one random number u between 0 and 1 and puts the probabilities side by side, in the order the links to the suppliers were created: with 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2, u below 0.5 chooses the first supplier, u from 0.5 to below 0.8 the second, and the rest the third. One number per order means that two runs with the same seed see the same numbers, so changing a probability a little changes only the few orders whose number falls near a boundary. The probabilities are the shares of the orders while every supplier can take orders. When a supplier or the link to it is disrupted, on_disruption decides what happens: "rescale" (the default): the order goes to one of the other suppliers, which keep their ratios. With 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 and the first supplier disrupted, the other two get 0.6 and 0.4. "block" : the draw uses the given probabilities as they are. If it chooses a disrupted supplier, the order is not placed and is counted as blocked ; the site orders again when a supplier or a link recovers, or when its inventory drops. So with disruptions, the shares of the orders at the end of a run differ from the probabilities. The link statistics ( link.stats ) record the real shares. The stored probabilities never change. The mode is always "dynamic" (a new choice for every order); "fixed" would keep the first random choice for ever, so it is rejected. When a site cannot fill an order at once, the customer either leaves without the units or, if a tolerance is set, waits for them. It supports: a lead time and a delivery cost for each customer order, partial deliveries for customers who wait ( order_min_split_ratio ), backorders at the site for customers who wait. Behavior Customer orders arrive at the site with the times and sizes given by order_arrival_model and order_quantity_model . If the site's inventory can fill an order, it is delivered at once. If not, a shortage is recorded at the site, and with no tolerance (the default), the customer leaves without the units; with consume_available , the customer takes the units that are there and leaves; with a tolerance, the customer waits for the units, up to the tolerance, and the order counts as a backorder at the site while they wait. Returns: – None Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 5282 5283 5284 5285 5286 5287 5288 5289 5290 5291 5292 5293 5294 5295 5296 5297 5298 5299 5300 5301 5302 5303 5304 5305 5306 5307 5308 5309 5310 5311 5312 5313 5314 5315 5316 5317 5318 5319 5320 5321 5322 5323 5324 5325 5326 5327 5328 5329 5330 5331 5332 5333 5334 5335 5336 5337 5338 5339 5340 5341 5342 5343 5344 5345 5346 5347 5348 5349 5350 5351 5352 5353 5354 5355 5356 5357 5358 5359 5360 5361 5362 5363 5364 5365 5366 5367 5368 5369 5370 5371 5372 5373 5374 5375 5376 5377 5378 5379 5380 5381 def wait_for_order ( self , customer_id , order_quantity ): """ Let a customer wait for the units of their order, up to their tolerance. While waiting, the customer's order is counted as a backorder at the site. The customer checks again each time units are added to the site's inventory. If the tolerance is infinite, the customer waits until the order is filled. Otherwise, the customer leaves as soon as their tolerance runs out, even if no new units have arrived, and whatever they were still owed is taken off the site's backorders. Parameters: order_quantity (float): Units ordered. customer_id (int): Customer ID for logging purposes. Attributes: customer_id (int): Customer ID for logging purposes. order_quantity (float): Units ordered. Returns: None """ self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . ID } :Customer { customer_id } :Order quantity: { order_quantity } not available! Order will be split if split ratio is provided." ) self . demand_node . stats . update_stats ( backorder = [ 1 , order_quantity ]) arrived = self . env . now # when the order arrived, for the waiting time if ( not self . demand_node . inventory_drop . triggered ): self . demand_node . inventory_drop . succeed () # a backorder lowers the inventory position, so let the replenishment policy check partial = order_quantity if self . min_split < 1 : partial = int ( order_quantity * self . min_split ) # The customer will wait until this moment and no longer. deadline = self . env . now + self . customer_tolerance while True : available = self . _available () # When there is enough, the units are taken out of the inventory # right here, in the same step as the check, and not later inside # ``_process_delivery``. That process only starts once this step is # over. If one delivery wakes several waiting customers at the same # moment, each of them would otherwise check the inventory before # any of them had taken anything, all would see the same units, and # all would think those units were theirs. if order_quantity <= available : # check if remaining order quantity is available get_event , _ = self . demand_node . inventory . get ( order_quantity ) self . env . process ( self . _process_delivery ( order_quantity , customer_id , get_event )) self . demand_node . stats . update_stats ( backorder = [ - 1 , - order_quantity ], waiting_time = self . env . now - arrived ) order_quantity = 0 break # ``partial`` can round down to 0 for a small order, so also check # that there is at least one unit to send. Asking the inventory for # 0 units is an error in SimPy. elif available > 0 and available >= partial : # or else at least the smallest partial delivery is there get_event , _ = self . demand_node . inventory . get ( available ) self . env . process ( self . _process_delivery ( available , customer_id , get_event )) # Partial delivery: the backorder still counts as 1 order (one customer # still waiting), and only its units go down. Each delivery adds 1 to the # order counts of fulfillment_received and demand_fulfilled (inside # _process_delivery), so 1 is taken off them here: the customer's order is # counted once, when it is finally filled. self . demand_node . stats . update_stats ( backorder = [ 0 , - available ], demand_fulfilled = [ - 1 , 0 ]) self . stats . update_stats ( fulfillment_received = [ - 1 , 0 ]) order_quantity -= available # update order quantity # Otherwise there is not enough yet, and the customer keeps waiting. # No shortage is recorded here: it was recorded once, when the order # arrived (in _enqueue_for_tolerance). Recording it again on every # check would count the same missing units many times. if self . env . now >= deadline : break # the customer's tolerance has run out # Wait for whichever comes first: new units arriving at the site, or # the end of the customer's tolerance. Without the second part, a # customer would only notice that their tolerance had run out when # units next arrived — and if none ever arrived, they would wait # (and stay counted as a backorder) forever. raised_event = self . demand_node . inventory_raised # the node's current "inventory raised" signal if deadline == float ( 'inf' ): yield raised_event # infinite tolerance: only new units can end the wait else : yield raised_event | self . env . timeout ( deadline - self . env . now ) # The "units arrived" signal can fire only once, so after it fires it # is swapped for a fresh one. Several customers may be waiting on the # same signal; only the first one to wake should swap it. If a later # customer swapped it again, the customers who had already moved on # to the first fresh signal would be left waiting on one that never # fires. Hence the check that the node still holds the signal we # waited on. If we woke because our tolerance ran out instead, the # signal has not fired and must be left alone for the others. if raised_event . triggered and self . demand_node . inventory_raised is raised_event : self . demand_node . inventory_raised = self . env . event () if order_quantity > 0 : # the customer gives up and leaves without the rest of the order # They are no longer waiting, so take what they were still owed off # the site's current backorders. (The count drops by 1 even after # partial deliveries: one customer is one backorder until they are # fully served or leave.) Without this, the site would keep placing # replenishment orders for a customer who has already gone. # The units they were still owed are never delivered: a lost sale. self . demand_node . stats . update_stats ( backorder = [ - 1 , - order_quantity ], lost_sales = [ 1 , order_quantity ]) self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . ID } :Customer { customer_id } : remaining order quantity: { order_quantity } not available! Customer leaves." ) customer customer ( customer_id , order_quantity ) Handle one customer order, by passing it to the helper for its case: the site is disrupted: the order is not placed. A disrupted site takes no new orders, so this is a sale it loses because of the disruption, recorded in its disruption_lost_sales (not as demand received, shortage or backorder). Customers who were already waiting when the disruption started keep waiting, and deliveries already on their way still arrive; the site can fill the whole order: _serve_in_full ; otherwise, with consume_available and some units there: _serve_partial_consume ; otherwise, for a customer with a tolerance: _enqueue_for_tolerance (or _discard_unservable if the order is too big for the site ever to hold); otherwise: _serve_no_tolerance . Returns: – None Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 5479 5480 5481 5482 5483 5484 5485 5486 5487 5488 5489 5490 5491 5492 5493 5494 5495 5496 5497 5498 5499 5500 5501 5502 5503 5504 5505 5506 5507 5508 5509 5510 5511 5512 5513 5514 5515 5516 5517 5518 5519 5520 5521 5522 5523 5524 5525 5526 5527 5528 5529 5530 def customer ( self , customer_id , order_quantity ): """ Handle one customer order, by passing it to the helper for its case: - the site is disrupted: the order is not placed. A disrupted site takes no new orders, so this is a sale it loses because of the disruption, recorded in its ``disruption_lost_sales`` (not as demand received, shortage or backorder). Customers who were already waiting when the disruption started keep waiting, and deliveries already on their way still arrive; - the site can fill the whole order: ``_serve_in_full``; - otherwise, with ``consume_available`` and some units there: ``_serve_partial_consume``; - otherwise, for a customer with a tolerance: ``_enqueue_for_tolerance`` (or ``_discard_unservable`` if the order is too big for the site ever to hold); - otherwise: ``_serve_no_tolerance``. Parameters: customer_id (int): Customer ID for logging purposes. order_quantity (float): Units ordered. Returns: None """ if self . demand_node . node_status != "active" : # A disrupted site takes no new orders, from other sites or from # customers (the same rule as Node.place_order). The customer goes # away, and the site loses the sale. This is not a shortage: the site # may have the units, it just cannot take the order. Nothing else is # recorded, and the customer's own demand_placed does not count it, # as for a replenishment order that is not placed. self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . ID } :Customer { customer_id } : { self . demand_node . ID } is disrupted, order of { order_quantity } units not placed (lost sale)." ) self . demand_node . stats . update_stats ( disruption_lost_sales = [ 1 , order_quantity ]) return available = self . _available () self . stats . update_stats ( demand_placed = [ 1 , order_quantity ]) # The smallest part this customer will take: the whole order when no # partial delivery is allowed (min_split >= 1), otherwise the smallest # partial delivery. This matches how ``wait_for_order`` computes ``partial``. min_chunk = order_quantity if self . min_split >= 1 else int ( order_quantity * self . min_split ) if order_quantity <= available : yield from self . _serve_in_full ( order_quantity , customer_id ) elif self . consume_available and available > 0 : yield from self . _serve_partial_consume ( order_quantity , available , customer_id ) elif self . customer_tolerance > 0 : if min_chunk > self . demand_node . inventory . capacity : # The order can never be served — even a full inventory cannot # cover the smallest part the customer accepts. Discard it # rather than create a backorder that would lead to a # replenishment order the inventory can't hold. yield from self . _discard_unservable ( order_quantity , customer_id ) else : yield from self . _enqueue_for_tolerance ( order_quantity , available , customer_id ) else : yield from self . _serve_no_tolerance ( order_quantity , available , customer_id ) behavior behavior () Create customer orders for the whole simulation: start a customer with an order of order_quantity_model() units, wait order_arrival_model() time units, and repeat. So the first customer order arrives at time 0. Number ): global_logger . error ( f "function { name } () must return a number (an int or a float)." ) raise ValueError ( f "function { name } () must be a number (an int or a float)." ) ensure_numeric_callable ensure_numeric_callable ( name : str , value ) Turn a value that is "a number, or a zero-arg function returning a number" into a zero-arg function. Many constructors accept either a plain number or a zero-arg function (lead times, arrival intervals, recovery times). The earlier version simply did if not callable(value): value = lambda val=value: val which accepted any function at all — even a class like int or a generator function — so the later value() call could fail deep inside a running simulation, far from where the mistake was made. This helper avoids that by calling the function once when it is set up and checking the result is a real number, so a bad value is reported right away, at construction, with a clear message naming the parameter at fault. Note The validation invocation samples the callable once at construction time. For stateful generators or iterators (rather than pure functions) this advances state before the simulation starts; if that matters, wrap the iterator in a closure that materialises the first sample lazily, or pass a numeric scalar instead. Parameters: name (str): Parameter name used in error messages. value: A number or a zero-arg callable returning a number. Returns: callable: A zero-arg callable. For stateful generators or iterators (rather than pure functions) this advances state before the simulation starts; if that matters, wrap the iterator in a closure that materialises the first sample lazily, or pass a numeric scalar instead. docs.text: The Components.core module provides the foundational building blocks for modeling and simulating supply chain networks in SupplyNetPy. It defines key classes representing entities and their interactions within a supply chain.
docs.title: SupplyNetPy Components.core Module

docs.text: Bases: str , Enum Canonical node types accepted by Node and create_sc_net . NodeType is a str subclass, so every existing comparison against a literal string ( node.node_type == "demand" , "supplier" in node.node_type , node.node_type.lower() ) continues to work unchanged. Users can pass either a plain string (case-insensitive, via _missing_ ) or a NodeType member: scm.Supplier(env=env, ID="S1", name="S1", node_type="supplier") scm.Supplier(env=env, ID="S1", name="S1", node_type=scm.NodeType.SUPPLIER) Some types are different names for the same kind of node: "manufacturer" and "factory" both create a manufacturer, and "warehouse" , "distributor" , "retailer" , "store" and "shop" all create an InventoryNode . "supplier" creates a raw-material supplier and "infinite_supplier" an infinite supplier. create_sc_net looks up which class to create for each type in a table ( _NODE_DISPATCH in utilities.py ). To add a new node type, add it to this enum and add an entry to that table.

docs.text: The NamedEntity class provides a standardized way to display names of the objects in the supply chain model. When printed or displayed, the object will show its name (if defined), otherwise its ID , or the class name as a fallback. This improves the readability and interpretability of simulation outputs by ensuring objects are easily identifiable. Methods: Name Description __str__ returns the name of the object if available, otherwise returns the class name __repr__ returns the name of the object if available, otherwise returns the class name

docs.text: Statistics ( node : object , periodic_update : bool = False , period : float = 1 ) Bases: InfoMixin The Statistics class tracks and summarizes key performance indicators for each node in the supply chain. It monitors essential metrics such as demand, inventory levels, shortages, backorders, costs, revenue, and profit. The class supports both automatic periodic updates and manual updates through the update_stats method, which can be called at any point in the simulation to immediately record changes. The _info_keys / _stats_keys / _cost_components declarations are class-level, making the tracked set of KPIs declaratively discoverable in one place. Statistics.__init__ copies the _stats_keys and _cost_components lists to the instance before any per-node extension runs ( Supplier.__init__ and Manufacturer.__init__ append their own subclass-specific KPIs), so those appends never leak into the class-level list and cross-contaminate other Statistics instances. docs.text: reset () Start the statistics again from zero, for example after a warm-up. A warm-up is an opening stretch of a run that is left out of the statistics, because a run starts in an unusual state (nothing in transit, no orders waiting). Run for the warm-up period, call reset() on each node, and carry on running. The simulation itself carries on unchanged; only the counting starts again: Running totals (orders, units, costs, shortage, expired units and so on) are set to zero, including those a Supplier or Manufacturer adds. Values that describe the present ( _live_keys ) are kept: backorder , what the node owes right now, and inventory_level , which is read again from the inventory. The holding cost is brought up to date first, so that after the reset it covers only the time since the reset. The once-per-time-unit record of the inventory level ( inventory.instantaneous_levels ) starts again. The inventory itself (inventory level, units in transit, waiting orders) is not touched. Each event is counted when it happens. So an order placed before the reset and received after it counts as received but not as placed, and units bought before the reset that expire after it count as expired units after it. A partial delivery to a customer takes 1 off the order count of demand_fulfilled when it is sent and adds 1 back when it arrives; if the reset falls in between, that customer order is counted twice in the order count (the units are counted correctly). Returns: – None Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 521 522 523 524 525 526 527 528 529 530 531 532 533 534 535 536 537 538 539 540 541 542 543 544 545 546 547 548 549 550 551 552 553 554 555 556 557 558 559 560 561 562 563 564 565 566 567 568 569 570 571 572 573 574 575 576 577 578 579 580 581 582 583 584 585 586 587 588 589 590 591 592 593 594 595 596 597 598 599 600 601 602 603 604 605 606 607 608 609 def reset ( self ): """ Start the statistics again from zero, for example after a warm-up. A warm-up is an opening stretch of a run that is left out of the statistics, because a run starts in an unusual state (nothing in transit, no orders waiting). Run for the warm-up period, call ``reset()`` on each node, and carry on running. The simulation itself carries on unchanged; only the counting starts again: - Running totals (orders, units, costs, shortage, expired units and so on) are set to zero, including those a ``Supplier`` or ``Manufacturer`` adds. - Values that describe the present (``_live_keys``) are kept: ``backorder``, what the node owes right now, and ``inventory_level``, which is read again from the inventory. - The holding cost is brought up to date first, so that after the reset it covers only the time since the reset. - The once-per-time-unit record of the inventory level (``inventory.instantaneous_levels``) starts again. - The inventory itself (inventory level, units in transit, waiting orders) is not touched. Each event is counted when it happens. So an order placed before the reset and received after it counts as received but not as placed, and units bought before the reset that expire after it count as expired units after it. A partial delivery to a customer takes 1 off the order count of ``demand_fulfilled`` when it is sent and adds 1 back when it arrives; if the reset falls in between, that customer order is counted twice in the order count (the units are counted correctly). Parameters: None Returns: None """ inventory = getattr ( self . node , 'inventory' , None ) # An infinite inventory (an infinite supplier) has no holding cost and # no inventory level worth recording, as in update_stats. finite_inventory = inventory is not None and inventory . level != float ( 'inf' ) if finite_inventory : # Charge the holding cost up to now, so that no time before the # reset is charged after it. inventory . update_carry_cost () # Pass 1: zero every statistic listed in _stats_keys (the list of # tracked statistics), except the values that describe the present and # the values worked out when read (properties such as # ``avg_inventory_level``), which follow from the totals. for key in self . _stats_keys : if not hasattr ( self , key ) or key == "name" or key in self . _live_keys : continue if isinstance ( getattr ( type ( self ), key , None ), property ): continue current = getattr ( self , key ) if isinstance ( current , list ): setattr ( self , key , [ 0 , 0 ]) elif isinstance ( current , ( int , float )): setattr ( self , key , 0 ) # Pass 2: a safety net for any counter that is not in the tracked list # but used to be reset by the old "reset everything" sweep. It looks # only at this Statistics object, never at the node's units or orders. for key , value in vars ( self ) . items (): if key . startswith ( "_" ) or key in self . _stats_keys or key in self . _live_keys : continue if isinstance ( value , list ): setattr ( self , key , [ 0 , 0 ]) elif isinstance ( value , ( int , float )): setattr ( self , key , 0 ) # Some counters live on the Inventory object, not on Statistics, so they # have to be reset here by hand. If you add a new Inventory counter that # should reset, add it to this block (or move the counter onto # Statistics by listing it in _stats_keys). if inventory is not None : inventory . carry_cost = 0 inventory . waste = 0 inventory . level_time = 0 inventory . zero_level_time = 0 inventory . instantaneous_levels = [] if finite_inventory : self . inventory_level = inventory . level # The clock starts again, so every average covers only the time since # the reset. A disruption going on now is counted from now on; it does # not add to ``disruptions``, because it started before the reset. now = self . node . env . now self . start_time = now self . _disrupted_time = 0 if self . _disrupted_since is not None : self . _disrupted_since = now

docs.text: LinkStatistics ( link ) Bases: InfoMixin The LinkStatistics class records what flows over one link: the replenishment orders its buyer placed over it, what arrived, how long the orders waited and travelled, what they cost, and the link's own disruptions. Every link has one, as link.stats , created with the link. Node statistics say how much a site ordered and received in total, but not from whom. A buyer with two suppliers has a link to each, and each link counts only the orders sent over it. A site finds the links it orders over in node.suppliers , and the links its buyers order over in node.buyers . The same events are counted in the node statistics too, so the totals over a buyer's links add up to the buyer's own figures. Customers do not order over links, so customer orders are not in any link (each Demand has its own statistics). Running totals are kept, not a record of each order. Values worked out when read are properties, and are None when there is nothing to divide by (a fill rate of 0 would look like a very bad link). Two spreads of order sizes. Both are sample standard deviations (how far values usually are from their average, dividing by one less than the number of values), and both are None with fewer than two values. order_size_std takes one value per order: the size of each order. units_per_time_unit_std takes one value per time unit: the units ordered in that time unit, with time units in which nothing was ordered counting as 0. The two can disagree completely. A distributor that orders 60 units at time 3 and 60 units at time 7, and nothing in between, has an order_size_std of 0 (every order is the same size) but a large units_per_time_unit_std (the orders come in bursts). The bullwhip effect (orders becoming more uneven as they pass from the customers towards the raw-material suppliers) is measured per time unit: compare a link's units_per_time_unit_std with the spread of customer demand per time unit. Parameters: link ( Link ) – The link whose statistics these are. Attributes: link ( Link ) – The link whose statistics these are. name ( str ) – Name of the statistics object: the link's ID followed by " statistics". start_time ( float ) – When counting began: the time the link was created, or the last reset . elapsed_time ( float ) – Time since start_time . Unlike backorder , it is a running total, so it still counts an order once the order is served. blocked ( list ) – Orders the buyer was about to send over this link but could not place, because the link or the supplier's site was disrupted by then, as [number of orders, units]. Orders blocked before any link was chosen (every supplier disrupted) are counted only in the buyer's node statistics. Worked out when read. avg_order_cycle_time ( float ) – Average time from placing an order until it arrives: avg_waiting_time + avg_lead_time . Worked out when read. fill_rate ( float ) – Share of the units ordered that the supplier sent at once: 1 - waited[1] / demand_placed[1] . An order that had to wait counts as not sent at once, even if part of it was there. Worked out when read. order_fill_rate ( float ) – The same share counted in orders: 1 - waited[0] / demand_placed[0] . Worked out when read. orders_per_time_unit ( float ) – Orders placed per time unit: demand_placed[0] / elapsed_time . Worked out when read. units_per_time_unit ( float ) – Units ordered per time unit: demand_placed[1] / elapsed_time . Worked out when read. order_size_mean ( float ) – Average size of the orders placed. Worked out when read. order_size_std ( float ) – Standard deviation of the size of the orders placed (see above). Worked out when read. units_per_time_unit_std ( float ) – Standard deviation of the units ordered in each time unit (see above). Time units are counted from start_time and are 1 long. The time unit still going on is left out. docs.text: reset () Start the statistics again from zero, for example after a warm-up (see Statistics.reset ). The simulation carries on unchanged; only the counting starts again: Running totals and both spreads of order sizes are set to zero. backorder is kept: orders waiting at the reset are still waiting after it. start_time becomes now, so every average and every value per time unit covers only the time since the reset. A disruption going on now is counted from now on. It does not add to disruptions , because it started before the reset. Each event is counted when it happens. So an order placed before the reset and received after it counts as received but not as placed. The averages stay correct, because each one divides by a count recorded at the same moment as its total. Returns: – None Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 1032 1033 1034 1035 1036 1037 1038 1039 1040 1041 1042 1043 1044 1045 1046 1047 1048 1049 1050 1051 1052 1053 1054 1055 1056 1057 1058 1059 1060 1061 def reset ( self ): """ Start the statistics again from zero, for example after a warm-up (see ``Statistics.reset``). The simulation carries on unchanged; only the counting starts again: - Running totals and both spreads of order sizes are set to zero. - ``backorder`` is kept: orders waiting at the reset are still waiting after it. - ``start_time`` becomes now, so every average and every value per time unit covers only the time since the reset. - A disruption going on now is counted from now on. It does not add to ``disruptions``, because it started before the reset. Each event is counted when it happens. So an order placed before the reset and received after it counts as received but not as placed. The averages stay correct, because each one divides by a count recorded at the same moment as its total. Parameters: None Returns: None """ self . _clear_totals () now = self . link . env . now self . start_time = now if self . _disrupted_since is not None : self . _disrupted_since = now

docs.text: InventoryReplenishment ( env : Environment , node : object , params : dict ) Bases: InfoMixin , NamedEntity The InventoryReplenishment class is the base for all replenishment policies in SupplyNetPy: the rules a site follows to decide when to place a replenishment order and how many units to order. This class is not used directly. Each policy is a subclass, such as the (s, S) policy ( SSReplenishment ), the (R, Q) policy ( RQReplenishment ) and the periodic policy ( PeriodicReplenishment ). A subclass overrides the run method with its rule. run runs as a SimPy process for the whole simulation. A policy usually checks the node's inventory position each time the node's inventory drops (the inventory_drop event), or at fixed intervals. How a custom policy should talk to its node. A policy should use these four helper methods instead of reaching into the node's internal attributes: self.node.position() — the inventory position: inventory level plus units in transit, minus units the node still owes (to other sites and to waiting customers). self.node.place_order(quantity) — picks a supplier using the node's supplier-selection policy and places the replenishment order. This replaces calling selection_policy.select(...) and env.process(process_order(...)) yourself. self.node.wait_for_drop() — used as yield from self.node.wait_for_drop() to wait until the inventory drops; on wake-up it safely replaces the inventory_drop event with a fresh one. Link.available_quantity() — lets a supplier-selection policy check a supplier's inventory level without reading link.source.inventory.level directly. Sticking to these helpers keeps a policy from depending on how a particular node is built, so it works with any future Node type that offers the same methods. Parameters: env ( Environment ) – Simulation environment. node ( object ) – Node to which this policy applies. params ( dict ) – Parameters for the replenishment policy. Parameters a policy does not use. Each built-in policy lists the keys it reads from params in _param_keys . Any other key is ignored by the policy, so a warning names it and asks whether another policy was meant (for example, 'T' is read only by the periodic policy). A custom policy can set its own _param_keys to get the same check; if it does not, nothing is checked. Attributes: _info_keys ( list ) – List of keys to include in the info dictionary. _param_keys ( tuple ) – Keys this policy reads from params , or None if it does not say. env ( Environment ) – Simulation environment. node ( object ) – Node to which this policy applies. params ( dict ) – Parameters for the replenishment policy. docs.text: SSReplenishment ( env , node , params ) Bases: InventoryReplenishment Implements the (s, S) replenishment policy, with an optional safety stock. When the inventory position falls to the reorder point s or below, the node places a replenishment order big enough to bring its inventory position back up to the order-up-to level S . If a safety stock is given, it is added to both s and S . The inventory position is checked each time the node's inventory drops, or every period time units if a period is given, starting after an optional first review delay. The supplier is chosen by the node's supplier-selection policy. Parameters: env ( Environment ) – Simulation environment. node ( object ) – Node to which this policy applies. params ( dict ) – Replenishment policy parameters (s, S) and optional parameters (safety_stock, first_review_delay, period). Attributes: _info_keys ( list ) – List of keys to include in the info dictionary. env ( Environment ) – Simulation environment. node ( object ) – Node to which this policy applies. params ( dict ) – Replenishment policy parameters. name ( str ) – Replenishment policy name. first_review_delay ( float ) – Time units to wait before the first check of the inventory position. period ( float ) – Time units between checks. 0 (the default) means checking each time the inventory drops. Methods: Name Description run Checks the inventory position and places replenishment orders by the (s, S) rule. Initialize the replenishment policy object. Parameters: env (simpy.Environment): simulation environment node (object): node to which this policy applies params (dict): parameters for the replenishment policy (s, S) Attributes: _info_keys (list): list of keys to include in the info dictionary env (simpy.Environment): simulation environment node (object): node to which this policy applies params (dict): parameters for the replenishment policy (s, S) name (str): replenishment policy name first_review_delay (float): time units to wait before the first check of the inventory position period (float): time units between checks; 0 means checking each time the inventory drops Returns: None """ validate_non_negative ( "Reorder point (s)" , params [ 's' ]) # s must not be negative validate_positive ( "Order-up-to level (S)" , params [ 'S' ]) # S must be positive if 's' not in params or 'S' not in params : raise ValueError ( "Parameters 's' and 'S' must be provided for the (s, S) replenishment policy." ) if params [ 's' ] > params [ 'S' ]: raise ValueError ( "Reorder point (s) must be less than or equal to order-up-to level (S)." ) super () . __init__ ( env , node , params ) self . name = "min-max replenishment (s, S)" self . first_review_delay = params . get ( 'first_review_delay' , 0 ) self . period = params . get ( 'period' , 0 )

docs.text: RQReplenishment ( env , node , params ) Bases: InventoryReplenishment Implements the (R, Q) replenishment policy. When the inventory position falls to the reorder point R or below, the node places a replenishment order of a fixed Q units. The inventory position is checked each time the node's inventory drops if period is 0 (the default), or every period time units if a positive period is given. An optional first review delay sets how long to wait before the first check. The supplier is chosen by the node's supplier-selection policy. If the supplier cannot fill the order at once, a shortage is recorded at the supplier. docs.text: SupplierSelectionPolicy ( node , mode = 'fixed' , params = None ) Bases: InfoMixin , NamedEntity The base for all supplier-selection policies: the rules a site follows to choose which of its suppliers receives a replenishment order. A site reaches each of its suppliers over a link, so the policy works with links: the site's suppliers are the links in node.suppliers , and select returns the link to the chosen supplier (the supplier itself is link.source ). There are two modes: (1) "dynamic": the supplier is chosen afresh for every replenishment order. (2) "fixed": the first supplier chosen is remembered and used for every later order (another one is used only while the remembered supplier or the link to it is disrupted). Every policy skips a supplier whose site or link is disrupted (see Link.can_take_order ). Node.place_order calls select only when at least one supplier can take the order. Each policy is a subclass that overrides the select method with its own rule. A site gives its policy the mode and the settings ( supplier_selection_param ) only when the user gives them, so each policy keeps its own default mode. A policy lists the settings it reads in _param_keys ; any other setting is ignored, so a warning names it. Parameters: node ( object ) – Node for which the supplier selection policy is applied. mode ( str , default: 'fixed' ) – Supplier selection mode. Must be "dynamic" or "fixed". params ( dict , default: None ) – Settings for the policy ( supplier_selection_param of the site), or None. Attributes: _info_keys ( list ) – List of keys to include in the info dictionary. _param_keys ( tuple ) – Settings this policy reads from params , or None if it does not say. node ( object ) – Node for which the supplier selection policy is applied. mode ( str ) – Supplier selection mode ("dynamic" or "fixed"). params ( dict ) – The settings given to the policy, or None. fixed_supplier ( Link ) – In "fixed" mode, the link to the remembered supplier (None until the first choice). Methods: Name Description select The policy's rule for choosing a supplier; each subclass overrides it. validate_suppliers Checks that the node has at least one supplier. check_links Checks the policy's settings against the site's links; does nothing here. Initialize the supplier selection policy object. Parameters: node ( object ) – Node for which the supplier selection policy is applied. mode ( str , default: 'fixed' ) – Supplier selection mode ("dynamic" or "fixed"). params ( dict , default: None ) – Settings for the policy ( supplier_selection_param of the site), or None. Attributes: _info_keys ( list ) – List of keys to include in the info dictionary. node ( object ) – Node for which the supplier selection policy is applied. mode ( str ) – Supplier selection mode ("dynamic" or "fixed"). params ( dict ) – The settings given to the policy, or None. fixed_supplier ( Link ) – In "fixed" mode, the link to the remembered supplier (None until the first choice). Returns: – None Raises: ValueError – If the mode is not "dynamic" or "fixed". TypeError – If the node is not an instance of Node class. Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 1758 1759 1760 1761 1762 1763 1764 1765 1766 1767 1768 1769 1770 1771 1772 1773 1774 1775 1776 1777 1778 1779 1780 1781 1782 1783 1784 1785 1786 1787 1788 1789 1790 1791 def __init__ ( self , node , mode = "fixed" , params = None ): """ Initialize the supplier selection policy object. Parameters: node (object): Node for which the supplier selection policy is applied. mode (str): Supplier selection mode ("dynamic" or "fixed"). params (dict): Settings for the policy (``supplier_selection_param`` of the site), or None. Attributes: _info_keys (list): List of keys to include in the info dictionary. node (object): Node for which the supplier selection policy is applied. mode (str): Supplier selection mode ("dynamic" or "fixed"). params (dict): The settings given to the policy, or None. fixed_supplier (Link): In "fixed" mode, the link to the remembered supplier (None until the first choice). docs.text: select ( order_quantity ) Chooses the first supplier whose inventory level can fill the whole order. Suppliers whose site or link is disrupted are skipped first. Among those left, it chooses the first one whose inventory level is at least order_quantity ; if none is, it chooses the first of them (the order then waits at that supplier until enough units arrive, and the supplier records a shortage and a backorder). In fixed mode, the first choice is remembered and used for later orders. While it or its link is disrupted, the policy uses another supplier, without forgetting the remembered one. Parameters: order_quantity ( float ) – Units in the replenishment order. Returns: Link – The link to the chosen supplier. Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 2027 2028 2029 2030 2031 2032 2033 2034 2035 2036 2037 2038 2039 2040 def select ( self , order_quantity ): """ Chooses the first supplier whose inventory level can fill the whole order. Suppliers whose site or link is disrupted are skipped first. Among those left, it chooses the first one whose inventory level is at least ``order_quantity``; if none is, it chooses the first of them (the order then waits at that supplier until enough units arrive, and the supplier records a shortage and a backorder). In fixed mode, the first choice is remembered and used for later orders. While it or its link is disrupted, the policy uses another supplier, without forgetting the remembered one. Parameters: order_quantity (float): Units in the replenishment order. Returns: Link: The link to the chosen supplier. """ self . validate_suppliers () candidates = self . _active_suppliers () available = [ s for s in candidates if s . available_quantity () >= order_quantity ] selected = available [ 0 ] if available else candidates [ 0 ] return self . _apply_mode ( selected )

docs.text: SelectProbabilistic ( node , mode = 'dynamic' , params = None ) Bases: SupplierSelectionPolicy Chooses the supplier of each replenishment order at random, with a probability for each supplier. For example, a retailer that sends half of its orders to distributor D1, 30% to D2 and 20% to D3 is given supplier_selection_param={"probabilities": {"D1": 0.5, "D2": 0.3, "D3": 0.2}} . The probabilities are keyed by supplier ID ( link.source.ID ), so they can be given before the links exist, and they must sum to 1. A supplier with probability 0 is never chosen. For every order the policy draws exactly one random number u between 0 and 1 and puts the probabilities side by side, in the order the links to the suppliers were created: with 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2, u below 0.5 chooses the first supplier, u from 0.5 to below 0.8 the second, and the rest the third. One number per order means that two runs with the same seed see the same numbers, so changing a probability a little changes only the few orders whose number falls near a boundary. The probabilities are the shares of the orders while every supplier can take orders. When a supplier or the link to it is disrupted, on_disruption decides what happens: "rescale" (the default): the order goes to one of the other suppliers, which keep their ratios. With 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 and the first supplier disrupted, the other two get 0.6 and 0.4. "block" : the draw uses the given probabilities as they are. If it chooses a disrupted supplier, the order is not placed and is counted as blocked ; the site orders again when a supplier or a link recovers, or when its inventory drops. So with disruptions, the shares of the orders at the end of a run differ from the probabilities. The link statistics ( link.stats ) record the real shares. The stored probabilities never change. The mode is always "dynamic" (a new choice for every order); "fixed" would keep the first random choice for ever, so it is rejected. Parameters: node ( object ) – The site that uses the policy. mode ( str , default: 'dynamic' ) – "dynamic" (the default and the only mode allowed). params ( dict , default: None ) – The settings, all optional: probabilities (dict from supplier ID to probability; may also be given later with set_probabilities ), on_disruption ( "rescale" or "block" ), and seed (a number or a string) or rng (a random.Random ) for the policy's own random numbers. With neither, a seed is drawn once from the site's random number generator ( node.rng ), so scm.set_seed still makes runs repeatable. Attributes: name ( str ) – Name of the selection policy. probabilities ( dict ) – The probability of each supplier, by supplier ID (None until given). on_disruption ( str ) – "rescale" or "block" . rng ( Random ) – The policy's own random number generator. Its numbers are used for nothing else. _info_keys ( list ) – List of keys to include in the info dictionary. docs.text: check_links () Check the probabilities against the links to the site's suppliers: the probabilities have been given, every link has a probability, every probability has a link, and no supplier has two links to this site (its ID would not say which link is meant). A link or ID left over is most likely a typo, so it is an error, not a probability of 0. create_sc_net calls this once every link is created, and select calls it before its first choice. Returns: – None Raises: ValueError – If any of these checks fails. ID } : SelectProbabilistic { reason } ." global_logger . error ( message ) raise ValueError ( message ) if self . probabilities is None : fail ( "has no probabilities. Give them in supplier_selection_param or with set_probabilities" ) linked = [ link . source . ID for link in self . node . suppliers ] twice = sorted ({ str ( i ) for i in linked if linked . count ( i ) > 1 }) if twice : fail ( f "cannot tell apart two links from the same supplier ( { ', ' . join ( twice ) } )" ) missing = [ str ( i ) for i in linked if i not in self . probabilities ] if missing : fail ( f "has no probability for the supplier(s) { ', ' . join ( missing ) } , linked to this site" ) unlinked = sorted ( str ( i ) for i in self . probabilities if i not in linked ) if unlinked : fail ( f "has a probability for the supplier(s) { ', ' . join ( unlinked ) } , which have no link to this site" ) self . _links_checked = True

docs.text: select ( order_quantity ) Chooses the supplier of one replenishment order at random. With "rescale" , the choice is made among the suppliers that can take the order (if none with a probability above 0 can, the chosen supplier is disrupted and the order is blocked). With "block" , the choice is made among all suppliers with a probability above 0. A disrupted supplier returned here is blocked by InventoryNode.process_order , which counts the order as blocked . Parameters: order_quantity ( float ) – Units in the replenishment order. Returns: Link – The link to the chosen supplier. Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 2369 2370 2371 2372 2373 2374 2375 2376 2377 2378 2379 2380 2381 2382 2383 2384 2385 2386 2387 2388 2389 2390 2391 2392 2393 2394 2395 2396 2397 2398 2399 2400 2401 2402 def select ( self , order_quantity ): """ Chooses the supplier of one replenishment order at random. With ``"rescale"``, the choice is made among the suppliers that can take the order (if none with a probability above 0 can, the chosen supplier is disrupted and the order is blocked). With ``"block"``, the choice is made among all suppliers with a probability above 0. A disrupted supplier returned here is blocked by ``InventoryNode.process_order``, which counts the order as ``blocked``. Parameters: order_quantity (float): Units in the replenishment order. Returns: Link: The link to the chosen supplier. """ if not self . _links_checked : self . check_links () u = self . rng . random () # exactly one number for every order candidates = [( link , self . probabilities [ link . source . ID ]) for link in self . node . suppliers if self . probabilities [ link . source . ID ] > 0 ] choices = candidates # the suppliers this order can go to if self . on_disruption == "rescale" : working = [( link , p ) for link , p in candidates if link . can_take_order ()] if working : choices = working # Scaling u by the total probability of these suppliers shares out the # probability of the suppliers left out, keeping their ratios. target = u * sum ( p for _ , p in choices ) running = 0.0 for link , p in choices : running += p if target < running : return link return choices [ - 1 ][ 0 ] # rounding left u just past the end

docs.text: Node ( env : Environment , ID : str , name : str , node_type : str , failure_p : float = 0.0 , node_disrupt_time : Callable = None , node_recovery_time : Callable = lambda : 1 , logging : bool = True , rng : Random = None , disruption_impact = None , disruption_loss_fraction = 1.0 , ** kwargs ) Bases: NamedEntity , InfoMixin Represents a node in the supply chain network: a raw-material supplier, a manufacturer, a warehouse, distributor or retailer, or a customer demand. This is the base class they all share. It handles disruption and recovery, and logging. A node can be disrupted at random (each time unit, a disruption starts with probability failure_p ) or at the times given by node_disrupt_time . While disrupted, its status is "inactive"; it recovers after node_recovery_time . The subclasses also keep statistics ( stats ): orders, shortages, costs, revenue and profit. Sites can use the built-in replenishment policies ((s, S), (R, Q) and periodic) or a custom one made by subclassing InventoryReplenishment , and the built-in supplier-selection policies ( SelectFirst , SelectAvailable , SelectCheapest , SelectFastest ) or a custom one made by subclassing SupplierSelectionPolicy . For the node types, see NodeType . Parameters: env ( Environment ) – Simulation environment. ID ( str ) – Unique node ID. name ( str ) – Node name. node_type ( str ) – Type of the node. failure_p ( float , default: 0.0 ) – Disruption probability: the chance, each time unit, that a disruption starts. node_disrupt_time ( callable , default: None ) – Time units until the next disruption (a number, or a function returning one each time). node_recovery_time ( callable , default: lambda: 1 ) – Time units a disruption lasts (a number, or a function returning one each time). logging ( bool , default: True ) – Flag to enable/disable logging. disruption_impact ( str | callable | None , default: None ) – What a disruption does to the units at the node, at the moment it starts. None (default) leaves them untouched. Built-in names: "destroy_all" destroys all units at the node (and a manufacturer's raw materials); "destroy_fraction" destroys disruption_loss_fraction × inventory level . For any other effect (partial spoilage, contamination, capacity damage), pass your own function f(node) -> None . It runs once per disruption; for an effect that builds up during the disruption, start a SimPy process inside the function. disruption_loss_fraction ( float | callable , default: 1.0 ) – Fraction between 0 and 1, used with disruption_impact="destroy_fraction" . May be a zero-arg function, so each disruption can destroy a different fraction. **kwargs – Additional arguments for the logger. Attributes: _info_keys ( list ) – List of keys to include in the info dictionary. env ( Environment ) – simulation environment ID ( str ) – ID of the node (alphanumeric) name ( str ) – name of the node node_type ( str ) – type of the node node_failure_p ( float ) – disruption probability (the chance, each time unit, that a disruption starts) node_status ( str ) – status of the node: "active", or "inactive" while disrupted node_disrupt_time ( callable ) – function giving the time units until the next disruption node_recovery_time ( callable ) – function giving the time units a disruption lasts disruption_impact – The disruption_impact setting as given (a name, a function, or None). _disruption_impact_fn ( callable | None ) – The function that disruption() calls when a disruption starts. logger ( GlobalLogger ) – logger object suppliers ( list ) – The links to this node's suppliers (links whose sink is this node); filled in by Link.__init__ through add_supplier_link . Environment ): raise ValueError ( "Invalid environment. Provide a valid SimPy environment." ) # Validate node_type via the NodeType enum — single source of truth # shared with create_sc_net. Accepts either a string (case-insensitive) # or a NodeType member. Stored as the normalized lowercase string so # every existing equality check against a literal (``== "demand"``, # ``"supplier" in node.node_type``) continues to work. try : node_type = NodeType ( node_type ) . value except ValueError : global_logger . error ( f "Invalid node type. Node type: { node_type } " ) raise ValueError ( f "Invalid node type: { node_type } ." ) # ``ensure_numeric_callable`` turns a plain number into a function that # returns it, and calls the function once to check that it returns a # number. A mistake (for example, passing a class such as ``int``) is # then reported here, instead of crashing later in the middle of a run. node_recovery_time = ensure_numeric_callable ( "node_recovery_time" , node_recovery_time ) if node_disrupt_time is not None : node_disrupt_time = ensure_numeric_callable ( "node_disrupt_time" , node_disrupt_time ) self . env = env # simulation environment self . ID = ID # ID of the node (alphanumeric) self . name = name # name of the node self . node_type = node_type # type of the node (see NodeType) self . node_failure_p = failure_p # disruption probability self . node_status = "active" # "active", or "inactive" while disrupted self . node_disrupt_time = node_disrupt_time # function: time units until the next disruption self . node_recovery_time = node_recovery_time # function: time units a disruption lasts self . rng = rng if rng is not None else _rng # random number generator for random disruptions; the library's default if none is given self . suppliers = [] # links to this node's suppliers; filled in by Link.__init__ through add_supplier_link self . buyers = [] # links to this node's buyers; filled in by Link.__init__ through add_buyer_link # Work out the disruption-impact function once, here. The setting as # given is kept as ``disruption_impact`` (shown by get_info); the # function that runs when a disruption starts is ``_disruption_impact_fn``. self . disruption_impact = disruption_impact self . _disruption_impact_fn = _resolve_disruption_impact ( disruption_impact , disruption_loss_fraction ) logger_name = self . ID # default logger name is the node ID if 'logger_name' in kwargs : logger_name = kwargs . pop ( 'logger_name' ) # Per-node loggers live as children of the library root ``"sim_trace"`` # so their records propagate up to the single set of handlers configured # on ``global_logger``. This avoids each Node opening its own # FileHandler on ``simulation_trace.log`` (which used to truncate the # file once per node at construction). Users who pass a custom # ``logger_name`` get the prefix added automatically; if they already # supplied the prefix we don't double it. if not logger_name . startswith ( "sim_trace." ): logger_name = f "sim_trace. { logger_name } " # Only forward kwargs that GlobalLogger actually accepts; ignore the rest # so unrelated keys (e.g. record_inv_levels, shelf_life) don't raise TypeError. logger_kwargs = { k : kwargs [ k ] for k in kwargs if k in _LOGGER_KWARGS } self . logger = GlobalLogger ( logger_name = logger_name , ** logger_kwargs ) # create a logger # Do NOT call enable_logging() here — the per-node logger inherits its # handlers from ``global_logger`` via propagation. The historical call # site re-attached a FileHandler in mode='w' on every Node, which # truncated the trace file N times during network construction (§4.8). if not logging : self . logger . disable_logging () # mute this node specifically if ( self . node_failure_p > 0 or self . node_disrupt_time ): # start the disruption process if the node can be disrupted self . env . process ( self . disruption ())

docs.text: disruption () Disrupts the node (its status becomes "inactive") and recovers it after the recovery time, for the whole simulation. Disruptions start either at the times given by node_disrupt_time , or at random: each time unit, a disruption starts with probability failure_p . Returns: – None Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 2737 2738 2739 2740 2741 2742 2743 2744 2745 2746 2747 2748 2749 2750 2751 2752 2753 2754 2755 2756 2757 2758 2759 2760 2761 2762 2763 2764 2765 2766 2767 2768 2769 2770 2771 2772 2773 2774 2775 2776 2777 2778 2779 2780 2781 2782 2783 2784 2785 2786 2787 2788 2789 2790 2791 2792 2793 2794 2795 2796 2797 2798 2799 2800 2801 2802 2803 2804 2805 2806 2807 2808 2809 2810 2811 def disruption ( self ): """ Disrupts the node (its status becomes "inactive") and recovers it after the recovery time, for the whole simulation. Disruptions start either at the times given by ``node_disrupt_time``, or at random: each time unit, a disruption starts with probability ``failure_p``. Parameters: None Attributes: None Returns: None """ # TODO: interrupt all ongoing processes spawned by this node on disruption, and resume them after recovery. while True : if ( self . node_status == "active" ): if ( self . node_disrupt_time ): # if node_disrupt_time is provided, wait for the disruption time disrupt_time = self . node_disrupt_time () # get the disruption time validate_positive ( name = "node_disrupt_time" , value = disrupt_time ) # check if disrupt_time is positive yield self . env . timeout ( disrupt_time ) self . node_status = "inactive" # change the node status to inactive self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now } : { self . ID } : Node disrupted." ) self . _record_disruption_start () # The disruption-impact effect runs once, at the moment the # node switches from active to inactive. Effects that should # build up *during* the disruption belong in a custom # function that starts its own process; checking once per # time unit here would wake the simulation up for nothing. if self . _disruption_impact_fn is not None : self . _disruption_impact_fn ( self ) else : # Random disruption: check once per time unit, so # ``node_failure_p`` acts as the chance that a disruption # starts in any one time unit. The ``yield env.timeout(1)`` below MUST run # whether or not this check succeeds. If it were skipped on a # miss, the ``while True`` loop would spin without advancing # simulation time, repeating the check over and over until one # finally succeeds — which would disrupt the node almost # immediately at t=0 no matter how small ``failure_p`` is. if ( self . rng . random () < self . node_failure_p ): self . node_status = "inactive" self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now } : { self . ID } : Node disrupted." ) self . _record_disruption_start () if self . _disruption_impact_fn is not None : self . _disruption_impact_fn ( self ) yield self . env . timeout ( 1 ) else : recovery_time = self . node_recovery_time () # get the recovery time validate_positive ( name = "node_recovery_time" , value = recovery_time ) # the recovery time must be positive yield self . env . timeout ( recovery_time ) self . node_status = "active" self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now } : { self . ID } : Node recovered from disruption." ) stats = getattr ( self , "stats" , None ) if stats is not None : stats . disruption_ended () # Orders from buyers were not placed while this node was # disrupted. Wake each buyer's replenishment policy so that it # checks its inventory position again now. Without this, a node with no units # left, no orders from buyers and no waiting customers would # never order again, for the same reason. It is woken after # its buyers, so that a run gives the same results as models # that woke the node with their own impact function before # the library did. self . wake_replenishment ()

docs.text: wake_replenishment () -> None Make this node's replenishment policy check its inventory position now. A policy without a review period checks only when it is woken, normally when the node's inventory drops. A supplier or a link that recovers from a disruption calls this on its buyer, because an order the policy tried to place during the disruption was not placed. A node that recovers also calls it on itself, because units destroyed by the disruption did not wake its policy. The policy then checks again and orders if its inventory position is too low. An extra wake-up does no harm: if the position is fine, the policy just waits again. A policy with a review period checks on its own timer and is not affected. Returns: None – None Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 2926 2927 2928 2929 2930 2931 2932 2933 2934 2935 2936 2937 2938 2939 2940 2941 2942 2943 2944 2945 2946 def wake_replenishment ( self ) -> None : """ Make this node's replenishment policy check its inventory position now. A policy without a review period checks only when it is woken, normally when the node's inventory drops. A supplier or a link that recovers from a disruption calls this on its buyer, because an order the policy tried to place during the disruption was not placed. A node that recovers also calls it on itself, because units destroyed by the disruption did not wake its policy. The policy then checks again and orders if its inventory position is too low. An extra wake-up does no harm: if the position is fine, the policy just waits again. A policy with a review period checks on its own timer and is not affected. Returns: None """ inventory_drop = getattr ( self , "inventory_drop" , None ) if inventory_drop is not None and not inventory_drop . triggered : inventory_drop . succeed ()

docs.text: position () -> float The inventory position, used by replenishment policies. The inventory position is what the node can count on: its inventory level plus the units in transit to it, minus the units it still owes (to other sites and to waiting customers). Replenishment policies use this one value instead of working it out themselves, so the arithmetic stays in one place. inventory.on_hand already holds most of it. The node's backorders hold two kinds of waiting orders, and only one of them is subtracted here: Replenishment orders from other sites. They were taken off on_hand when they were placed (those still waiting are in the inventory's line, see Inventory.waiting_site_orders ), so subtracting them again would count them twice and make the node order too much. Customers waiting for units. They were not taken off on_hand , so they are subtracted here. Returns: float ( float ) – The inventory position. Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 2957 2958 2959 2960 2961 2962 2963 2964 2965 2966 2967 2968 2969 2970 2971 2972 2973 2974 2975 2976 2977 2978 2979 2980 2981 2982 2983 def position ( self ) -> float : """ The inventory position, used by replenishment policies. The inventory position is what the node can count on: its inventory level plus the units in transit to it, minus the units it still owes (to other sites and to waiting customers). Replenishment policies use this one value instead of working it out themselves, so the arithmetic stays in one place. ``inventory.on_hand`` already holds most of it. The node's backorders hold two kinds of waiting orders, and only one of them is subtracted here: - Replenishment orders from other sites. They were taken off ``on_hand`` when they were placed (those still waiting are in the inventory's line, see ``Inventory.waiting_site_orders``), so subtracting them again would count them twice and make the node order too much. - Customers waiting for units. They were not taken off ``on_hand``, so they are subtracted here. Returns: float: The inventory position. """ customer_backorders = self . stats . backorder [ 1 ] - self . inventory . waiting_site_orders () return self . inventory . on_hand - customer_backorders

docs.text: place_order ( quantity ) -> None Choose a supplier with this node's supplier-selection policy and place a replenishment order with it. First it checks that some supplier can take the order (see can_place_order ). If none can, no order is placed. The replenishment policy then goes back to waiting, and it is woken when a supplier or a link recovers (see wake_replenishment ), or when units leave the inventory. Otherwise it does in one call what a replenishment policy would otherwise do in two steps: selection_policy.select(...) , which chooses among the suppliers that can take the order, and env.process(process_order(...)) . The order itself is handled by process_order , which runs as its own SimPy process: it reduces the order to fit the node's capacity and records the order at the supplier. This method returns at once. Parameters: quantity ( float ) – Units to order. process_order may still reduce this to fit the capacity. Returns: None – None Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 2985 2986 2987 2988 2989 2990 2991 2992 2993 2994 2995 2996 2997 2998 2999 3000 3001 3002 3003 3004 3005 3006 3007 3008 3009 3010 3011 3012 3013 3014 3015 3016 3017 3018 3019 3020 3021 3022 3023 3024 3025 3026 3027 3028 3029 3030 3031 3032 3033 3034 3035 def place_order ( self , quantity ) -> None : """ Choose a supplier with this node's supplier-selection policy and place a replenishment order with it. First it checks that some supplier can take the order (see ``can_place_order``). If none can, no order is placed. The replenishment policy then goes back to waiting, and it is woken when a supplier or a link recovers (see ``wake_replenishment``), or when units leave the inventory. Otherwise it does in one call what a replenishment policy would otherwise do in two steps: ``selection_policy.select(...)``, which chooses among the suppliers that can take the order, and ``env.process(process_order(...))``. The order itself is handled by ``process_order``, which runs as its own SimPy process: it reduces the order to fit the node's capacity and records the order at the supplier. This method returns at once. Parameters: quantity (float): Units to order. ``process_order`` may still reduce this to fit the capacity. Returns: None """ if not self . can_place_order (): if self . has_suppliers (): self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . ID } : No supplier can take an order (every supplier or the link to it is disrupted). Order not placed." ) # A blocked order: not lost, because the policy orders again # when a supplier or a link recovers. self . stats . update_stats ( blocked = [ 1 , quantity ]) else : # Not a disruption: the site has no supplier to order from at # all, a mistake in how the network is built. No recovery will # ever let the order through, so it is not counted as blocked. # The user is warned once for each site (the warning text # leaves out the site, so Python shows it once in all). self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . ID } : The site has no supplier to order from. Order not placed." ) if not getattr ( self , "_warned_no_supplier" , False ): self . _warned_no_supplier = True message = ( "A site has no supplier to place replenishment orders with (a manufacturer needs a " "raw-material supplier for every raw material), so its orders are not placed. " "Connect a supplier to it with a link." ) self . logger . warning ( f " { self . ID } : { message } " ) warnings . warn ( message , UserWarning , stacklevel = 2 ) return # The order is really placed when process_order runs, a moment later # at this same time. It checks the chosen supplier again then. supplier = self . selection_policy . select ( quantity ) self . env . process ( self . process_order ( supplier , quantity ))

docs.text: wait_for_drop () Wait until the node's inventory drops, then get ready for the next drop. Replenishment policies use it as yield from node.wait_for_drop() . It waits on the node's inventory_drop event, which fires when the inventory drops, and also when the node itself, one of its suppliers or the link to it recovers from a disruption (see wake_replenishment ). A SimPy event can fire only once, so after it fires it is replaced with a fresh one, ready for the next drop. Doing this here keeps that replacing step in one place. Yields: – simpy.Event: The current inventory_drop event. Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 3062 3063 3064 3065 3066 3067 3068 3069 3070 3071 3072 3073 3074 3075 3076 3077 def wait_for_drop ( self ): """ Wait until the node's inventory drops, then get ready for the next drop. Replenishment policies use it as ``yield from node.wait_for_drop()``. It waits on the node's ``inventory_drop`` event, which fires when the inventory drops, and also when the node itself, one of its suppliers or the link to it recovers from a disruption (see ``wake_replenishment``). A SimPy event can fire only once, so after it fires it is replaced with a fresh one, ready for the next drop. Doing this here keeps that replacing step in one place. Yields: simpy.Event: The current ``inventory_drop`` event. """ yield self . inventory_drop self . inventory_drop = self . env . event ()

A link can be disrupted at random (each time unit, a disruption starts with probability link_failure_p ) or at the times given by link_disrupt_time ; it recovers after link_recovery_time . While a link is disrupted, no new orders are sent over it; orders already in transit still arrive. Parameters: env ( Environment ) – Simulation environment.
