docs.text: disruption () Disrupts the link (its status becomes "inactive") and recovers it after the recovery time, for the whole simulation. Disruptions start either at the times given by link_disrupt_time , or at random: each time unit, a disruption starts with probability link_failure_p . Returns: – None Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 3257 3258 3259 3260 3261 3262 3263 3264 3265 3266 3267 3268 3269 3270 3271 3272 3273 3274 3275 3276 3277 3278 3279 3280 3281 3282 3283 3284 3285 3286 3287 3288 3289 3290 3291 3292 3293 3294 3295 3296 3297 3298 3299 3300 3301 3302 3303 3304 3305 3306 3307 3308 def disruption ( self ): """ Disrupts the link (its status becomes "inactive") and recovers it after the recovery time, for the whole simulation. Disruptions start either at the times given by ``link_disrupt_time``, or at random: each time unit, a disruption starts with probability ``link_failure_p``. Parameters: None Attributes: None Returns: None """ # Orders already in transit over this link are not stopped when the # link is disrupted; only *new* orders are not sent (see # Node.place_order, which checks Link.can_take_order). # Stopping orders in transit would need each one tracked as its own # process; that is left for later. while True : if ( self . status == "active" ): if ( self . link_disrupt_time ): # if link_disrupt_time is provided, wait for the disruption time disrupt_time = self . link_disrupt_time () # get the disruption time validate_positive ( name = "link_disrupt_time" , value = disrupt_time ) # the disruption time must be positive yield self . env . timeout ( disrupt_time ) self . status = "inactive" # change the link status to inactive global_logger . info ( f " { self . env . now } : { self . ID } : Link disrupted." ) self . stats . disruption_started () else : # Random disruption: check once per time unit. The # ``yield env.timeout(1)`` below must run whether or not the # check succeeds (same as in ``Node.disruption``). Without # it, a miss would spin through ``while True`` without # advancing simulation time, making ``link_failure_p`` turn # into near-certain disruption at t=0. if ( self . rng . random () < self . link_failure_p ): self . status = "inactive" global_logger . info ( f " { self . env . now } : { self . ID } : Link disrupted." ) self . stats . disruption_started () yield self . env . timeout ( 1 ) else : recovery_time = self . link_recovery_time () # get the recovery time validate_positive ( name = "link_recovery_time" , value = recovery_time ) # the recovery time must be positive yield self . env . timeout ( recovery_time ) self . status = "active" global_logger . info ( f " { self . env . now } : { self . ID } : Link recovered from disruption." ) self . stats . disruption_ended () # Orders were not sent over this link while it was disrupted. # Wake the buyer's replenishment policy so it checks again now # (see Node.wake_replenishment). self . sink . wake_replenishment ()

docs.text: Inventory ( env : Environment , capacity : float , initial_level : float , node : Node , replenishment_policy : InventoryReplenishment , holding_cost : float = 0.0 , shelf_life : float = 0 , inv_type : str = 'non-perishable' , record_inv_levels = False ) Bases: NamedEntity , InfoMixin The Inventory class holds the units at a node and its records about them. It keeps the inventory level within the capacity, keeps the inventory position ( on_hand ), and tells the node when its inventory drops, so that its replenishment policy can check whether to order. For perishable goods it keeps the list of batches and throws away expired units. It also works out the holding cost, and can record the inventory level once per time unit. docs.text: waiting_orders () How many units are asked for by orders still waiting at this inventory. An order the inventory cannot fill right away (for example, a replenishment order bigger than the inventory level) joins a line and is served, in turn, when enough units arrive. Orders are served strictly in the order they arrived, so an order can also wait behind an earlier one. Besides replenishment orders from other sites, the line can hold other orders made with get . All of these units have already been taken off on_hand but have not left the inventory yet. (Expired and destroyed units never wait in this line: they are removed at once.) Returns: float – the units asked for by all waiting orders, or 0 if none are waiting. Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 3628 3629 3630 3631 3632 3633 3634 3635 3636 3637 3638 3639 3640 3641 3642 3643 3644 def waiting_orders ( self ): """ How many units are asked for by orders still waiting at this inventory. An order the inventory cannot fill right away (for example, a replenishment order bigger than the inventory level) joins a line and is served, in turn, when enough units arrive. Orders are served strictly in the order they arrived, so an order can also wait behind an earlier one. Besides replenishment orders from other sites, the line can hold other orders made with `get`. All of these units have already been taken off `on_hand` but have not left the inventory yet. (Expired and destroyed units never wait in this line: they are removed at once.) Returns: float: the units asked for by all waiting orders, or 0 if none are waiting. """ return sum ( request . amount for request in self . inventory . get_queue )

docs.text: put ( amount : float , manufacturing_date : float = None ) Add units to the inventory. For perishable goods, they are added as a new batch with their manufacturing date. Parameters: amount ( float ) – units to add manufacturing_date ( float , default: None ) – the units' manufacturing date (needed for perishable goods only) Returns: float – the units actually accepted. Less than amount when they do not all fit within the capacity, and 0 when the inventory is infinite, already full, or amount <= 0 . Callers that keep on_hand must take any shortfall ( requested - accepted ) back off it. Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 3676 3677 3678 3679 3680 3681 3682 3683 3684 3685 3686 3687 3688 3689 3690 3691 3692 3693 3694 3695 3696 3697 3698 3699 3700 3701 3702 3703 3704 3705 3706 3707 3708 3709 3710 3711 3712 3713 3714 3715 3716 3717 3718 3719 3720 3721 3722 3723 3724 3725 3726 3727 3728 3729 3730 3731 def put ( self , amount : float , manufacturing_date : float = None ): """ Add units to the inventory. For perishable goods, they are added as a new batch with their manufacturing date. Parameters: amount (float): units to add manufacturing_date (float): the units' manufacturing date (needed for perishable goods only) Returns: float: the units actually accepted. Less than ``amount`` when they do not all fit within the capacity, and 0 when the inventory is infinite, already full, or ``amount <= 0``. Callers that keep ``on_hand`` must take any shortfall (``requested - accepted``) back off it. """ # Use ``>=``, not ``==``. When the inventory is filled exactly to # capacity, floating-point rounding can leave the level a hair ABOVE # capacity (e.g. 99.99000000000001 for a capacity of 99.99). A plain # ``== capacity`` check would miss that case, so ``>=`` is used to # correctly spot an inventory that is already full. if self . inventory . level == float ( 'inf' ) or amount <= 0 or self . inventory . level >= self . capacity : return 0 if amount + self . inventory . level > self . capacity : # adjust amount if it exceeds capacity old_amount = amount amount = self . capacity - self . inventory . level # Safety net: if the rounding above left the level just over # capacity, this leftover space comes out as zero or negative. # SimPy's Container.put rejects a non-positive amount with an error, # so we treat the inventory as already full and simply accept nothing. if amount <= 0 : return 0 self . node . logger . warning ( f "Inventory capacity exceeded. Only { amount } of { old_amount } units added to inventory." ) if self . inv_type == "perishable" : if manufacturing_date is None : self . node . logger . error ( "Manufacturing date must be provided for perishable inventory." ) raise ValueError ( "Manufacturing date must be provided for perishable inventory." ) # ``perish_queue`` is a heap ordered by manufacturing date, so the # oldest batch (the first to expire) is always at position 0. Adding # a batch with ``heapq.heappush`` is fast. new_batch = ( manufacturing_date , amount ) heapq . heappush ( self . perish_queue , new_batch ) # Only wake ``remove_expired`` when this new batch becomes the oldest # one (position 0) — either because the list was empty, or because # this batch is older than every batch already there. For ordinary # deliveries (newer dates than what is there) the oldest batch does # not change, so ``remove_expired`` is left alone. if self . perish_queue [ 0 ] is new_batch and not self . perish_changed . triggered : self . perish_changed . succeed () self . update_carry_cost () # add the holding cost up to now, before the level changes self . inventory . put ( amount ) if ( not self . node . inventory_raised . triggered ): self . node . inventory_raised . succeed () # signal that inventory has been raised return amount

docs.text: get ( amount : float , site_order : bool = False ) Take units out of the inventory for an order. For perishable goods, the units come from the oldest batch first. If the inventory level is too low, the order waits until enough units arrive (see _InventoryContainer ). Either way, the units are taken off the inventory position ( on_hand ) straight away. Parameters: amount ( float ) – units to take. site_order ( bool , default: False ) – True for a replenishment order from another site, False for a customer order (see waiting_site_orders ). Defaults to False. Returns: tuple – (SimPy event, list of (manufacturing_date, quantity)). The event fires when the order is served. The list holds the batches the units came from (perishable goods only; empty otherwise). It is filled in when the units really leave the inventory: at once if the inventory level is high enough, or later, when an order that had to wait is served. So read it after yielding the event. Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 3733 3734 3735 3736 3737 3738 3739 3740 3741 3742 3743 3744 3745 3746 3747 3748 3749 3750 3751 3752 3753 3754 3755 3756 3757 3758 3759 3760 3761 3762 3763 3764 3765 3766 3767 def get ( self , amount : float , site_order : bool = False ): """ Take units out of the inventory for an order. For perishable goods, the units come from the oldest batch first. If the inventory level is too low, the order waits until enough units arrive (see `_InventoryContainer`). Either way, the units are taken off the inventory position (``on_hand``) straight away. Parameters: amount (float): units to take. site_order (bool): True for a replenishment order from another site, False for a customer order (see `waiting_site_orders`). Defaults to False. Returns: tuple: (SimPy event, list of (manufacturing_date, quantity)). The event fires when the order is served. The list holds the batches the units came from (perishable goods only; empty otherwise). It is filled in when the units really leave the inventory: at once if the inventory level is high enough, or later, when an order that had to wait is served. So read it after yielding the event. """ # The order is labelled, so that among the orders still waiting the # node can tell replenishment orders from other sites apart from # customer orders (see `waiting_site_orders`). if self . inventory . level == float ( 'inf' ): get_event = self . inventory . get ( amount , site_order = site_order ) return get_event , get_event . batches self . update_carry_cost () get_event = self . inventory . get ( amount , site_order = site_order ) self . on_hand -= amount # the inventory position drops at once self . _signal_inventory_drop () return get_event , get_event . batches

docs.text: remove_expired () Throw away expired units (perishable goods only). This runs as a SimPy process for the whole simulation. Instead of checking every time unit, it sleeps exactly until the oldest batch is due to expire. It wakes up early through the perish_changed event when put adds a batch that becomes the new oldest one (or arrives while the list is empty), so a batch that expires sooner is handled without waiting for the old timer. After each wake-up it creates a fresh perish_changed event so an already-used one cannot fire again by mistake — the same pattern as Node.wait_for_drop . Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 3826 3827 3828 3829 3830 3831 3832 3833 3834 3835 3836 3837 3838 3839 3840 3841 3842 3843 3844 3845 3846 3847 3848 3849 3850 3851 3852 3853 3854 3855 3856 3857 3858 3859 3860 3861 3862 3863 3864 3865 3866 3867 3868 3869 3870 3871 3872 3873 3874 3875 3876 3877 3878 3879 3880 3881 3882 3883 def remove_expired ( self ): """ Throw away expired units (perishable goods only). This runs as a SimPy process for the whole simulation. Instead of checking every time unit, it sleeps exactly until the oldest batch is due to expire. It wakes up early through the ``perish_changed`` event when ``put`` adds a batch that becomes the new oldest one (or arrives while the list is empty), so a batch that expires sooner is handled without waiting for the old timer. After each wake-up it creates a fresh ``perish_changed`` event so an already-used one cannot fire again by mistake — the same pattern as ``Node.wait_for_drop``. """ while True : if not self . perish_queue : # Nothing to expire: wait until ``put`` adds a batch. yield self . perish_changed self . perish_changed = self . env . event () continue # The oldest batch sits at position 0 of the heap, so one look is # enough to find when the next expiry is due. ``max(0, ...)`` keeps # the sleep time from going negative for a batch whose expiry time # has already passed (e.g. one given an old manufacturing date). next_expiry = self . perish_queue [ 0 ][ 0 ] + self . shelf_life sleep_dt = max ( 0 , next_expiry - self . env . now ) timer = self . env . timeout ( sleep_dt ) result = yield timer | self . perish_changed if self . perish_changed in result : # A new oldest batch arrived (or the list was empty and now has # a batch). Make a fresh event and start over from the new # oldest batch — even if the timer also fired, the next loop will # see a sleep time of 0 and remove the expired units right away. self . perish_changed = self . env . event () continue # The timer fired — remove every batch that has now expired. The # test is written as ``env.now >= mfg_date + shelf_life`` to match # how the expiry time was worked out above. The other form, # ``env.now - mfg_date >= shelf_life``, is unreliable with # fractional shelf lives because of floating-point rounding (e.g. # ``9.2 - 8`` becomes ``1.1999999999999993`` and fails a ``>= 1.2`` # check), which could make this helper skip the removal and loop # forever at the same time. # # Expired units are thrown away at once, even when an order is # waiting. Every batch in the list is still physically in the # inventory (a batch leaves the list only when its units leave the # inventory), so the units are there to remove. Queueing the # removal behind a waiting order would leave the expired units in # the inventory, where that order could take them once it is served. while self . perish_queue and self . env . now >= self . perish_queue [ 0 ][ 0 ] + self . shelf_life : mfg_date , qty = heapq . heappop ( self . perish_queue ) # take the oldest batch off the list if qty > 0 : self . update_carry_cost () removed = self . inventory . remove_now ( qty ) # and the same units out of the inventory self . on_hand -= removed self . waste += removed # expired units thrown away so far self . node . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { removed } units expired (Mgf date: { mfg_date } )." ) self . _signal_inventory_drop ()

docs.text: update_carry_cost () Add the holding cost since the last update: inventory level × time units since then × holding cost per unit per time unit. It is called before every change of the inventory level, so each stretch of time is charged at the level the inventory really had. The same stretch is also added, without the holding cost, to level_time (inventory level × time) and, if the level was 0, to zero_level_time . Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 3885 3886 3887 3888 3889 3890 3891 3892 3893 3894 3895 3896 3897 3898 3899 3900 3901 3902 3903 def update_carry_cost ( self ): """ Add the holding cost since the last update: inventory level × time units since then × holding cost per unit per time unit. It is called before every change of the inventory level, so each stretch of time is charged at the level the inventory really had. The same stretch is also added, without the holding cost, to ``level_time`` (inventory level × time) and, if the level was 0, to ``zero_level_time``. """ carry_period = self . env . now - self . last_update_t self . carry_cost += self . inventory . level * ( carry_period ) * self . holding_cost # holding cost for the time since the last update if self . inventory . level != float ( 'inf' ): # The same stretch of time, kept without the holding cost: the # inventory level × time (for the average inventory level), and the # time spent at level 0. The tolerance ignores rounding dust. self . level_time += self . inventory . level * carry_period if self . inventory . level <= 1e-9 : self . zero_level_time += carry_period self . last_update_t = self . env . now # update the last update time

docs.text: destroy ( amount : float = None , reason : str = 'disruption' ) -> float Destroy units now, for a physical loss in a disruption (natural disaster, contamination, theft, etc.). Removes the units right away, even when orders are waiting, so the caller (usually a Node disruption handler) sees the new level on the very next line. The method does not fire inventory_drop for nodes with a replenishment policy. That event wakes the policy, and a disrupted node can still place replenishment orders, so the node would order while it is disrupted. Instead the node wakes its own policy when it recovers (see Node.disruption ), and the policy then orders if its inventory position is too low. It does wake a raw-material supplier (which then mines to refill its inventory, as it does whenever its inventory drops) and a manufacturer (which can make more now that there is free capacity). For perishable goods the oldest batches are destroyed first, the same as for orders: destroying part of the oldest batch lowers its quantity but keeps its manufacturing date. waste (which counts only expired units) is left unchanged — destroyed units are counted separately, in Statistics.destroyed_qty / destroyed_value , which the caller fills in. For an infinite supplier ( level == float('inf') ) this does nothing: it stands for an unlimited supply of raw material, not a real pile that can be destroyed. Parameters: amount ( float , default: None ) – Units to destroy. None (default) destroys all units (the whole inventory level). Values larger than the inventory level are reduced to it. Zero or negative values do nothing. reason ( str , default: 'disruption' ) – Free-form label written to the per-node logger so the trace makes the distinction between expiry, consumption, and destruction visible. Default "disruption" . Returns: float ( float ) – The units actually destroyed ( 0 in the cases above where float – nothing happens). Callers usually multiply this by the value of one float – unit to record destroyed_value on Statistics . Removes the units right away, even when orders are waiting, so the caller (usually a ``Node`` disruption handler) sees the new ``level`` on the very next line. The method does **not** fire ``inventory_drop`` for nodes with a replenishment policy. That event wakes the policy, and a disrupted node can still place replenishment orders, so the node would order while it is disrupted. Instead the node wakes its own policy when it recovers (see ``Node.disruption``), and the policy then orders if its inventory position is too low. It does wake a raw-material supplier (which then mines to refill its inventory, as it does whenever its inventory drops) and a manufacturer (which can make more now that there is free capacity). For perishable goods the oldest batches are destroyed first, the same as for orders: destroying part of the oldest batch lowers its quantity but keeps its manufacturing date. ``waste`` (which counts only expired units) is left unchanged — destroyed units are counted separately, in ``Statistics.destroyed_qty`` / ``destroyed_value``, which the caller fills in. For an infinite supplier (``level == float('inf')``) this does nothing: it stands for an unlimited supply of raw material, not a real pile that can be destroyed. Parameters: amount (float, optional): Units to destroy. ``None`` (default) destroys all units (the whole inventory level). Values larger than the inventory level are reduced to it. Zero or negative values do nothing. reason (str, optional): Free-form label written to the per-node logger so the trace makes the distinction between expiry, consumption, and destruction visible. Default ``"disruption"``. Returns: float: The units actually destroyed (``0`` in the cases above where nothing happens). Callers usually multiply this by the value of one unit to record ``destroyed_value`` on ``Statistics``. """ if self . inventory . level == float ( 'inf' ): return 0 # infinite_supplier — nothing physical to destroy available = self . inventory . level if amount is None : amount = available amount = max ( 0.0 , min ( amount , available )) if amount <= 0 : return 0 # Add the holding cost up to now, so the destroyed units are not # charged holding cost afterwards. self . update_carry_cost () # Destroy the oldest batches first (perishable goods only), and take the # same units out of the inventory at once — even when an order is # waiting. An ordinary request would wait in line behind that order, # so the units would stay in the inventory and would instead be # taken from the next delivery. self . _pick_oldest_batches ( amount ) amount = self . inventory . remove_now ( amount ) self . on_hand -= amount self . node . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . node . ID } : { amount } units destroyed ( { reason } ). " f "Level= { self . inventory . level } , on_hand= { self . on_hand } ." ) # There is free capacity again. A raw-material supplier whose inventory # was full starts mining again, and a manufacturer that stopped because # its inventory was full carries on. Other nodes are not told, so their # replenishment policies do not order while the node is disrupted; the # node wakes its policy when it recovers (see above). # Raw-material suppliers have no replenishment policy, so for them the # "inventory dropped" signal only restarts mining. if isinstance ( self . node , Supplier ): inventory_drop = getattr ( self . node , "inventory_drop" , None ) if inventory_drop is not None and not inventory_drop . triggered : inventory_drop . succeed () wake_production = getattr ( self . node , "wake_production" , None ) if wake_production is not None : wake_production () return amount

It has no supplier of its own. SupplyNetPy does not model perishable raw materials yet, so its inventory is always non-perishable. A raw-material supplier with finite inventory ( node_type="supplier" ) mines RawMaterial.extraction_quantity units every RawMaterial.extraction_time time units, as long as its inventory is not full. docs.text: behavior () Mine raw material for the whole simulation: extraction_quantity units every extraction_time time units, as long as the inventory is not full. When it is full, wait until the inventory drops, then mine again. A raw-material supplier mines a single raw material. Returns: – None Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 4117 4118 4119 4120 4121 4122 4123 4124 4125 4126 4127 4128 4129 4130 4131 4132 4133 4134 4135 4136 4137 4138 4139 4140 4141 4142 4143 4144 4145 4146 def behavior ( self ): """ Mine raw material for the whole simulation: `extraction_quantity` units every `extraction_time` time units, as long as the inventory is not full. When it is full, wait until the inventory drops, then mine again. A raw-material supplier mines a single raw material. Parameters: None Attributes: None Returns: None """ while True : if ( self . inventory . level < self . inventory . capacity ): # check if the inventory is not full mined_quantity = self . raw_material . extraction_quantity if (( self . inventory . level + self . raw_material . extraction_quantity ) > self . inventory . capacity ): # mine only what fits within the capacity mined_quantity = self . inventory . capacity - self . inventory . level self . inventory . put ( mined_quantity ) self . stats . update_stats ( total_raw_materials_mined = mined_quantity , total_material_cost = mined_quantity * self . raw_material . mining_cost ) self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . ID } :Raw material mined/extracted. Inventory level: { self . inventory . level } " ) yield self . env . timeout ( self . raw_material . extraction_time ) else : # The inventory is full. Wait until it drops (a buyer takes # units, and Inventory.get signals inventory_drop), then mine # again, instead of checking the inventory every time unit. yield from self . wait_for_drop () self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . ID } : Inventory level: { self . inventory . level } " ) # log on each event-driven wake-up

docs.text: process_order ( supplier , reorder_quantity ) Place a replenishment order with one supplier, and add the units to the inventory when they arrive. This runs as a SimPy process ( place_order starts it). place_order has already checked that some supplier can take the order. This method checks the chosen supplier again when it starts, because that is when the order is really placed. If the supplier's site or the link to it is disrupted by then, the order is not placed. Parameters: supplier ( Link ) – The link to the supplier, not the supplier itself (the supplier is supplier.source ). reorder_quantity ( float ) – Units to order. Reduced if they would not fit within the capacity. This method checks the chosen supplier again when it starts, because that is when the order is really placed. If the supplier's site or the link to it is disrupted by then, the order is not placed. Reduced if they would not fit within the capacity. Attributes: None Returns: None """ # Check the order against the capacity using the inventory position # (inventory level plus units in transit, minus units owed to other # sites and to waiting customers). Processes queued before it run first, and at time 0 these # include the start of every disruption process, whose first random # draw can disrupt the chosen supplier or link. So check again now. A # blocked order records nothing (no shortage, backorder or pending # order). The replenishment policy is woken when the supplier or the # link recovers (see Node.wake_replenishment). if not supplier . can_take_order (): self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . ID } :Supplier: { supplier . source . name } or link: { supplier . ID } is disrupted. ID } :shipment in transit from supplier: { supplier . source . name } ." ) # log the shipment lead_time = supplier . lead_time () # draw the lead time from the link validate_non_negative ( name = "lead_time" , value = lead_time ) # check if lead_time is non-negative yield self . env . timeout ( lead_time ) # lead time for the order # Add the delivered units to the inventory, one part that fits at a time. # # Why loop instead of a single put()? A replenishment order can be # bigger than the free capacity. This is normal, not a mistake: when # the node owes units to waiting customers (backorders), the (s, S) # policy orders enough to BOTH refill the inventory AND cover those # backorders. That combined amount can be more than the inventory # can hold at once, because the backordered units are meant to pass # straight through to customers, not to stay in the inventory. A # single put() would simply drop whatever did not fit — and the node # would still have paid for those dropped units. # # So we add what fits right now, then pause for one instant of # simulation time. `env.timeout(0)` does not advance the clock; it just # lets other events scheduled for this same instant run. During that # pause, the units we just added are handed to the waiting customers, # which frees capacity again. We then add the next part, and repeat # until the whole order has been added or handed out. # # Safety stop: if a pause frees no capacity at all, the inventory is # genuinely full and the leftover cannot be stored. We stop there (so # the loop can never run forever inside a single instant) and drop the # leftover. `on_hand` (the inventory position, apart from units owed # to waiting customers) was increased by the full order amount when # the order was placed, so we subtract the undeliverable leftover # back out to keep it correct. if man_date_ls : # the supplier sent batches with their manufacturing dates (perishable goods) batches = [( ele [ 0 ], ele [ 1 ]) for ele in man_date_ls ] elif self . inventory . inv_type == "perishable" : # perishable, but we set the manufacturing date ourselves mfg = self . manufacture_date ( self . env . now ) if self . manufacture_date else self . env . now batches = [( mfg , reorder_quantity )] else : # ordinary (non-perishable) goods batches = [( None , reorder_quantity )] accepted = 0 # how many units actually made it into the inventory for mfg_date , qty in batches : # `remaining > 1e-9` rather than `> 0`: a tiny tolerance so # floating-point rounding dust never triggers one extra loop. remaining = qty while remaining > 1e-9 : # put() returns how many units it actually accepted — it # never goes over the capacity, so this can be less than asked. if mfg_date is None : put_now = self . inventory . put ( remaining ) else : put_now = self . inventory . put ( remaining , mfg_date ) accepted += put_now remaining -= put_now if remaining <= 1e-9 : break # the whole part is in the inventory; done # The inventory is full. This usually means the node's storage # capacity is too small for the order sizes flowing # through it. self . logger . warning ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . ID } :Dropped { remaining } units from the " f "delivered shipment — the shelf is full and no waiting customer " f "could take them. The node's storage capacity " f "( { self . inventory . capacity } ) may be too small for this order size." ) self . stats . update_stats ( dropped_qty = remaining ) self . inventory . on_hand -= remaining remaining = 0 break self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . ID } :Inventory replenished. reorder_quantity= { reorder_quantity } , accepted= { accepted } , Inventory levels: { self . inventory . level } " ) # Record what actually arrived (`accepted`), not what was ordered. # In the normal case these are equal. They differ only when part of an # order could not be stored (the "safety stop" above), and in that case # the node should be billed for, and credited with, only the units it # truly received. self . stats . update_stats ( fulfillment_received = [ 1 , accepted ], inventory_spend_cost = accepted * self . buy_price ) supplier . source . stats . update_stats ( demand_fulfilled = [ 1 , accepted ]) # The link adds the order's waiting time and lead time now, on arrival, # with fulfillment_received, so that their averages divide by a count # recorded at the same moment (this matters after a reset). supplier . stats . update_stats ( fulfillment_received = [ 1 , accepted ], inventory_spend_cost = accepted * self . buy_price , waiting_time = waited_for , lead_time = lead_time ) self . pending_orders -= 1

docs.text: Manufacturer ( env : Environment , ID : str , name : str , capacity : float , initial_level : float , inventory_holding_cost : float , product_sell_price : float , replenishment_policy : InventoryReplenishment , policy_param : dict , product : Product = None , inventory_type : str = 'non-perishable' , shelf_life : float = 0.0 , supplier_selection_policy : SupplierSelectionPolicy = SelectFirst , supplier_selection_mode : str = None , supplier_selection_param : dict = None , ** kwargs ) Bases: Node The Manufacturer class represents a manufacturer: a site that turns raw materials into a product and sells the product to buyers (other sites) and customers. It keeps its raw materials apart from its inventory of the product. Its replenishment policy watches the product's inventory position and decides when to plan production; the manufacturer then orders the raw materials needed from its raw-material suppliers, one for each raw material. Parameters: env ( Environment ) – Simulation environment. ID ( str ) – Unique identifier for the manufacturer. name ( str ) – Name of the manufacturer. capacity ( float ) – The largest inventory level of the product it can hold. initial_level ( float ) – Inventory level of the product at the start. inventory_holding_cost ( float ) – Holding cost per unit of the product per time unit. product_sell_price ( float ) – Sell price per unit of the product. replenishment_policy ( InventoryReplenishment ) – The replenishment policy class (for example scm.SSReplenishment ), not an object: the manufacturer creates the policy itself. It decides when to plan production. None for no replenishment policy. policy_param ( dict ) – Parameters for the replenishment policy (for example {'s': 20, 'S': 60} ). product ( Product , default: None ) – The product it makes (required). If the product's buy price is not set, it is set to the cost of making one unit: the manufacturing cost plus the cost of its raw materials. inventory_type ( str , default: 'non-perishable' ) – Type of inventory ("non-perishable" or "perishable"). shelf_life ( float , default: 0.0 ) – Shelf life of the product, in time units (perishable goods only). supplier_selection_policy ( SupplierSelectionPolicy , default: SelectFirst ) – The supplier-selection policy class (default SelectFirst ). supplier_selection_mode ( str , default: None ) – "fixed" or "dynamic"; see SupplierSelectionPolicy . If it is not given, the policy's own default is used ("fixed" for the built in policies except SelectProbabilistic ). supplier_selection_param ( dict , default: None ) – Settings for the supplier-selection policy (optional), for example the probabilities of SelectProbabilistic . **kwargs – Additional keyword arguments for the Node class and logger. Also accepts periodic_stats (bool, default False: if True, its statistics are updated every stats_period time units) and stats_period (float, default 1). Attributes: _info_keys ( list ) – List of keys to include in the info dictionary. replenishment_policy ( InventoryReplenishment ) – The replenishment policy object the manufacturer created (or None). inventory ( Inventory ) – Its inventory of the product. inventory_drop ( Event ) – Fires when its inventory drops. inventory_raised ( Event ) – Fires when units are added to its inventory. product ( Product ) – The product it makes. suppliers ( list ) – The links to its raw-material suppliers. sell_price ( float ) – Sell price per unit of the product. production_cycle ( bool ) – True while a production batch is being made. raw_inventory_counts ( dict ) – Units of each raw material it holds, by raw material ID. (Raw materials are counted here, not in inventory .) pending_orders ( int ) – Number of its raw-material replenishment orders placed but not yet arrived. selection_policy ( SupplierSelectionPolicy ) – The supplier-selection policy object. stats ( Statistics ) – Its statistics. Besides the usual ones, total_products_manufactured (units made so far) and total_manufacturing_cost (manufacturing cost so far, part of node_cost ). production_wake ( Event ) – Event that wakes the production loop when it is waiting (see wake_production ). Methods: Name Description manufacture_product Makes one production batch, using up raw materials and adding the units made to the inventory. behavior Production loop that keeps making production batches while there are planned units left to make. wake_production Wakes the production loop if it is waiting. process_order Plans production and orders the raw materials needed for it. process_order_raw Places one replenishment order for one raw material with one raw-material supplier. Behavior When the replenishment policy asks for more units, the manufacturer plans that many units and orders the raw materials needed to make them. It then makes the planned units in production batches: each makes at most product.batch_size units and takes product.manufacturing_time . Production batches follow one another until every planned unit is made. If one cannot start (no raw material yet, or no free capacity), the manufacturer waits until raw material arrives, a new plan comes in, or units leave its inventory, and then carries on. Assumptions The manufacturer makes a single product. Raw materials are kept apart from the inventory of the product. Only the product's inventory position is watched by the replenishment policy. Raw materials are ordered when production is planned, for exactly the planned units. The manufacturer starts with no raw materials. Initialize the manufacturer object. Attributes: _info_keys (list): List of keys to include in the info dictionary. replenishment_policy (InventoryReplenishment): The replenishment policy object the manufacturer created (or None). inventory (Inventory): Its inventory of the product. inventory_drop (simpy.Event): Fires when its inventory drops. inventory_raised (simpy.Event): Fires when units are added to its inventory. product (Product): The product it makes. suppliers (list): The links to its raw-material suppliers. sell_price (float): Sell price per unit of the product. production_cycle (bool): True while a production batch is being made. raw_inventory_counts (dict): Units of each raw material it holds, by raw material ID. (Raw materials are counted here, not in ``inventory``.) pending_orders (int): Number of its raw-material replenishment orders placed but not yet arrived. selection_policy (SupplierSelectionPolicy): The supplier-selection policy object. stats (Statistics): Its statistics. Besides the usual ones, ``total_products_manufactured`` (units made so far) and ``total_manufacturing_cost`` (manufacturing cost so far, part of ``node_cost``). production_wake (simpy.Event): Event that wakes the production loop when it is waiting (see `wake_production`). Returns: None """ # Take the statistics options out of kwargs before passing the rest on # to Node. ID } : { message } " ) warnings . warn ( message , UserWarning , stacklevel = 2 ) # A policy with its own random numbers (SelectProbabilistic) given no # seed or rng would draw its seed from this site's random number # generator, which is usually the library's. docs.text: manufacture_product () Make one production batch. A production batch makes at most product.batch_size units and takes product.manufacturing_time . It can be smaller when there is only raw material, free capacity, or planned units left for fewer units. The raw materials are used up when the production batch starts, and the units made are added to the inventory when it ends. Returns: int – Number of units made in this production batch (0 if nothing could be made). Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 4740 4741 4742 4743 4744 4745 4746 4747 4748 4749 4750 4751 4752 4753 4754 4755 4756 4757 4758 4759 4760 4761 4762 4763 4764 4765 4766 4767 4768 4769 4770 4771 4772 4773 4774 4775 4776 4777 4778 4779 4780 4781 4782 4783 4784 4785 4786 4787 4788 4789 4790 4791 4792 4793 4794 4795 4796 4797 4798 4799 def manufacture_product ( self ): """ Make one production batch. A production batch makes at most `product.batch_size` units and takes `product.manufacturing_time`. It can be smaller when there is only raw material, free capacity, or planned units left for fewer units. The raw materials are used up when the production batch starts, and the units made are added to the inventory when it ends. Parameters: None Attributes: None Returns: int: Number of units made in this production batch (0 if nothing could be made). """ max_producible_units = self . product . batch_size for raw_material in self . product . raw_materials : raw_mat_id = raw_material [ 0 ] . ID required_amount = raw_material [ 1 ] current_raw_material_level = self . raw_inventory_counts [ raw_mat_id ] max_producible_units = min ( max_producible_units , int ( current_raw_material_level / required_amount )) if (( self . inventory . level + max_producible_units ) > self . inventory . capacity ): # make only what fits within the capacity max_producible_units = self . inventory . capacity - self . inventory . level # Don't make more than the manufacturer has planned to make. When it # plans production, it adds those units to on_hand straight away # (§3.11), so on_hand = inventory level + units still to be made - # replenishment orders from other sites that are waiting at its # inventory (those were taken off on_hand when they were placed). # Units still to be made is therefore on_hand - inventory level + # waiting orders. # # Leaving out the waiting orders makes this number too small, by # exactly the amount the manufacturer owes. docs.text: behavior () The production loop, for the whole simulation: make one production batch after another while there are planned units left to make; when nothing can be made, wait until something may change that (see wake_production ). It first checks the manufacturer's suppliers: each must be a raw-material supplier with a raw material, and there should be at least one for each raw material of the product. Returns: – None Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 4814 4815 4816 4817 4818 4819 4820 4821 4822 4823 4824 4825 4826 4827 4828 4829 4830 4831 4832 4833 4834 4835 4836 4837 4838 4839 4840 4841 4842 4843 4844 4845 4846 4847 4848 4849 4850 4851 4852 4853 4854 4855 4856 4857 4858 4859 4860 4861 4862 4863 4864 4865 4866 4867 def behavior ( self ): """ The production loop, for the whole simulation: make one production batch after another while there are planned units left to make; when nothing can be made, wait until something may change that (see `wake_production`). It first checks the manufacturer's suppliers: each must be a raw-material supplier with a raw material, and there should be at least one for each raw material of the product. Parameters: None Attributes: None Returns: None """ if ( len ( self . suppliers ) == 0 ): self . logger . error ( "No suppliers connected to the manufacturer." ) raise ValueError ( "No suppliers connected to the manufacturer." ) if ( len ( self . suppliers ) > 0 ): # start a count of 0 units for each raw material (key: raw material ID) for supplier in self . suppliers : # iterate over supplier links if ( supplier . source . raw_material is None ): # check if the supplier has a raw material self . logger . error ( f " { self . ID } :Supplier { supplier . source . ID } does not have a raw material. Please provide a raw material for the supplier." ) raise ValueError ( f "Supplier { supplier . source . ID } does not have a raw material." ) self . raw_inventory_counts [ supplier . source . raw_material . ID ] = 0 # store initial levels if ( len ( self . suppliers ) < len ( self . product . raw_materials )): message = ( f "Manufacturer { self . ID } ( { self . name } ) has fewer suppliers ( { len ( self . suppliers ) } ) than the raw " f "materials its product needs ( { len ( self . product . raw_materials ) } ), so it cannot make any units. " f "Connect a raw-material supplier for each raw material." ) self . logger . warning ( message ) warnings . warn ( message , UserWarning ) # Production loop: make one production batch after another for as long # as there are planned units left to make. The manufacturer makes only # one production batch at a time (we wait for each to finish before # starting the next). # # When nothing can be made (nothing planned, no raw material yet, or no # free capacity), wait for something that may change that: raw # material arriving, a new production plan, or units leaving the # inventory. Waking only on raw-material deliveries is not enough. # Picture a manufacturer that plans 25 units with a batch size of 5: # one delivery of raw material covers all 25, but would start only the # first production batch, leaving the manufacturer idle with raw # material for 20 units. while len ( self . suppliers ) >= len ( self . product . raw_materials ): # check if required number of suppliers are connected made = yield self . env . process ( self . manufacture_product ()) if made > 0 : continue # go straight on to the next batch yield self . production_wake # Replace the used event with a new one for the next wait. self . production_wake = self . env . event ()

This runs as a SimPy process ( process_order starts it). Parameters: raw_mat_id ( str ) – ID of the raw material to order. supplier ( Link ) – The link to the raw-material supplier, not the supplier itself (the supplier is supplier.source ). reorder_quantity ( float ) – Units of the raw material to order. Returns: – None Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 4869 4870 4871 4872 4873 4874 4875 4876 4877 4878 4879 4880 4881 4882 4883 4884 4885 4886 4887 4888 4889 4890 4891 4892 4893 4894 4895 4896 4897 4898 4899 4900 4901 4902 4903 4904 4905 4906 4907 4908 4909 4910 4911 4912 4913 4914 4915 4916 4917 4918 4919 4920 4921 4922 4923 4924 4925 4926 4927 4928 4929 4930 4931 4932 4933 4934 4935 4936 4937 4938 4939 4940 4941 4942 def process_order_raw ( self , raw_mat_id , supplier , reorder_quantity ): """ Place a replenishment order for one raw material with one raw-material supplier, and add the units to the manufacturer's raw materials when they arrive. This runs as a SimPy process (``process_order`` starts it). Parameters: raw_mat_id (str): ID of the raw material to order. supplier (Link): The **link** to the raw-material supplier, not the supplier itself (the supplier is ``supplier.source``). reorder_quantity (float): Units of the raw material to order. Attributes: None Returns: None """ # This order is always placed. `process_order` has already chosen a # supplier whose site and link are not disrupted, and has already # counted the units this raw material is for as planned production. This process starts at the same moment, before the clock # moves on, so neither can have become disrupted in between. # # Raw material the manufacturer already holds is not a reason to skip # the order: it is set aside for units planned earlier. Using it for # these new units would leave some planned units with no raw material # to make them from, and the manufacturer would wait for them forever. if supplier . source . inventory . level < reorder_quantity : # the supplier cannot fill this order right away: record the shortage shortage = reorder_quantity - supplier . source . inventory . level supplier . source . stats . update_stats ( shortage = [ 1 , shortage ]) supplier . stats . update_stats ( shortage = [ 1 , shortage ]) self . pending_orders += 1 # count this raw-material order as placed self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . ID } :Replenishing raw material: { supplier . source . raw_material . name } from supplier: { supplier . source . ID } , order placed for { reorder_quantity } units. Current inventory level: { self . raw_inventory_counts } ." ) # The order counts as placed now, when it is placed, as in # InventoryNode.process_order, even if the supplier makes it wait. # It is recorded at the manufacturer and on the link (see LinkStatistics). self . stats . update_stats ( demand_placed = [ 1 , reorder_quantity ], transportation_cost = supplier . cost ) supplier . stats . update_stats ( demand_placed = [ 1 , reorder_quantity ], transportation_cost = supplier . cost ) supplier . stats . record_order ( reorder_quantity ) self . _warn_if_supplier_cannot_hold ( supplier , reorder_quantity ) event , man_date_ls = supplier . source . inventory . get ( reorder_quantity , site_order = True ) supplier . source . stats . update_stats ( demand_received = [ 1 , reorder_quantity ]) # update the supplier statistics for demand received # The supplier owes this order only while it waits for units: count # it as a backorder now and remove it once it is served (the same as # for other replenishment orders, see InventoryNode.process_order). order_waits = not event . triggered ordered_at = self . env . now if order_waits : supplier . source . stats . update_stats ( backorder = [ 1 , reorder_quantity ], waited = [ 1 , reorder_quantity ]) supplier . stats . update_stats ( backorder = [ 1 , reorder_quantity ], waited = [ 1 , reorder_quantity ]) yield event waited_for = self . env . now - ordered_at # 0 if the order was served at once if order_waits : # Served at last: the supplier no longer owes this order, and it # adds how long the order waited. supplier . source . stats . update_stats ( backorder = [ - 1 , - reorder_quantity ], waiting_time = waited_for ) supplier . stats . update_stats ( backorder = [ - 1 , - reorder_quantity ]) self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . ID } :shipment in transit from supplier: { supplier . source . name } ." ) lead_time = supplier . lead_time () # draw the lead time from the link validate_non_negative ( name = "lead_time" , value = lead_time ) # check if lead_time is non-negative yield self . env . timeout ( lead_time ) # lead time for the order self . stats . update_stats ( fulfillment_received = [ 1 , reorder_quantity ], inventory_spend_cost = reorder_quantity * supplier . source . sell_price ) supplier . source . stats . update_stats ( demand_fulfilled = [ 1 , reorder_quantity ]) # update the supplier statistics for demand fulfilled # On arrival, as in InventoryNode.process_order. supplier . stats . update_stats ( fulfillment_received = [ 1 , reorder_quantity ], inventory_spend_cost = reorder_quantity * supplier . source . sell_price , waiting_time = waited_for , lead_time = lead_time ) self . raw_inventory_counts [ raw_mat_id ] += reorder_quantity self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . docs.text: process_order ( supplier , reorder_quantity ) Plan the production of more product units and order the raw materials needed to make them. Each raw material is ordered from the first raw-material supplier of that raw material whose link and site are both not disrupted. place_order starts this as a SimPy process only when every raw material has such a supplier (see can_place_order ). Parameters: supplier ( Link ) – The link chosen by the supplier-selection policy. Not used: each raw material is ordered from its own raw-material supplier, as described above. reorder_quantity ( float ) – Number of product units to plan. Returns: – None Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 4990 4991 4992 4993 4994 4995 4996 4997 4998 4999 5000 5001 5002 5003 5004 5005 5006 5007 5008 5009 5010 5011 5012 5013 5014 5015 5016 5017 5018 5019 5020 5021 5022 5023 5024 5025 5026 5027 5028 5029 5030 5031 5032 5033 5034 5035 5036 5037 5038 5039 5040 5041 5042 5043 5044 5045 5046 5047 5048 5049 5050 5051 5052 5053 5054 5055 5056 5057 5058 5059 5060 def process_order ( self , supplier , reorder_quantity ): """ Plan the production of more product units and order the raw materials needed to make them. Each raw material is ordered from the first raw-material supplier of that raw material whose link and site are both not disrupted. ``place_order`` starts this as a SimPy process only when every raw material has such a supplier (see ``can_place_order``). Parameters: supplier (Link): The link chosen by the supplier-selection policy. Not used: each raw material is ordered from its own raw-material supplier, as described above. reorder_quantity (float): Number of product units to plan. Attributes: None Returns: None """ # Check the order against the capacity using the inventory position, # as InventoryNode.process_order does. Units owed to waiting customers # leave the inventory as soon as they are made, so they do not take up # space. See §3.10 for details. gross = self . position () if ( gross + reorder_quantity > self . inventory . capacity ): # check if the inventory can accommodate the reordered quantity reorder_quantity = self . inventory . capacity - gross # if not, adjust reorder quantity to order only what can fit if reorder_quantity <= 0 : return # no need to place an order if reorder quantity is zero # Units count as planned only if all their raw materials really get # ordered. Otherwise the manufacturer would count on units it can # never make: its inventory position would include them, so the policy # would not order again, and orders waiting for those units would wait # forever. place_order has already checked that every raw material can # be ordered (can_place_order); here we choose the supplier for each. # The check below matters only if a supplier was disrupted after # place_order checked (possible at time 0, see # InventoryNode.process_order), or if process_order is called directly. raw_orders = [] # (raw material ID, supplier link, quantity to order) for raw_mat , qty_per_unit , supplier_link in self . _raw_material_links (): if supplier_link is None : self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . ID } :No supplier can take an order for raw material { raw_mat . name } . No production planned." ) if self . has_suppliers (): # Every supplier of this raw material is disrupted: a # blocked order. With no supplier at all, it is not one. self . stats . update_stats ( blocked = [ 1 , reorder_quantity ]) return raw_orders . append (( raw_mat . ID , supplier_link , qty_per_unit * reorder_quantity )) # Count the planned production in on_hand right away (the same thing # InventoryNode.process_order does). Without this, the replenishment # policy could check again before the next production batch, see an # out-of-date on_hand, and order raw materials a second time for units # that are already planned. self . inventory . on_hand += reorder_quantity # New units are planned, so let the production loop know. Raw material # already on hand may be enough to start on them. self . wake_production () # Order the raw materials for these units. This happens even if an # earlier raw-material order is still on its way: that order is for # units planned earlier, so these new units need their own. for raw_mat_id , supplier_link , quantity in raw_orders : self . env . process ( self . process_order_raw ( raw_mat_id , supplier_link , quantity )) # This method runs via ``env.process``, so it must be a generator and # therefore must yield at least once — but it has nothing to wait for. # Each raw-material order is started as its own separate process and is # not awaited here (the production loop is woken when the raw material # arrives, see `wake_production`). So we yield a zero-length timeout, which # satisfies that requirement without pausing for any real time. (An # earlier version waited one time unit here for no real reason.) yield self . env . timeout ( 0 )

docs.text: Demand ( env : Environment , ID : str , name : str , order_arrival_model : Callable , order_quantity_model : Callable , demand_node : Node , tolerance : float = 0.0 , order_min_split_ratio : float = 1.0 , delivery_cost : Callable = lambda : 0 , lead_time : Callable = lambda : 0 , consume_available : bool = False , ** kwargs ) Bases: Node The Demand class represents a customer demand: a stream of customer orders arriving at one site (the demand_node ). The time between orders and the units in each order are given by functions, so they can be random. When a site cannot fill an order at once, the customer either leaves without the units or, if a tolerance is set, waits for them. It supports: a lead time and a delivery cost for each customer order, partial deliveries for customers who wait ( order_min_split_ratio ), backorders at the site for customers who wait. Parameters: env ( Environment ) – Simulation environment. ID ( str ) – Unique identifier for the customer demand. name ( str ) – Name of the customer demand. order_arrival_model ( callable ) – Time units between one customer order and the next (a number, or a function returning one each time). order_quantity_model ( callable ) – Units in each customer order (a number, or a function returning one each time). demand_node ( Node ) – The site the customers order from. (Despite its name, this is not the customer demand itself.) It cannot be a raw-material supplier. tolerance ( float , default: 0.0 ) – How long, in time units, a customer is willing to wait for units that are not there. 0 (the default) means the customer leaves at once. order_min_split_ratio ( float , default: 1.0 ) – For a customer who waits: the smallest partial delivery they accept, as a fraction of the order (more than 0, at most 1). 1 (the default) means no partial deliveries. delivery_cost ( callable , default: lambda: 0 ) – Cost of delivering each customer order (a number or a function); recorded as this customer demand's transportation cost. lead_time ( callable , default: lambda: 0 ) – Lead time of each customer order: time units from the site to the customer (a number or a function). consume_available ( bool , default: False ) – If True, a customer whose order cannot be filled in full takes the units that are there and leaves; the rest is recorded as a shortage. **kwargs – Additional keyword arguments for Node and GlobalLogger. Also accepts periodic_stats (bool, default False: if True, its statistics are updated every stats_period time units) and stats_period (float, default 1). Attributes: _info_keys ( list ) – List of keys to include in the info dictionary. order_arrival_model ( callable ) – Function giving the time units between customer orders. order_quantity_model ( callable ) – Function giving the units in each customer order. demand_node ( Node ) – The site the customers order from. customer_tolerance ( float ) – How long a customer is willing to wait (the tolerance parameter). delivery_cost ( callable ) – Function giving the cost of delivering each customer order. lead_time ( callable ) – Function giving the lead time of each customer order. min_split ( float ) – The smallest partial delivery a waiting customer accepts, as a fraction of the order. consume_available ( bool ) – If True, a customer takes the units that are there when the order cannot be filled in full. stats ( Statistics ) – Its statistics: the customer orders placed ( demand_placed ) and received ( fulfillment_received ), and the delivery costs ( transportation_cost ). Shortages and backorders are recorded at the site ( demand_node ). Methods: Name Description _process_delivery Delivers one customer order: records the delivery cost and waits for the lead time. wait_for_order Lets a customer wait for units, up to their tolerance, when the order cannot be filled at once. customer Handles one customer order. behavior Creates customer orders for the whole simulation. Behavior Customer orders arrive at the site with the times and sizes given by order_arrival_model and order_quantity_model . If the site's inventory can fill an order, it is delivered at once. If not, a shortage is recorded at the site, and with no tolerance (the default), the customer leaves without the units; with consume_available , the customer takes the units that are there and leaves; with a tolerance, the customer waits for the units, up to the tolerance, and the order counts as a backorder at the site while they wait. They may accept partial deliveries, if order_min_split_ratio is below 1. If the tolerance runs out, they leave without the rest. Assumptions The time between customer orders follows order_arrival_model ; the first order arrives at time 0. The units in each order follow order_quantity_model . The delivery cost and lead time are drawn afresh for each customer order. The site ( demand_node ) cannot be a raw-material supplier; it is usually a retailer or a distributor. Shortages and backorders are recorded at the site (``demand_node``). Returns: None """ # Take the statistics options out of kwargs before passing the rest on # to Node. They belong to Statistics, but are accepted here so users can # ask for regular statistics updates. periodic_stats = kwargs . pop ( 'periodic_stats' , False ) stats_period = kwargs . pop ( 'stats_period' , 1 ) if periodic_stats : validate_positive ( name = "stats_period" , value = stats_period ) super () . __init__ ( env = env , ID = ID , name = name , node_type = "demand" , ** kwargs ) if order_arrival_model is None or order_quantity_model is None : raise ValueError ( "Order arrival and quantity models cannot be None." ) # Turn each of these settings into a function and check that it returns # a number (see ``ensure_numeric_callable``). order_arrival_model = ensure_numeric_callable ( "order_arrival_model" , order_arrival_model ) order_quantity_model = ensure_numeric_callable ( "order_quantity_model" , order_quantity_model ) delivery_cost = ensure_numeric_callable ( "delivery_cost" , delivery_cost ) lead_time = ensure_numeric_callable ( "lead_time" , lead_time ) if demand_node is None or "supplier" in demand_node . node_type : raise ValueError ( "Demand node must be a valid non-supplier node." ) validate_non_negative ( "Customer tolerance" , tolerance ) validate_positive ( "Order Min Split Ratio" , order_min_split_ratio ) if order_min_split_ratio > 1 : self . logger . error ( "Order Min Split Ratio must be in the range (0, 1]." ) raise ValueError ( "Order Min Split Ratio must be in the range (0, 1]." ) validate_number ( name = "order_time" , value = order_arrival_model ()) validate_number ( name = "order_quantity" , value = order_quantity_model ()) validate_number ( name = "delivery_cost" , value = delivery_cost ()) # check if delivery_cost is a number validate_number ( name = "lead_time" , value = lead_time ()) # check if lead_time is a number self . order_arrival_model = order_arrival_model self . order_quantity_model = order_quantity_model self . demand_node = demand_node self . customer_tolerance = tolerance self . delivery_cost = delivery_cost self . lead_time = lead_time self . min_split = order_min_split_ratio self . consume_available = consume_available # if True, a customer takes the units that are there and leaves self . env . process ( self . behavior ()) self . stats = Statistics ( self , periodic_update = periodic_stats , period = stats_period ) # docs.text: wait_for_order ( customer_id , order_quantity ) Let a customer wait for the units of their order, up to their tolerance. While waiting, the customer's order is counted as a backorder at the site. The customer checks again each time units are added to the site's inventory. If the tolerance is infinite, the customer waits until the order is filled. Otherwise, the customer leaves as soon as their tolerance runs out, even if no new units have arrived, and whatever they were still owed is taken off the site's backorders. Parameters: order_quantity ( float ) – Units ordered. customer_id ( int ) – Customer ID for logging purposes. Attributes: customer_id ( int ) – Customer ID for logging purposes. order_quantity ( float ) – Units ordered. Returns: – None Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 5282 5283 5284 5285 5286 5287 5288 5289 5290 5291 5292 5293 5294 5295 5296 5297 5298 5299 5300 5301 5302 5303 5304 5305 5306 5307 5308 5309 5310 5311 5312 5313 5314 5315 5316 5317 5318 5319 5320 5321 5322 5323 5324 5325 5326 5327 5328 5329 5330 5331 5332 5333 5334 5335 5336 5337 5338 5339 5340 5341 5342 5343 5344 5345 5346 5347 5348 5349 5350 5351 5352 5353 5354 5355 5356 5357 5358 5359 5360 5361 5362 5363 5364 5365 5366 5367 5368 5369 5370 5371 5372 5373 5374 5375 5376 5377 5378 5379 5380 5381 def wait_for_order ( self , customer_id , order_quantity ): """ Let a customer wait for the units of their order, up to their tolerance. While waiting, the customer's order is counted as a backorder at the site. The customer checks again each time units are added to the site's inventory. If the tolerance is infinite, the customer waits until the order is filled. Otherwise, the customer leaves as soon as their tolerance runs out, even if no new units have arrived, and whatever they were still owed is taken off the site's backorders. Parameters: order_quantity (float): Units ordered. customer_id (int): Customer ID for logging purposes. Attributes: customer_id (int): Customer ID for logging purposes. order_quantity (float): Units ordered. Returns: None """ self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . ID } :Customer { customer_id } :Order quantity: { order_quantity } not available! Order will be split if split ratio is provided." ) self . demand_node . stats . update_stats ( backorder = [ 1 , order_quantity ]) arrived = self . env . now # when the order arrived, for the waiting time if ( not self . demand_node . inventory_drop . triggered ): self . demand_node . inventory_drop . succeed () # a backorder lowers the inventory position, so let the replenishment policy check partial = order_quantity if self . min_split < 1 : partial = int ( order_quantity * self . min_split ) # The customer will wait until this moment and no longer. deadline = self . env . now + self . customer_tolerance while True : available = self . _available () # When there is enough, the units are taken out of the inventory # right here, in the same step as the check, and not later inside # ``_process_delivery``. That process only starts once this step is # over. If one delivery wakes several waiting customers at the same # moment, each of them would otherwise check the inventory before # any of them had taken anything, all would see the same units, and # all would think those units were theirs. if order_quantity <= available : # check if remaining order quantity is available get_event , _ = self . demand_node . inventory . get ( order_quantity ) self . env . process ( self . _process_delivery ( order_quantity , customer_id , get_event )) self . demand_node . stats . update_stats ( backorder = [ - 1 , - order_quantity ], waiting_time = self . env . now - arrived ) order_quantity = 0 break # ``partial`` can round down to 0 for a small order, so also check # that there is at least one unit to send. Asking the inventory for # 0 units is an error in SimPy. elif available > 0 and available >= partial : # or else at least the smallest partial delivery is there get_event , _ = self . demand_node . inventory . get ( available ) self . env . process ( self . _process_delivery ( available , customer_id , get_event )) # Partial delivery: the backorder still counts as 1 order (one customer # still waiting), and only its units go down. Each delivery adds 1 to the # order counts of fulfillment_received and demand_fulfilled (inside # _process_delivery), so 1 is taken off them here: the customer's order is # counted once, when it is finally filled. self . demand_node . stats . update_stats ( backorder = [ 0 , - available ], demand_fulfilled = [ - 1 , 0 ]) self . stats . update_stats ( fulfillment_received = [ - 1 , 0 ]) order_quantity -= available # update order quantity # Otherwise there is not enough yet, and the customer keeps waiting. # No shortage is recorded here: it was recorded once, when the order # arrived (in _enqueue_for_tolerance). Recording it again on every # check would count the same missing units many times. if self . env . now >= deadline : break # the customer's tolerance has run out # Wait for whichever comes first: new units arriving at the site, or # the end of the customer's tolerance. Without the second part, a # customer would only notice that their tolerance had run out when # units next arrived — and if none ever arrived, they would wait # (and stay counted as a backorder) forever. raised_event = self . demand_node . inventory_raised # the node's current "inventory raised" signal if deadline == float ( 'inf' ): yield raised_event # infinite tolerance: only new units can end the wait else : yield raised_event | self . env . timeout ( deadline - self . env . now ) # The "units arrived" signal can fire only once, so after it fires it # is swapped for a fresh one. Several customers may be waiting on the # same signal; only the first one to wake should swap it. If a later # customer swapped it again, the customers who had already moved on # to the first fresh signal would be left waiting on one that never # fires. Hence the check that the node still holds the signal we # waited on. If we woke because our tolerance ran out instead, the # signal has not fired and must be left alone for the others. if raised_event . triggered and self . demand_node . inventory_raised is raised_event : self . demand_node . inventory_raised = self . env . event () if order_quantity > 0 : # the customer gives up and leaves without the rest of the order # They are no longer waiting, so take what they were still owed off # the site's current backorders. (The count drops by 1 even after # partial deliveries: one customer is one backorder until they are # fully served or leave.) Without this, the site would keep placing # replenishment orders for a customer who has already gone. # The units they were still owed are never delivered: a lost sale. self . demand_node . stats . update_stats ( backorder = [ - 1 , - order_quantity ], lost_sales = [ 1 , order_quantity ]) self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . ID } :Customer { customer_id } : remaining order quantity: { order_quantity } not available! Customer leaves." )

docs.text: customer ( customer_id , order_quantity ) Handle one customer order, by passing it to the helper for its case: the site is disrupted: the order is not placed. A disrupted site takes no new orders, so this is a sale it loses because of the disruption, recorded in its disruption_lost_sales (not as demand received, shortage or backorder). Customers who were already waiting when the disruption started keep waiting, and deliveries already on their way still arrive; the site can fill the whole order: _serve_in_full ; otherwise, with consume_available and some units there: _serve_partial_consume ; otherwise, for a customer with a tolerance: _enqueue_for_tolerance (or _discard_unservable if the order is too big for the site ever to hold); otherwise: _serve_no_tolerance . Parameters: customer_id ( int ) – Customer ID for logging purposes. order_quantity ( float ) – Units ordered. Returns: – None Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 5479 5480 5481 5482 5483 5484 5485 5486 5487 5488 5489 5490 5491 5492 5493 5494 5495 5496 5497 5498 5499 5500 5501 5502 5503 5504 5505 5506 5507 5508 5509 5510 5511 5512 5513 5514 5515 5516 5517 5518 5519 5520 5521 5522 5523 5524 5525 5526 5527 5528 5529 5530 def customer ( self , customer_id , order_quantity ): """ Handle one customer order, by passing it to the helper for its case: - the site is disrupted: the order is not placed. A disrupted site takes no new orders, so this is a sale it loses because of the disruption, recorded in its ``disruption_lost_sales`` (not as demand received, shortage or backorder). Customers who were already waiting when the disruption started keep waiting, and deliveries already on their way still arrive; - the site can fill the whole order: ``_serve_in_full``; - otherwise, with ``consume_available`` and some units there: ``_serve_partial_consume``; - otherwise, for a customer with a tolerance: ``_enqueue_for_tolerance`` (or ``_discard_unservable`` if the order is too big for the site ever to hold); - otherwise: ``_serve_no_tolerance``. Parameters: customer_id (int): Customer ID for logging purposes. order_quantity (float): Units ordered. Returns: None """ if self . demand_node . node_status != "active" : # A disrupted site takes no new orders, from other sites or from # customers (the same rule as Node.place_order). The customer goes # away, and the site loses the sale. This is not a shortage: the site # may have the units, it just cannot take the order. Nothing else is # recorded, and the customer's own demand_placed does not count it, # as for a replenishment order that is not placed. self . logger . info ( f " { self . env . now : .4f } : { self . ID } :Customer { customer_id } : { self . demand_node . ID } is disrupted, order of { order_quantity } units not placed (lost sale)." ) self . demand_node . stats . update_stats ( disruption_lost_sales = [ 1 , order_quantity ]) return available = self . _available () self . stats . update_stats ( demand_placed = [ 1 , order_quantity ]) # The smallest part this customer will take: the whole order when no # partial delivery is allowed (min_split >= 1), otherwise the smallest # partial delivery. This matches how ``wait_for_order`` computes ``partial``. min_chunk = order_quantity if self . min_split >= 1 else int ( order_quantity * self . min_split ) if order_quantity <= available : yield from self . _serve_in_full ( order_quantity , customer_id ) elif self . consume_available and available > 0 : yield from self . _serve_partial_consume ( order_quantity , available , customer_id ) elif self . customer_tolerance > 0 : if min_chunk > self . demand_node . inventory . capacity : # The order can never be served — even a full inventory cannot # cover the smallest part the customer accepts. Discard it # rather than create a backorder that would lead to a # replenishment order the inventory can't hold. yield from self . _discard_unservable ( order_quantity , customer_id ) else : yield from self . _enqueue_for_tolerance ( order_quantity , available , customer_id ) else : yield from self . _serve_no_tolerance ( order_quantity , available , customer_id )

docs.text: ensure_numeric_callable ( name : str , value ) Turn a value that is "a number, or a zero-arg function returning a number" into a zero-arg function. Many constructors accept either a plain number or a zero-arg function (lead times, arrival intervals, recovery times). The earlier version simply did if not callable(value): value = lambda val=value: val which accepted any function at all — even a class like int or a generator function — so the later value() call could fail deep inside a running simulation, far from where the mistake was made. This helper avoids that by calling the function once when it is set up and checking the result is a real number, so a bad value is reported right away, at construction, with a clear message naming the parameter at fault. Parameters: name ( str ) – Parameter name used in error messages. value – A number or a zero-arg callable returning a number. Returns: callable – A zero-arg callable. If value was a scalar it is wrapped; if it was already callable the original is returned unchanged. Raises: TypeError – If value is callable but invoking it raises (the original exception is chained). ValueError – If the (wrapped) callable returns a non-numeric value. Note The validation invocation samples the callable once at construction time. For stateful generators or iterators (rather than pure functions) this advances state before the simulation starts; if that matters, wrap the iterator in a closure that materialises the first sample lazily, or pass a numeric scalar instead. Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/core.py 185 186 187 188 189 190 191 192 193 194 195 196 197 198 199 200 201 202 203 204 205 206 207 208 209 210 211 212 213 214 215 216 217 218 219 220 221 222 223 224 225 226 227 228 229 230 231 232 233 234 235 236 237 238 239 240 241 242 243 244 245 def ensure_numeric_callable ( name : str , value ): """ Turn a value that is "a number, or a zero-arg function returning a number" into a zero-arg function. Many constructors accept either a plain number or a zero-arg function (lead times, arrival intervals, recovery times). The earlier version simply did ```python if not callable(value): value = lambda val=value: val ``` which accepted any function at all — even a class like ``int`` or a generator function — so the later ``value()`` call could fail deep inside a running simulation, far from where the mistake was made. This helper avoids that by calling the function once when it is set up and checking the result is a real number, so a bad value is reported right away, at construction, with a clear message naming the parameter at fault. Parameters: name (str): Parameter name used in error messages. value: A number or a zero-arg callable returning a number. Returns: callable: A zero-arg callable. If ``value`` was a scalar it is wrapped; if it was already callable the original is returned unchanged. Raises: TypeError: If ``value`` is callable but invoking it raises (the original exception is chained). ValueError: If the (wrapped) callable returns a non-numeric value. Note: The validation invocation samples the callable once at construction time. For stateful generators or iterators (rather than pure functions) this advances state before the simulation starts; if that matters, wrap the iterator in a closure that materialises the first sample lazily, or pass a numeric scalar instead. """ if not callable ( value ): scalar = value value = lambda val = scalar : val try : sample = value () except Exception as e : global_logger . error ( f " { name } : callable raised { type ( e ) . __name__ } on validation call: { e } " ) raise TypeError ( f " { name } must be a number or a zero-arg callable returning a number; " f "calling it raised { type ( e ) . __name__ } : { e } " ) from e if not isinstance ( sample , numbers . Number ): global_logger . error ( f " { name } must be a number or a zero-arg callable returning a number; " f "got { type ( sample ) . __name__ } ( { sample !r} )." ) raise ValueError ( f " { name } must be a number or a zero-arg callable returning a number; " f "got { type ( sample ) . __name__ } ." ) return value
