docs.text: The GlobalLogger class provides a flexible logging system for the SupplyNetPy simulations. It allows logging messages to both the console and a file, and can be easily enabled or disabled during runtime. SupplyNetPy.Components.logger GlobalLogger GlobalLogger ( logger_name = _LIBRARY_LOGGER_NAME , log_to_file = False , log_file = 'simulation_trace.log' , log_to_screen = False ) Bases: LoggerAdapter Library-wide logging.LoggerAdapter with on/off file and screen handlers. Subclasses logging.LoggerAdapter so callers can write node.logger.info(...) (and debug / warning / error / critical ) directly. (Older code had to write node.logger.logger.info(...) with two .logger steps; that is no longer needed.) The underlying logging.Logger is still reachable as self.logger (the standard adapter attribute), so older code that goes through that attribute keeps working. The wrapper does nothing by default. GlobalLogger() attaches only a logging.NullHandler and does not open any file — output is opt-in. Call enable_logging (or pass log_to_file=True / log_to_screen=True to the constructor) to attach real handlers. This is the documented Python-library logging pattern; see https://docs.python.org/3/howto/logging.html#configuring-logging-for-a-library The library exports a module-level global_logger = GlobalLogger() from core.py whose underlying logging.Logger is named "sim_trace" . Every per-node logger created by Node lives at "sim_trace.<node.ID>" and propagates up to "sim_trace" — so all log routing is configured in one place by calling scm.global_logger.enable_logging(...) . simulate_sc_net(logging=True) does this automatically; users who drive env.run(...) themselves and want a log file must call it explicitly. Parameters: logger_name ( str , default: _LIBRARY_LOGGER_NAME ) – Name of the underlying logging.Logger . Defaults to "sim_trace" . log_to_file ( bool , default: False ) – Attach a logging.FileHandler writing to log_file (mode 'w' ). Defaults to False — opt-in. log_file ( str , default: 'simulation_trace.log' ) – Destination file path. Only opened when log_to_file is True . Defaults to "simulation_trace.log" . log_to_screen ( bool , default: False ) – Attach a logging.StreamHandler . Defaults to False — opt-in. Attributes: logger ( Logger ) – The underlying logger instance (inherited from logging.LoggerAdapter ). log_to_file ( bool ) – Current file-handler flag. log_to_screen ( bool ) – Current screen-handler flag. log_file ( str ) – Current destination file path. Methods: Name Description debug/info/warning/error/critical/log/exception Inherited from logging.LoggerAdapter — call them directly on the adapter (e.g. logger.info(...) ) instead of going through .logger . set_log_file Set the destination file and re-attach handlers. get_log_file Return the current log file path. set_logger Rebind self.logger to a different name. configure_logger Re-build handlers from current flags. Always attaches logging.NullHandler . enable_logging Opt-in: attach handlers and unmute the logger. disable_logging Mute the logger and drop handlers (NullHandler stays). Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/logger.py 94 95 96 97 98 99 100 101 102 103 104 105 106 107 108 109 110 111 112 113 114 115 116 117 118 def __init__ ( self , logger_name = _LIBRARY_LOGGER_NAME , log_to_file = False , log_file = 'simulation_trace.log' , log_to_screen = False ): logger = logging . getLogger ( logger_name ) logger . setLevel ( logging . DEBUG ) # Stop this main logger from passing its messages further up to # Python's own root logger — otherwise our log lines would also land in # whatever logging the host application has set up. (Per-node loggers # still pass their messages up to this one; only this top logger stops # here.) if logger_name == _LIBRARY_LOGGER_NAME : logger . propagate = False # Start clean: an earlier GlobalLogger may have muted this same # underlying Python logger by setting disabled=True. logger . disabled = False # extra=None: we add no extra fields to each message, so the base # LoggerAdapter passes the message through unchanged. super () . __init__ ( logger , extra = None ) self . log_to_file = log_to_file self . log_to_screen = log_to_screen self . log_file = log_file self . configure_logger () set_log_file set_log_file ( filename ) Set the destination log file and re-attach handlers. Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/logger.py 120 121 122 123 def set_log_file ( self , filename ): """Set the destination log file and re-attach handlers.""" self . log_file = filename self . configure_logger () get_log_file get_log_file () Return the current log file path. Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/logger.py 125 126 127 def get_log_file ( self ): """Return the current log file path.""" return self . log_file set_logger set_logger ( logger_name ) Rebind the underlying logger to a different name. Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/logger.py 129 130 131 def set_logger ( self , logger_name ): """Rebind the underlying logger to a different name.""" self . logger = logging . getLogger ( logger_name ) configure_logger configure_logger () Replace this logger's handlers based on current log_to_file / log_to_screen flags. A logging.NullHandler is always attached so the logger never triggers Python's "No handlers could be found" stderr fallback — the recommended default for library loggers. Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/logger.py 133 134 135 136 137 138 139 140 141 142 143 144 145 146 147 148 149 150 151 152 153 154 def configure_logger ( self ): """ Replace this logger's handlers based on current ``log_to_file`` / ``log_to_screen`` flags. A `logging.NullHandler` is always attached so the logger never triggers Python's "No handlers could be found" stderr fallback — the recommended default for library loggers. """ self . _replace_handlers ([ logging . NullHandler ()]) if self . log_to_screen : screen_handler = logging . StreamHandler () screen_handler . setLevel ( logging . DEBUG ) screen_handler . setFormatter ( logging . Formatter ( _LOG_FORMAT )) screen_handler . addFilter ( _ShortNameFilter ()) self . logger . addHandler ( screen_handler ) if self . log_to_file : file_handler = logging . FileHandler ( self . log_file , mode = 'w' ) file_handler . setLevel ( logging . DEBUG ) file_handler . setFormatter ( logging . Formatter ( _LOG_FORMAT )) file_handler . addFilter ( _ShortNameFilter ()) self . logger . addHandler ( file_handler ) enable_logging enable_logging ( log_to_file = True , log_to_screen = True ) Opt-in. Unmute the logger and (re)attach screen and/or file handlers according to the arguments. Defaults are True for both so a bare enable_logging() call gives the user the historical "noisy" behavior on demand. Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/logger.py 156 157 158 159 160 161 162 163 164 def enable_logging ( self , log_to_file = True , log_to_screen = True ): """Opt-in. Unmute the logger and (re)attach screen and/or file handlers according to the arguments. Defaults are ``True`` for both so a bare ``enable_logging()`` call gives the user the historical "noisy" behavior on demand.""" self . logger . disabled = False self . log_to_file = log_to_file self . log_to_screen = log_to_screen self . configure_logger () disable_logging disable_logging () Mute the logger. Sets self.logger.disabled = True and drops all handlers (a logging.NullHandler is re-attached so the logger remains well-formed). Note: this only affects self.logger — it does not touch the global logging.disable switch, which would suppress the host application's own logging. Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/logger.py 166 167 168 169 170 171 172 173 174 175 def disable_logging ( self ): """Mute the logger. Sets ``self.logger.disabled = True`` and drops all handlers (a `logging.NullHandler` is re-attached so the logger remains well-formed). Note: this only affects ``self.logger`` — it does not touch the global ``logging.disable`` switch, which would suppress the host application's own logging.""" self . logger . disabled = True self . _replace_handlers ([ logging . NullHandler ()]) self . log_to_file = False self . log_to_screen = False

Call enable_logging (or pass log_to_file=True / log_to_screen=True to the constructor) to attach real handlers. This is the documented Python-library logging pattern; see https://docs.python.org/3/howto/logging.html#configuring-logging-for-a-library The library exports a module-level global_logger = GlobalLogger() from core.py whose underlying logging.Logger is named "sim_trace" . Every per-node logger created by Node lives at "sim_trace.<node.ID>" and propagates up to "sim_trace" — so all log routing is configured in one place by calling scm.global_logger.enable_logging(...) . simulate_sc_net(logging=True) does this automatically; users who drive env.run(...) themselves and want a log file must call it explicitly. Defaults to "sim_trace" . log_to_file ( bool , default: False ) – Attach a logging.FileHandler writing to log_file (mode 'w' ). Defaults to False — opt-in. log_file ( str , default: 'simulation_trace.log' ) – Destination file path. Only opened when log_to_file is True . Defaults to "simulation_trace.log" . log_to_screen ( bool , default: False ) – Attach a logging.StreamHandler . Defaults to False — opt-in. docs.text: The utility module offers various functions to create, simulate, access information, and visualize the supply chain network more effectively. SupplyNetPy.Components.utilities create_sc_net create_sc_net ( nodes : list , links : list , demands : list , env : Environment = None ) Takes the node, link, and demand descriptions, builds the matching supply chain node, link, and demand objects, and gathers them all into one dictionary that represents the network. Each of nodes , links , and demands must be all one kind — either all dicts (the description style) or all ready-made objects ( Node / Link / Demand instances). You cannot mix the two in a single list, because the fresh simpy.Environment made for the dict items would not match the one the ready-made objects were built with. If any list contains ready-made objects, you must pass env yourself, and each object's own env must be that same environment. Parameters: nodes ( list ) – The nodes (sites): dicts, or Node objects. links ( list ) – The links between them: dicts, or Link objects. demands ( list ) – The customer demands: dicts, or Demand objects. env ( Environment , default: None ) – A SimPy Environment object. If not provided, a new environment will be created. Attributes: global_logger ( GlobalLogger ) – The global logger instance used for logging messages. supplychainnet ( dict ) – A dictionary representing the supply chain network. used_ids ( set ) – The IDs used so far, to catch duplicates. num_suppliers ( int ) – Number of raw-material suppliers (finite and infinite). num_manufacturers ( int ) – Number of manufacturers. num_distributors ( int ) – Number of distributors and warehouses. num_retailers ( int ) – Number of retailers, stores and shops. Raises: ValueError – If the SimPy Environment object is not provided or if there are duplicate IDs in nodes, links, or demands. ValueError – If any of nodes / links / demands mixes dicts and pre-built domain objects. ValueError – If a pre-built object's env does not match the provided env . ValueError – If an invalid node type is encountered. ValueError – If an invalid source or sink node is specified in a link. ValueError – If a customer demand names a demand_node (the site its customers order from) that is not among the nodes. Returns: dict – A dictionary representing the supply chain network. Each of ``nodes``, ``links``, and ``demands`` must be all one kind — either all dicts (the description style) or all ready-made objects (``Node`` / ``Link`` / ``Demand`` instances). You cannot mix the two in a single list, because the fresh ``simpy.Environment`` made for the dict items would not match the one the ready-made objects were built with. If any list contains ready-made objects, you must pass ``env`` yourself, and each object's own ``env`` must be that same environment. Parameters: nodes (list): The nodes (sites): dicts, or `Node` objects. links (list): The links between them: dicts, or `Link` objects. demands (list): The customer demands: dicts, or `Demand` objects. env (simpy.Environment, optional): A SimPy Environment object. If not provided, a new environment will be created. Attributes: global_logger (GlobalLogger): The global logger instance used for logging messages. supplychainnet (dict): A dictionary representing the supply chain network. used_ids (set): The IDs used so far, to catch duplicates. num_suppliers (int): Number of raw-material suppliers (finite and infinite). num_manufacturers (int): Number of manufacturers. num_distributors (int): Number of distributors and warehouses. num_retailers (int): Number of retailers, stores and shops. Raises: ValueError: If the SimPy Environment object is not provided or if there are duplicate IDs in nodes, links, or demands. ValueError: If any of ``nodes`` / ``links`` / ``demands`` mixes dicts and pre-built domain objects. ValueError: If a pre-built object's ``env`` does not match the provided ``env``. ValueError: If an invalid node type is encountered. ValueError: If an invalid source or sink node is specified in a link. """ # Reject lists that mix dicts and pre-built objects, right at the start. We # check every element, not just the first one. ID ) global_logger . error ( f "Invalid node type { node . node_type } " ) raise ValueError ( "Invalid node type" ) counters [ _NODE_DISPATCH [ nt ][ 1 ]] += 1 for link in links : if isinstance ( link , dict ): check_duplicate_id ( used_ids , link [ "ID" ], "link ID" ) source = None sink = None node_ids = supplychainnet [ "nodes" ] . keys () if ( link [ "source" ] in node_ids ): source_id = link [ "source" ] source = supplychainnet [ "nodes" ][ f " { source_id } " ] if ( link [ "sink" ] in node_ids ): sink_id = link [ "sink" ] sink = supplychainnet [ "nodes" ][ f " { sink_id } " ] if ( source is None or sink is None ): global_logger . error ( f "Invalid source or sink node { link [ 'source' ] } { link [ 'sink' ] } " ) raise ValueError ( "Invalid source or sink node" ) exclude_keys = { 'source' , 'sink' } params = { k : v for k , v in link . items () if k not in exclude_keys } link_id = params [ 'ID' ] supplychainnet [ "links" ][ f " { link_id } " ] = Link ( env = env , source = source , sink = sink , ** params ) elif isinstance ( link , Link ): check_duplicate_id ( used_ids , link . docs.text: create_sc_net ( nodes : list , links : list , demands : list , env : Environment = None ) Takes the node, link, and demand descriptions, builds the matching supply chain node, link, and demand objects, and gathers them all into one dictionary that represents the network. Each of nodes , links , and demands must be all one kind — either all dicts (the description style) or all ready-made objects ( Node / Link / Demand instances). You cannot mix the two in a single list, because the fresh simpy.Environment made for the dict items would not match the one the ready-made objects were built with. If any list contains ready-made objects, you must pass env yourself, and each object's own env must be that same environment. Parameters: nodes ( list ) – The nodes (sites): dicts, or Node objects. links ( list ) – The links between them: dicts, or Link objects. demands ( list ) – The customer demands: dicts, or Demand objects. env ( Environment , default: None ) – A SimPy Environment object. If not provided, a new environment will be created. Attributes: global_logger ( GlobalLogger ) – The global logger instance used for logging messages. supplychainnet ( dict ) – A dictionary representing the supply chain network. used_ids ( set ) – The IDs used so far, to catch duplicates. num_suppliers ( int ) – Number of raw-material suppliers (finite and infinite). num_manufacturers ( int ) – Number of manufacturers. num_distributors ( int ) – Number of distributors and warehouses. num_retailers ( int ) – Number of retailers, stores and shops. Raises: ValueError – If the SimPy Environment object is not provided or if there are duplicate IDs in nodes, links, or demands. ValueError – If any of nodes / links / demands mixes dicts and pre-built domain objects. ValueError – If a pre-built object's env does not match the provided env . ValueError – If an invalid node type is encountered. ValueError – If an invalid source or sink node is specified in a link. ValueError – If a customer demand names a demand_node (the site its customers order from) that is not among the nodes. Returns: dict – A dictionary representing the supply chain network. Environment = None ): """ Takes the node, link, and demand descriptions, builds the matching supply chain node, link, and demand objects, and gathers them all into one dictionary that represents the network. Each of ``nodes``, ``links``, and ``demands`` must be all one kind — either all dicts (the description style) or all ready-made objects (``Node`` / ``Link`` / ``Demand`` instances). You cannot mix the two in a single list, because the fresh ``simpy.Environment`` made for the dict items would not match the one the ready-made objects were built with. If any list contains ready-made objects, you must pass ``env`` yourself, and each object's own ``env`` must be that same environment. Parameters: nodes (list): The nodes (sites): dicts, or `Node` objects. links (list): The links between them: dicts, or `Link` objects. demands (list): The customer demands: dicts, or `Demand` objects. env (simpy.Environment, optional): A SimPy Environment object. If not provided, a new environment will be created. Attributes: global_logger (GlobalLogger): The global logger instance used for logging messages. supplychainnet (dict): A dictionary representing the supply chain network. used_ids (set): The IDs used so far, to catch duplicates. num_suppliers (int): Number of raw-material suppliers (finite and infinite). num_manufacturers (int): Number of manufacturers. num_distributors (int): Number of distributors and warehouses. num_retailers (int): Number of retailers, stores and shops. Raises: ValueError: If the SimPy Environment object is not provided or if there are duplicate IDs in nodes, links, or demands. ValueError: If any of ``nodes`` / ``links`` / ``demands`` mixes dicts and pre-built domain objects. ValueError: If a pre-built object's ``env`` does not match the provided ``env``. ValueError: If an invalid node type is encountered. ValueError: If an invalid source or sink node is specified in a link. ValueError: If a customer demand names a ``demand_node`` (the site its customers order from) that is not among the nodes. Returns: dict: A dictionary representing the supply chain network. """ # Reject lists that mix dicts and pre-built objects, right at the start. We # check every element, not just the first one. An earlier version only # looked at element 0, so a list like ``[dict, Node_instance, ...]`` slipped # past the "env required" check (because ``nodes[0]`` was a dict) and then # built the later object with a fresh env, throwing away the env that object # was actually created with. def _check_homogeneous ( items , obj_cls , list_name ): has_dict = any ( isinstance ( x , dict ) for x in items ) has_obj = any ( isinstance ( x , obj_cls ) for x in items ) if has_dict and has_obj : global_logger . error ( f " { list_name } list mixes dicts and { obj_cls . __name__ } instances." ) raise ValueError ( f " { list_name } list mixes dicts and { obj_cls . __name__ } instances; " f "use all dicts or all { obj_cls . __name__ } instances." ) _check_homogeneous ( nodes , Node , "nodes" ) _check_homogeneous ( links , Link , "links" ) _check_homogeneous ( demands , Demand , "demands" ) # ``env`` is required whenever ANY list contains a pre-built domain object, # regardless of the element's position. Scanning each list (rather than # indexing [0]) also avoids an IndexError on legitimately empty lists. any_object = ( any ( isinstance ( x , Node ) for x in nodes ) or any ( isinstance ( x , Link ) for x in links ) or any ( isinstance ( x , Demand ) for x in demands ) ) if any_object and env is None : global_logger . error ( "Please provide SimPy Environment object env" ) raise ValueError ( "A SimPy Environment object is required!" ) if len ( nodes ) == 0 or len ( links ) == 0 or len ( demands ) == 0 : global_logger . error ( "Nodes, links, and demands cannot be empty" ) raise ValueError ( "Nodes, links, and demands cannot be empty" ) if ( env is None ): env = simpy . Environment () # When the user supplied both ``env`` and pre-built objects, each object's # own ``env`` must match — otherwise the returned supplychainnet would # combine processes from two different environments and nothing would run # consistently. The old code simply ignored the object's env; this check # surfaces the mismatch loudly. def _check_env_match ( items , obj_cls , list_name ): for i , x in enumerate ( items ): if isinstance ( x , obj_cls ) and getattr ( x , "env" , None ) is not env : global_logger . error ( f " { list_name } [ { i } ] ( { getattr ( x , 'ID' , '<no ID>' ) } ) was built against a " f "different simpy.Environment than the one passed to create_sc_net." ) raise ValueError ( f " { list_name } [ { i } ] env does not match the env passed to create_sc_net." ) _check_env_match ( nodes , Node , "nodes" ) _check_env_match ( links , Link , "links" ) _check_env_match ( demands , Demand , "demands" ) supplychainnet = { "nodes" :{}, "links" :{}, "demands" :{}} # create empty supply chain network # Use a set, not a list: checking membership and adding/removing items are # all fast (constant time), so building a network with many nodes stays # fast. ``check_duplicate_id`` works with either a set or a list. used_ids = set () # Counts of each node category, keyed by the names used in # ``_NODE_DISPATCH``. Using one dict (instead of four separate ``num_*`` # variables) lets us count with a single ``counters[category] += 1`` rather # than a long if/else chain. counters = { "num_suppliers" : 0 , "num_manufacturers" : 0 , "num_distributors" : 0 , "num_retailers" : 0 } for node in nodes : if isinstance ( node , dict ): check_duplicate_id ( used_ids , node [ "ID" ], "node ID" ) node_id = node [ "ID" ] try : nt = NodeType ( node [ "node_type" ]) except ValueError : used_ids . remove ( node [ "ID" ]) global_logger . error ( f "Invalid node type { node [ 'node_type' ] } " ) raise ValueError ( "Invalid node type" ) cls , counter_key , drop_node_type = _NODE_DISPATCH [ nt ] # ``Manufacturer.__init__`` is the only constructor that does not # accept ``node_type``, so for it we drop that key. The # ``drop_node_type`` flag records this one difference. kwargs = { k : v for k , v in node . items () if not ( drop_node_type and k == "node_type" )} supplychainnet [ "nodes" ][ f " { node_id } " ] = cls ( env = env , ** kwargs ) counters [ counter_key ] += 1 elif isinstance ( node , Node ): check_duplicate_id ( used_ids , node . ID , "node ID" ) node_id = node . ID supplychainnet [ "nodes" ][ f " { node_id } " ] = node try : nt = NodeType ( node . node_type ) except ValueError : used_ids . remove ( node . ID ) global_logger . error ( f "Invalid node type { node . node_type } " ) raise ValueError ( "Invalid node type" ) counters [ _NODE_DISPATCH [ nt ][ 1 ]] += 1 for link in links : if isinstance ( link , dict ): check_duplicate_id ( used_ids , link [ "ID" ], "link ID" ) source = None sink = None node_ids = supplychainnet [ "nodes" ] . keys () if ( link [ "source" ] in node_ids ): source_id = link [ "source" ] source = supplychainnet [ "nodes" ][ f " { source_id } " ] if ( link [ "sink" ] in node_ids ): sink_id = link [ "sink" ] sink = supplychainnet [ "nodes" ][ f " { sink_id } " ] if ( source is None or sink is None ): global_logger . error ( f "Invalid source or sink node { link [ 'source' ] } { link [ 'sink' ] } " ) raise ValueError ( "Invalid source or sink node" ) exclude_keys = { 'source' , 'sink' } params = { k : v for k , v in link . items () if k not in exclude_keys } link_id = params [ 'ID' ] supplychainnet [ "links" ][ f " { link_id } " ] = Link ( env = env , source = source , sink = sink , ** params ) elif isinstance ( link , Link ): check_duplicate_id ( used_ids , link . ID , "link ID" ) supplychainnet [ "links" ][ f " { link . ID } " ] = link # Every link is known now, so each site's supplier-selection policy can # check its settings against the links (SelectProbabilistic: every link # has a probability). Mistakes then show before the run, not at the first # order. A manufacturer does not use its policy yet, so it is skipped. for node in supplychainnet [ "nodes" ] . values (): check_links = getattr ( getattr ( node , "selection_policy" , None ), "check_links" , None ) if check_links is not None and not isinstance ( node , Manufacturer ): check_links () for d in demands : if isinstance ( d , dict ): check_duplicate_id ( used_ids , d [ "ID" ], "demand ID" ) demand_node = None # the site this customer demand's customers order from node_ids = supplychainnet [ "nodes" ] . keys () if d [ 'demand_node' ] in node_ids : demand_node_id = d [ 'demand_node' ] demand_node = supplychainnet [ "nodes" ][ f " { demand_node_id } " ] if ( demand_node is None ): global_logger . error ( f "Invalid demand node { d [ 'demand_node' ] } " ) raise ValueError ( "Invalid demand node" ) exclude_keys = { 'demand_node' , 'node_type' } params = { k : v for k , v in d . items () if k not in exclude_keys } demand_id = params [ 'ID' ] supplychainnet [ "demands" ][ f " { demand_id } " ] = Demand ( env = env , demand_node = demand_node , ** params ) elif isinstance ( d , Demand ): check_duplicate_id ( used_ids , d . ID , "demand ID" ) supplychainnet [ "demands" ][ f " { d . ID } " ] = d supplychainnet [ "env" ] = env supplychainnet [ "num_of_nodes" ] = sum ( counters . values ()) supplychainnet [ "num_of_links" ] = len ( links ) supplychainnet . update ( counters ) return supplychainnet

docs.text: check_duplicate_id ( used_ids , new_id , entity_type = 'ID' ) Checks if new_id is already in used_ids . If it is, logs an error and raises ValueError ; otherwise inserts it. Accepts either a set (preferred — O(1) membership and insert) or a list (kept for backward compatibility with external callers — O(n) on both operations). create_sc_net passes a set ; the helper duck-types the insert call so existing user code that builds its own list keeps working unchanged. Parameters: used_ids ( set | list ) – Container of already-used IDs. Mutated in place. new_id ( str ) – The new ID to check and insert. entity_type ( str , default: 'ID' ) – Type of the entity for which the ID is being checked (e.g., "node ID" , "link ID" ). Returns: – None Raises: ValueError – If new_id is already in used_ids . If it is, logs an error and raises ``ValueError``; otherwise inserts it. Accepts either a ``set`` (preferred — O(1) membership and insert) or a ``list`` (kept for backward compatibility with external callers — O(n) on both operations). ``create_sc_net`` passes a ``set``; the helper duck-types the insert call so existing user code that builds its own ``list`` keeps working unchanged. Parameters: used_ids (set | list): Container of already-used IDs. Mutated in place. new_id (str): The new ID to check and insert. entity_type (str): Type of the entity for which the ID is being checked (e.g., ``"node ID"``, ``"link ID"``). Returns: None Raises: ValueError: If ``new_id`` is already in ``used_ids``. """ if new_id in used_ids : global_logger . error ( f "Duplicate { entity_type } { new_id } " ) raise ValueError ( f "Duplicate { entity_type } " ) # A ``set`` adds items with ``.add`` and a ``list`` with ``.append``. We # use whichever method the passed-in container has, instead of checking its # exact type, so other set-like or list-like containers work too. insert = getattr ( used_ids , "add" , None ) or used_ids . append insert ( new_id )

docs.text: reset_stats ( supplychainnet ) Start the statistics of the whole network again from zero: every node, every customer demand and every link. This is what a warm-up uses. A warm-up is an opening stretch of a run that is left out of the statistics, because a run starts in an unusual state (nothing in transit, no orders waiting). Run for the warm-up period, reset, and carry on running: scm.simulate_sc_net(sc, sim_time=31) # warm-up scm.reset_stats(sc) scm.simulate_sc_net(sc, sim_time=T + 1) The simulation carries on unchanged and only the counting starts again. Each node, customer demand and link keeps what describes the present (see Statistics.reset and LinkStatistics.reset ). The network results in supplychainnet are not cleared here; simulate_sc_net works them out again from the statistics when it next stops. Parameters: supplychainnet ( dict ) – The supply chain network, as returned by create_sc_net . Returns: – None Source code in src/SupplyNetPy/Components/utilities.py 844 845 846 847 848 849 850 851 852 853 854 855 856 857 858 859 860 861 862 863 864 865 866 867 868 869 870 871 872 873 874 def reset_stats ( supplychainnet ): """ Start the statistics of the whole network again from zero: every node, every customer demand and every link. This is what a warm-up uses. A warm-up is an opening stretch of a run that is left out of the statistics, because a run starts in an unusual state (nothing in transit, no orders waiting). Run for the warm-up period, reset, and carry on running: ```python scm.simulate_sc_net(sc, sim_time=31) # warm-up scm.reset_stats(sc) scm.simulate_sc_net(sc, sim_time=T + 1) ``` The simulation carries on unchanged and only the counting starts again. Each node, customer demand and link keeps what describes the present (see ``Statistics.reset`` and ``LinkStatistics.reset``). The network results in ``supplychainnet`` are not cleared here; ``simulate_sc_net`` works them out again from the statistics when it next stops. Parameters: supplychainnet (dict): The supply chain network, as returned by `create_sc_net`. Returns: None """ for group in ( "nodes" , "demands" , "links" ): for item in supplychainnet . get ( group , {}) . values (): item . stats . reset ()

docs.text: A National Scale Milk Supply Chain (India) Milk is one of the most perishable goods distributed at national scale. A packet leaves the processing plant with a shelf life of only a few days, and India, the largest producer of milk in the world, moves it through thousands of distributors and retailers every day. Every site in that chain faces the same tension. Holding too few units loses sales, while holding too many means units expire before they sell. This case study models a national scale milk supply chain for India using SupplyNetPy. The network has three levels, with 31 manufacturers supplying 282 distributors, which in turn supply 1,498 retailers placed according to census town populations. The study performs an exhaustive evaluation and simulation based optimization to find near optimal replenishment settings, namely the reorder point fraction (alpha) and the order up to fraction (beta), for a given degree of disruption (controlled by the disruption probability, p_fail) and a given network structure (controlled by the number of backup distributors per retailer, n_backup). Goal of the Study The goal is to study the combined effect of perishability and disruption on supply chain network performance, measured by profit, service level, and waste. These two forces pull replenishment policy in opposite directions. Perishability punishes holding too many units, because they expire before they sell. Disruption punishes holding too few, because a site that loses its inventory leaves its buyers and customers unserved. The experiments quantify this tension and identify the replenishment settings that balance it best at each disruption level, with and without backup distributors. The Network The network is built entirely from public data. Towns are taken from the Census of India 2011, and each town receives a retailer whose demand is proportional to its population. Distributors and manufacturers are placed in larger towns and cities, weighted by state level milk production statistics, and every site is placed at its real coordinates. Sites are then connected by nearest neighbor links. Each distributor buys from its nearest manufacturer, and each retailer is linked to its three nearest distributors. One of the three is the primary source and the other two serve as backups. A link is created only when its lead time is shorter than the shelf life of the product, so milk can never be sent along a path on which it would expire in transit. Lead times and transportation costs are worked out from road distances. Capacities are sized from the daily demand of the population each site serves. The result is a network of about 3,300 nodes and 6,300 links spanning the country. The complete network can be explored in the interactive map below. Layers for primary and backup links can be toggled on and off. 🔗 Open the interactive supply chain network map (opens in a new tab, about 5 MB) Modeling with SupplyNetPy The study exercises several capabilities of the library together. Perishable inventory with first in, first out expiry, so each batch carries its manufacturing date and is thrown away when it passes its shelf life. (s, S) replenishment at every distributor and retailer, with s and S worked out from alpha, beta, and the capacity of the node. Supplier-selection policies, so a retailer with backup links switches to a distributor that is not disrupted when its primary distributor is. Disruptions that destroy the units at the disrupted site, followed by recovery after a while. Statistics for each node that report profit, service, waste, and costs for every site in the network. Each site is described by a plain dictionary, and the whole network is just a list of such dictionaries, created by a program from the data files. A distributor, a retailer with a backup link, and the links between them look like this. import random import SupplyNetPy.Components as scm P_FAIL = 0.005 # chance a disruption starts each day (one every 200 days on average) distributor = {'ID': 'D042', 'name': 'Distributor 42', 'node_type': 'distributor', 'capacity': 11200, 'initial_level': 11200, 'inventory_type': 'perishable', 'shelf_life': 5, 'inventory_holding_cost': 0.75, 'replenishment_policy': scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s': 1792, 'S': 4480}, # S = beta * capacity, s = alpha * S 'node_disrupt_time': lambda: random.expovariate(P_FAIL), # time until the next disruption 'node_recovery_time': lambda: 1.0, # each disruption lasts one day 'disruption_impact': 'destroy_all', # a disrupted site loses all its units 'product_buy_price': 20, 'product_sell_price': 24} retailer = {'ID': 'R0731', 'name': 'Retailer 731', 'node_type': 'retailer', 'capacity': 1400, 'initial_level': 1400, 'inventory_type': 'perishable', 'shelf_life': 5, 'inventory_holding_cost': 0.6, 'replenishment_policy': scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s': 224, 'S': 560}, 'supplier_selection_policy': scm.SelectAvailable, # a distributor that is not disrupted and has enough units 'supplier_selection_mode': 'dynamic', 'product_buy_price': 24, 'product_sell_price': 29} links = [ {'ID': 'L1', 'source': 'P007', 'sink': 'D042', 'cost': 950.0, 'lead_time': lambda: 0.20}, {'ID': 'L2', 'source': 'D042', 'sink': 'R0731', 'cost': 120.0, 'lead_time': lambda: 0.05}, # primary {'ID': 'L3', 'source': 'D118', 'sink': 'R0731', 'cost': 180.0, 'lead_time': lambda: 0.08}, # backup ] # costs and lead times come from road distances net = scm.create_sc_net(nodes=nodes, links=links, demands=demands) net = scm.simulate_sc_net(net, sim_time=180) Experiments The experiments sweep a full factorial grid over the four factors. The replenishment settings alpha and beta, the disruption probability p_fail, and the number of backup distributors n_backup are varied together, and every configuration is simulated for a 180 day horizon with multiple independent replications. The sweep amounts to roughly 24,000 simulation runs, executed in parallel on an 80 core server. Each run records network profit, customer service level, and waste, with waste split into units lost to expiry and units destroyed by disruptions. Insights Four findings stand out from the sweep. For perishables, more inventory is not safer. Beyond a modest level, raising the order up to fraction beta reduces both profit and service, because the extra units expire before they can be sold. Disruption shifts the optimum. As disruptions become more frequent, the best policy keeps more units in inventory. The buffer that perishability punishes in calm conditions becomes worth paying for when sites keep losing their inventory. Backup distributors pay off. Every near optimal configuration found by the sweep uses all the backup distributors available. Backup links soften the profit and service loss caused by disruptions at little cost in calm conditions. A profitable network can hide a struggling level. Under heavy disruption the network as a whole remains profitable while the retail level runs at a loss, a pattern that only becomes visible when performance is examined per node. The figures below show expected profit as a surface over the alpha and beta grid. The plots are interactive, so they can be rotated, zoomed, and hovered to read individual values. The first surface uses two backups per retailer, and rotating it shows the best (alpha, beta) region moving as disruption grows. The second surface fixes the disruption probability at one disruption every 200 days on average and shows how profit responds to the replenishment settings at that disruption level. The per node view behind the fourth finding is available as a second interactive map. It shows the measured profit and the expiry waste of every retailer in the country at the best configuration found for each disruption level, with one toggleable layer per disruption level. 🔗 Open the interactive retailer profit and waste map (opens in a new tab, about 15 MB) Further work The exhaustive sweep produced a large volume of simulation data, and a related research thread builds on it. We are exploring graph neural network (GNN) metamodels for simulation based optimization of supply chains. A metamodel trained on this data may learn to predict near optimal values of alpha, beta, and n_backup for a given disruption degree directly from the network, without running thousands of simulations.

A distributor, a retailer with a backup link, and the links between them look like this. import random import SupplyNetPy.Components as scm P_FAIL = 0.005 # chance a disruption starts each day (one every 200 days on average) distributor = {'ID': 'D042', 'name': 'Distributor 42', 'node_type': 'distributor', 'capacity': 11200, 'initial_level': 11200, 'inventory_type': 'perishable', 'shelf_life': 5, 'inventory_holding_cost': 0.75, 'replenishment_policy': scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s': 1792, 'S': 4480}, # S = beta * capacity, s = alpha * S 'node_disrupt_time': lambda: random.expovariate(P_FAIL), # time until the next disruption 'node_recovery_time': lambda: 1.0, # each disruption lasts one day 'disruption_impact': 'destroy_all', # a disrupted site loses all its units 'product_buy_price': 20, 'product_sell_price': 24} retailer = {'ID': 'R0731', 'name': 'Retailer 731', 'node_type': 'retailer', 'capacity': 1400, 'initial_level': 1400, 'inventory_type': 'perishable', 'shelf_life': 5, 'inventory_holding_cost': 0.6, 'replenishment_policy': scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s': 224, 'S': 560}, 'supplier_selection_policy': scm.SelectAvailable, # a distributor that is not disrupted and has enough units 'supplier_selection_mode': 'dynamic', 'product_buy_price': 24, 'product_sell_price': 29} links = [ {'ID': 'L1', 'source': 'P007', 'sink': 'D042', 'cost': 950.0, 'lead_time': lambda: 0.20}, {'ID': 'L2', 'source': 'D042', 'sink': 'R0731', 'cost': 120.0, 'lead_time': lambda: 0.05}, # primary {'ID': 'L3', 'source': 'D118', 'sink': 'R0731', 'cost': 180.0, 'lead_time': lambda: 0.08}, # backup ] # costs and lead times come from road distances net = scm.create_sc_net(nodes=nodes, links=links, demands=demands) net = scm.simulate_sc_net(net, sim_time=180)
docs.title: Modeling with SupplyNetPy

docs.text: The experiments sweep a full factorial grid over the four factors. The replenishment settings alpha and beta, the disruption probability p_fail, and the number of backup distributors n_backup are varied together, and every configuration is simulated for a 180 day horizon with multiple independent replications. The sweep amounts to roughly 24,000 simulation runs, executed in parallel on an 80 core server. Each run records network profit, customer service level, and waste, with waste split into units lost to expiry and units destroyed by disruptions.
docs.title: Experiments

docs.text: Four findings stand out from the sweep. For perishables, more inventory is not safer. Beyond a modest level, raising the order up to fraction beta reduces both profit and service, because the extra units expire before they can be sold. Disruption shifts the optimum. As disruptions become more frequent, the best policy keeps more units in inventory. The buffer that perishability punishes in calm conditions becomes worth paying for when sites keep losing their inventory. Backup distributors pay off. Every near optimal configuration found by the sweep uses all the backup distributors available. Backup links soften the profit and service loss caused by disruptions at little cost in calm conditions. A profitable network can hide a struggling level. Under heavy disruption the network as a whole remains profitable while the retail level runs at a loss, a pattern that only becomes visible when performance is examined per node. The figures below show expected profit as a surface over the alpha and beta grid. The plots are interactive, so they can be rotated, zoomed, and hovered to read individual values. The first surface uses two backups per retailer, and rotating it shows the best (alpha, beta) region moving as disruption grows. The second surface fixes the disruption probability at one disruption every 200 days on average and shows how profit responds to the replenishment settings at that disruption level. The per node view behind the fourth finding is available as a second interactive map. It shows the measured profit and the expiry waste of every retailer in the country at the best configuration found for each disruption level, with one toggleable layer per disruption level. 🔗 Open the interactive retailer profit and waste map (opens in a new tab, about 15 MB)
docs.title: Insights

docs.text: The exhaustive sweep produced a large volume of simulation data, and a related research thread builds on it. We are exploring graph neural network (GNN) metamodels for simulation based optimization of supply chains. A metamodel trained on this data may learn to predict near optimal values of alpha, beta, and n_backup for a given disruption degree directly from the network, without running thousands of simulations.

docs.text: Customer Demand Imagine a bakery. Customers come in through the day, one every few minutes, and each buys a few loaves. Some days are busy and some are quiet. A customer who finds too little bread may walk out, may take the loaves that are left, or may wait for the next batch from the oven. In SupplyNetPy, this stream of customers is a customer demand, and each customer places one customer order at a site. This guide shows how to create a customer demand, how to set how often customers order and how many units, at random or from recorded data, what customers do when the site is short of units, and how their orders are delivered. The words used here are explained in the Glossary . Creating a customer demand A customer demand needs an ID, a name, the site its customers order from ( demand_node ), the time units between one customer order and the next ( order_arrival_model ), and the units in each order ( order_quantity_model ). In a dict netlist, the site is given by its ID. demand = {'ID': 'd1', 'name': 'Bakery customers', 'demand_node': 'R1', 'order_arrival_model': lambda: 1, 'order_quantity_model': lambda: 10} Created as an object, the customer demand takes the site itself. demand = scm.Demand(env=env, ID='d1', name='Bakery customers', demand_node=retailer, order_arrival_model=lambda: 1, order_quantity_model=lambda: 10) The site can be any site except a raw-material supplier, usually a retailer or a distributor. Every setting is listed under Demand in the API reference . How often and how many units Both settings can be a number or a function with no arguments that returns one. The function is called again for every customer order, so a random function gives every order its own time and size. The first customer order arrives at time 0, and each later one after the time units that order_arrival_model returns. import random 'order_arrival_model': lambda: random.expovariate(1 / 2), # one order every 2 time units on average 'order_quantity_model': lambda: random.randint(1, 6), # between 1 and 6 units Every customer order must be for more than 0 units. If order_quantity_model returns 0, the run stops with an error, so a distribution that can give 0 must be kept at 1 or more. These functions use Python's own random numbers, so to repeat the same demand in another run, seed them with random.seed(n) . scm.set_seed(n) seeds only the random numbers of the library itself, such as those of random disruptions. Demand from recorded data To replay past sales, pick each value from a list by the simulation time, as below, rather than with a counter that moves on at every call. SupplyNetPy calls the function when the customer demand is created, to check that it returns a number, so a counter would skip values. sales = [4, 7, 2, 9, 5] # units sold on each day env = simpy.Environment() demand = {'ID': 'd1', 'name': 'Past sales', 'demand_node': 'R1', 'order_arrival_model': lambda: 1, 'order_quantity_model': lambda: sales[int(env.now) % len(sales)]} sc = scm.create_sc_net(nodes, links, [demand], env=env) The function reads the simulation time from env , so create the environment yourself and pass it to create_sc_net . The % len(sales) starts the list again when it runs out. When the site is short of units When a customer order arrives and the site has enough units, the customer gets the whole order. When it does not, what the customer does depends on the settings below. Setting What the customer does None of them (the default) Leaves at once without any units consume_available=True Takes the units that are there and leaves tolerance above 0 Waits up to tolerance time units for the units, then leaves without the rest tolerance , and order_min_split_ratio below 1 Waits, and accepts partial deliveries of at least that share of the order With both consume_available and a tolerance , the customer takes the units that are there, and waits only if there are none at all. A waiting customer's order counts as a backorder at the site, and the site's replenishment policy checks at once whether to order. The customer checks again each time units arrive at the site. If the tolerance runs out first, the customer leaves, and the units still missing are lost sales. With a tolerance of float('inf') , the customer waits as long as it takes. Say a customer orders 20 units when the site has 15, with order_min_split_ratio=0.5 . The smallest partial delivery they accept is then 10 units, so they get the 15 at once and wait for the other 5. With 0.9 , the smallest partial delivery is 18 units, so the 15 are not enough and the customer waits for all 20. Either way, the order counts as fulfilled once, when its last units are delivered. If even the smallest part a waiting customer accepts is more than the capacity of the site, the order can never be filled. The customer is not left waiting, and the whole order is recorded at once as a shortage and as lost sales. How each case shows up in shortage , backorder and lost_sales is explained, with the same order of 20 units, in the Statistics and Results guide. A customer who arrives while the site is disrupted is turned away, as described in the Disruptions guide. Delivering the order By default, a customer gets the units at once. lead_time sets the time units from the site to the customer, and delivery_cost the cost of delivering each customer order. Both can be a number or a function. The units leave the site's inventory when the order is served, but the order counts as fulfilled, at the site and for the customer demand, only when it reaches the customer. The site's revenue is counted then too. The delivery cost is recorded as the transportation cost of the customer demand, not of the site. So it is part of the total cost and profit of the network, but not of the site's node cost. Several customer demands A site can have more than one customer demand, for example customers who come to the shop and customers who order online, with a lead time and a delivery cost. Each is its own customer demand with the same demand_node . demands = [{'ID': 'walk_in', 'name': 'Walk in', 'demand_node': 'R1', 'order_arrival_model': lambda: 1, 'order_quantity_model': lambda: 4}, {'ID': 'online', 'name': 'Online', 'demand_node': 'R1', 'order_arrival_model': lambda: 2, 'order_quantity_model': lambda: 6, 'lead_time': 3, 'delivery_cost': 2}] The customer demands share the site's inventory. The site's statistics count the orders of all of them together, and each customer demand keeps its own. A distributor can also have its own customers while it supplies retailers. Statistics of a customer demand A customer demand records the customer orders placed ( demand_placed ), those that reached the customers ( fulfillment_received ) and the delivery costs ( transportation_cost ), read with demand.stats.get_statistics() . Everything about shortages, backorders, lost sales and waiting is recorded at the site. See the Statistics and Results guide.

docs.text: Disruptions Imagine a distributor whose warehouse is flooded for a week. While the water is there, its retailers cannot order from it, and the customers who come to its door are turned away. The trucks already on the road still arrive, and once the water is gone, the distributor works as before. Some of the units inside may be ruined. In SupplyNetPy, such an event is called a disruption, and it can hit a site or a link. This guide shows how to make sites and links disrupted, at fixed times or at random, what happens to orders while they are, how the disruptions show up in the statistics, and how to model units lost in a disruption. The words used here are explained in the Glossary . What a disruption does A disrupted site takes no new orders, neither replenishment orders from its buyers nor orders from customers. A disrupted link carries no new orders. Everything else goes on as before. Orders the site took before the disruption are still served, and customers who were already waiting keep waiting and are served. Shipments in transit still arrive, even over a disrupted link. See Known Issues . The site itself still places its own replenishment orders and receives deliveries. A raw-material supplier still mines, and a manufacturer still makes its product. The units at the site are left alone, unless you set a disruption impact, described at the end of this guide. Scheduled and random disruptions Sites and links take the same three settings, with slightly different names. What it sets Site Link Time units until the next disruption, for scheduled disruptions node_disrupt_time link_disrupt_time Disruption probability, the chance each time unit that a disruption starts failure_p link_failure_p Time units a disruption lasts, 1 if not given node_recovery_time link_recovery_time Each of them can be a number or a function with no arguments that returns one, so every disruption can be different. A scheduled disruption starts after node_disrupt_time time units, counted from the start of the run and then from each recovery. So the settings below disrupt the site from 30 to 35, from 65 to 70, and so on. 'node_disrupt_time': 30, 'node_recovery_time': 5 A random disruption can start in any time unit, with the chance failure_p . The settings below give a link a 2% chance each time unit of a disruption that lasts between 1 and 4 time units. 'link_failure_p': 0.02, 'link_recovery_time': lambda: random.uniform(1, 4) If both are given, the scheduled disruption is used and failure_p is ignored. Remember to give a recovery time. Without it, every disruption lasts only 1 time unit. Random disruptions draw random numbers, so two runs give different results. To repeat exactly the same run, call scm.set_seed(n) once before you build the network. What happens to orders Replenishment orders. When a buyer orders, its supplier-selection policy skips every supplier whose site or link is disrupted. If no supplier can take the order, the order is not placed. It is counted in the buyer's blocked statistic, and the buyer's replenishment policy checks again as soon as a supplier or a link recovers. Manufacturers. A manufacturer plans production only when it can order every raw material. If every raw-material supplier of even one raw material is disrupted, it plans nothing until one recovers. Customers. A customer who arrives at a disrupted site is turned away. The order is counted in the site's disruption_lost_sales , and not in its shortage, because the site did not run out of units. It could not take the order. Disruptions in the statistics The statistics of every site, and of every link in link.stats , record its disruptions. Statistic Meaning disruptions How many disruptions started disrupted_time How many time units the site or link was disrupted in all availability The share of time it was not disrupted blocked Replenishment orders a buyer could not place because every supplier, or the link to it, was disrupted. Recorded at the buyer disruption_lost_sales Customer orders a site lost because it was disrupted when they arrived A retailer disrupted from 30 to 35 and from 65 to 70 in a run of 100 time units has disruptions 2, disrupted_time 10 and availability 0.9. What a disruption does to stored inventory A disruption in the real world can take many forms, such as a natural disaster, a power cut, contamination, theft or a strike, and each affects the units at a site differently. The settings above only mark the site as disrupted. They do not describe what happens to the units already there. If you want the simulation to also account for units that are physically lost in a disruption, set the disruption_impact argument when you create the site (and, if you choose "destroy_fraction" , also disruption_loss_fraction ). The available choices are listed below. disruption_impact value What happens the moment a disruption starts None (the default) or "none" The site is disrupted, but its units are left alone. "destroy_all" All units at the site are lost. For a Manufacturer , its raw materials are lost too, since the idea behind this choice is that every physical thing at the site is gone. Infinite suppliers (which never run out) are skipped, since destroying an unlimited supply has no meaning. "destroy_fraction" A share of the inventory level is lost. The share is given by disruption_loss_fraction , which can be a fixed number between 0 and 1 (for example 0.3 to lose 30%) or a small function that returns a different number each time, if you want random losses. A function f(node) For anything more specific. You write a short Python function describing the effect, and the simulator calls it with the site when a disruption starts. For example, a contamination that destroys only certain batches, damage that reduces capacity, or a lead time penalty that applies once the site recovers. The effect is applied once , exactly at the moment the site goes from active to inactive, both for scheduled and random disruptions. It is not applied again while the site stays disrupted. If you want a loss that grows over time during a disruption (slow spoilage from a long loss of cooling, ongoing theft), write that inside your own function, where you can start your own SimPy process and time it against node_recovery_time . The two built in choices call Inventory.destroy(amount, reason) , a public method on Inventory that removes the units at once, even when orders are waiting at the site. For perishable products, the oldest batches are destroyed first. One subtle but important detail is that destroy does not wake up the replenishment policy, because a site should not place replenishment orders while it is disrupted. Instead, the site wakes its replenishment policy when it recovers. The policy then checks the inventory position and orders if it is too low, so a site that lost all its units refills its inventory as soon as it is working again. Note that a disrupted site can still order in two cases. A replenishment policy with a period orders when its time comes, and a policy is woken when one of the site's suppliers, or the link to it, recovers during the site's disruption. destroy also wakes a raw-material supplier, which then mines again to refill its inventory, and a manufacturer, which can then make more. If you write your own impact function that destroys units, call Inventory.destroy(...) for the same reasons, and do not change level , on_hand or perish_queue by hand. The units destroyed ( destroyed_qty ) and their value ( destroyed_value ) are recorded in the site's statistics. destroyed_value is one of the site's costs, so it is automatically included in node_cost and therefore in profit , and you do not need to subtract it yourself. In your own impact function, report losses the same way, with node.stats.update_stats(destroyed_qty=qty, destroyed_value=qty * unit_cost) , rather than inventing separate statistics that the simulator will not know about. A short example. import random import SupplyNetPy.Components as scm # Destroy all units when a disruption starts, as in a natural disaster. distributor = scm.InventoryNode( env=env, ID="D1", name="D1", node_type="warehouse", capacity=200, initial_level=120, inventory_holding_cost=0.2, replenishment_policy=scm.SSReplenishment, policy_param={'s': 100, 'S': 200}, product_sell_price=10, product_buy_price=5, node_disrupt_time=lambda: 30, node_recovery_time=lambda: 5, disruption_impact="destroy_all", ) # Like a power cut, each disruption destroys between 10% and 40% of the inventory level. warehouse = scm.InventoryNode( ..., disruption_impact="destroy_fraction", disruption_loss_fraction=lambda: random.uniform(0.1, 0.4), )

For example, a contamination that destroys only certain batches, damage that reduces capacity, or a lead time penalty that applies once the site recovers. The effect is applied once , exactly at the moment the site goes from active to inactive, both for scheduled and random disruptions. It is not applied again while the site stays disrupted. If you want a loss that grows over time during a disruption (slow spoilage from a long loss of cooling, ongoing theft), write that inside your own function, where you can start your own SimPy process and time it against node_recovery_time . The two built in choices call Inventory.destroy(amount, reason) , a public method on Inventory that removes the units at once, even when orders are waiting at the site. For perishable products, the oldest batches are destroyed first. One subtle but important detail is that destroy does not wake up the replenishment policy, because a site should not place replenishment orders while it is disrupted. Instead, the site wakes its replenishment policy when it recovers. The policy then checks the inventory position and orders if it is too low, so a site that lost all its units refills its inventory as soon as it is working again. Note that a disrupted site can still order in two cases. A replenishment policy with a period orders when its time comes, and a policy is woken when one of the site's suppliers, or the link to it, recovers during the site's disruption. destroy also wakes a raw-material supplier, which then mines again to refill its inventory, and a manufacturer, which can then make more. If you write your own impact function that destroys units, call Inventory.destroy(...) for the same reasons, and do not change level , on_hand or perish_queue by hand. The units destroyed ( destroyed_qty ) and their value ( destroyed_value ) are recorded in the site's statistics. destroyed_value is one of the site's costs, so it is automatically included in node_cost and therefore in profit , and you do not need to subtract it yourself. In your own impact function, report losses the same way, with node.stats.update_stats(destroyed_qty=qty, destroyed_value=qty * unit_cost) , rather than inventing separate statistics that the simulator will not know about. A short example. import random import SupplyNetPy.Components as scm # Destroy all units when a disruption starts, as in a natural disaster. distributor = scm.InventoryNode( env=env, ID="D1", name="D1", node_type="warehouse", capacity=200, initial_level=120, inventory_holding_cost=0.2, replenishment_policy=scm.SSReplenishment, policy_param={'s': 100, 'S': 200}, product_sell_price=10, product_buy_price=5, node_disrupt_time=lambda: 30, node_recovery_time=lambda: 5, disruption_impact="destroy_all", ) # Like a power cut, each disruption destroys between 10% and 40% of the inventory level. warehouse = scm.InventoryNode( ..., disruption_impact="destroy_fraction", disruption_loss_fraction=lambda: random.uniform(0.1, 0.4), )

docs.text: Perishable Products Imagine a dairy that makes milk which can be sold for 5 days after it is made. A distributor buys the milk and sends it on to retailers, 2 days away. By the time a packet reaches a retailer, it has only 3 days left, and whatever is not sold by then is thrown away. Holding too few packets loses sales, while holding too many means packets expire before they sell. In SupplyNetPy, such a product is perishable, and every site that holds it keeps track of when its units were made. This guide shows how to make a product perishable, how batches and their manufacturing dates move through the supply chain, when units expire, and how expired units show up in the statistics. The words used here are explained in the Glossary . Making a product perishable Give each site that holds the product inventory_type="perishable" and a shelf_life , the time units a unit can be sold after it is made. retailer = {'ID': 'R1', 'name': 'Retailer 1', 'node_type': 'retailer', 'capacity': 100, 'initial_level': 60, 'inventory_holding_cost': 0.1, 'replenishment_policy': scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s': 20, 'S': 60}, 'product_buy_price': 1, 'product_sell_price': 3, 'inventory_type': 'perishable', 'shelf_life': 5} Distributors, retailers and other inventory sites ( InventoryNode ) and manufacturers ( Manufacturer ) can hold a perishable product. SupplyNetPy does not model perishable raw materials yet, so the inventory of a raw-material supplier and the raw materials a manufacturer holds are always non-perishable. A site without these settings keeps its units forever, even when its supplier's units are perishable. Batches and manufacturing dates A perishable inventory keeps its units as batches, units with the same manufacturing date. A unit expires shelf_life time units after its manufacturing date. Where the date comes from depends on how the units arrive. Units Manufacturing date The initial units of a site Time 0 Units a manufacturer makes The time their production batch is finished Units from a supplier whose product is perishable The date they already have, so they keep it from site to site Units from a supplier whose product is not perishable, such as an infinite supplier The time they arrive, or manufacture_date(t) if you give it manufacture_date is a function that takes the arrival time and returns a manufacturing date. It describes units that were made before they reached the site. For example, lambda t: t - 1 dates every delivery 1 time unit before it arrives. Oldest units first Every order takes units from the oldest batch first, then from the next oldest, and so on. This holds for customer orders and for replenishment orders from other sites. The batches go with the units to the buyer. Say a retailer has 10 units made at time 0 and 20 units made at time 3. A customer who orders 15 units gets the 10 from time 0 and 5 from time 3, and the retailer keeps 15 units made at time 3. When units expire The moment a batch reaches the end of its shelf life, its units are thrown away, even if orders are waiting at the site. The inventory level drops, so the site's replenishment policy checks at once whether to order. A unit's shelf life is counted from its manufacturing date, not from its arrival, so the lead time uses up part of it. In the dairy above, milk made at time 0 that reaches a retailer at time 2 expires there at time 5. Units do not expire while they are in transit. Units whose shelf life ends on the way are thrown away when they arrive, after the buyer has paid for them, so if a lead time is as long as the shelf life, every unit arrives already expired. So keep every lead time shorter than the shelf life. Each site uses its own shelf_life with the date the units carry. A retailer with a shelf life of 10 that buys units made at time 0 from a distributor with a shelf life of 5 keeps them until time 10. Give every site that holds the same product the same shelf life, unless the sites really do keep it differently, for example one with cooling and one without. Expired units in the statistics A site's expired units are counted in inventory_waste , and simulate_sc_net adds them up for the whole network in sc["inventory_waste"] . A warm-up resets the count, as described in the Statistics and Results guide. SupplyNetPy does not give expired units a price of their own. The site paid for them when they arrived, which is in inventory_spend_cost , it was charged the holding cost until they expired, and they bring in no revenue, so they already lower its profit. If your study gives waste a cost of its own, multiply inventory_waste by that cost. Choosing the replenishment settings A replenishment policy looks at the inventory position, and counts units that are about to expire the same as fresh ones. For a perishable product, holding more is not always safer. Once a site holds more than it sells within the shelf life, every extra unit expires, so a higher S or a larger safety stock can lower both the profit and the share of customers served. Compare a few settings by running them, as in the Milk Supply Chain (India) case study. The Pharmacy Supply Chain case study is another worked example with a perishable product.

docs.text: Replenishment Policies Imagine a small shop that sells about 30 loaves of bread a day. Again and again, the owner has to decide two things, when to order more bread from the bakery and how many loaves to order. One owner orders whenever the count gets low. Another orders the same amount every Monday. In SupplyNetPy, such a rule is called a replenishment policy. Every distributor, retailer and manufacturer follows one, and you choose it when you create the site. This guide shows how to choose a built in policy and set it up, and how to write your own policy when none of them fits. The words used here are explained in the Glossary . Giving a site its policy A policy is given with two settings. replenishment_policy is the policy's class, and policy_param is a dictionary with its parameters. Pass the class itself, such as scm.SSReplenishment , without creating an object from it. The site creates its policy when the site itself is created. retailer = {'ID': 'R1', 'name': 'Retailer1', 'node_type': 'retailer', 'capacity': 300, 'initial_level': 100, 'inventory_holding_cost': 0.2, 'replenishment_policy': scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s': 80, 'S': 300}, 'product_buy_price': 100, 'product_sell_price': 105} The same two settings work when you create an InventoryNode or a Manufacturer object yourself. The built in policies The (s, S) and (R, Q) policies decide using the inventory position, the units the site can count on. It is the inventory level, plus the units in transit to the site, minus the units the site still owes to other sites and to waiting customers. The periodic policy orders on a timer instead. Policy When it orders How many units Parameters Class (s, S) policy The inventory position falls to s or below Enough to bring the inventory position back up to S s , S , and optionally safety_stock , period , first_review_delay SSReplenishment (R, Q) policy The inventory position falls to R or below Always Q R , Q , and optionally period , first_review_delay RQReplenishment Periodic policy Every T time units Q , plus any units missing from the safety stock T , Q , and optionally safety_stock , first_review_delay PeriodicReplenishment Which one to choose depends on how the real site orders. The (s, S) policy suits a site that can order any amount and wants each order to fill its inventory up again. The size of each order depends on how much was sold. The (R, Q) policy suits a site that orders a fixed amount each time, such as one full truck or one pallet. The periodic policy suits a site whose supplier delivers on fixed days, such as once a week. It orders Q units every time, whatever the inventory position. If customers buy fewer than Q units in T time units, the inventory fills up, and later orders are reduced to fit the site's capacity. Every policy chooses how many units to order, but not from whom. When a site has more than one supplier, its supplier-selection policy chooses which one receives each order. When a policy checks By default, the (s, S) and (R, Q) policies check the inventory position each time units leave the site's inventory, so they never miss the moment it reaches the reorder point. Many real sites count their inventory only now and then, for example once a week. To model this, give period , and the policy checks only every period time units. Between two checks it does nothing, even if the inventory position has fallen below the reorder point. first_review_delay sets how long a policy waits before its first check, or, for the periodic policy, before its first order. 'policy_param': {'s': 80, 'S': 300, 'period': 5, 'first_review_delay': 1} # checks at 1, 6, 11, 16, ... A policy without a period is also woken when the site itself recovers from a disruption. A disruption that destroys units does not wake the policy, so the site checks its inventory position again the moment it is working again. The policy is also woken when one of the site's suppliers, or the link to it, recovers. While every supplier is disrupted, the site cannot place an order, so the policy checks again the moment one recovers, instead of waiting for the next sale. A policy with a period keeps to its own timer. Safety stock Safety stock is extra units kept as a buffer against uncertain demand or lead times. The two policies that take a safety_stock use it differently. The (s, S) policy adds safety_stock to both s and S . So {'s': 80, 'S': 300, 'safety_stock': 20} behaves like {'s': 100, 'S': 320} . The periodic policy looks at the inventory level when it orders. If the level is below safety_stock , the order gets the missing units on top of Q . The (R, Q) policy has no safety stock. To keep a buffer with it, raise R . Mistakes caught when the network is created A policy ignores any parameter it does not read. So that a typing mistake, or a parameter meant for another policy, does not go unnoticed, a built in policy warns about such a parameter. Passing T to the (s, S) policy, for example, gives this warning. UserWarning: SSReplenishment does not use the parameter(s) 'T' in policy_param, so they are ignored. It uses only 's', 'S', 'safety_stock', 'first_review_delay', 'period'. Check whether you meant to use another replenishment policy. Settings that cannot work stop with an error, for example an s larger than S , a negative reorder point, or a Q , S or T that is not positive. Writing your own policy When no built in policy fits, write your own as a subclass of InventoryReplenishment . Suppose the retailer above orders up to S like the (s, S) policy, but its supplier accepts at most 100 units in one order. class CappedSSReplenishment(scm.InventoryReplenishment): _param_keys = ("s", "S", "max_order") def run(self): s, S = self.params["s"], self.params["S"] max_order = self.params["max_order"] while True: position = self.node.position() if position <= s: self.node.place_order(min(S - position, max_order)) yield from self.node.wait_for_drop() Give it to a site like a built in policy. 'replenishment_policy': CappedSSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s': 80, 'S': 300, 'max_order': 100}, In the policy, self.node is the site, self.params is its policy_param , and self.env is the SimPy environment. The run method runs for the whole simulation. It loops forever, and in each round it checks, perhaps orders, and then pauses with yield , either until the next drop in inventory with yield from self.node.wait_for_drop() , or for a fixed time with yield self.env.timeout(t) . The policy works with its site through a small set of helper methods on Node , rather than reading or changing the site's internal attributes directly. The built in policies use the same helpers, so a policy written this way does not depend on how Node is built inside. node.position() returns the inventory position. Use it instead of working the position out yourself from node.inventory.on_hand and node.stats.backorder . node.place_order(quantity) first checks that some supplier can take the order, then chooses a supplier with the site's supplier-selection policy and places the replenishment order. If every supplier, or the link to it, is disrupted, no order is placed. Use it instead of calling selection_policy.select(...) and env.process(process_order(...)) yourself. node.wait_for_drop() waits until the site's inventory drops, until the site recovers from a disruption, or until one of its suppliers or the link to it recovers, then gets ready for the next time. A policy that found no supplier to order from is woken this way, so it can check again. Use it as yield from node.wait_for_drop() . To give your policy the warning about unused parameters, list the keys it reads in the class attribute _param_keys , as in the example. A policy without such a list is not checked.
