docs.text: Running Experiments Imagine a shop manager who wants to know whether to reorder when 60 units are left or when 120 are left. One simulated year gives an answer, but customers arrive at random, so another year could give a different one. To answer the question properly, the manager simulates many years with each setting, compares the averages, and checks how precise they are. Each of these runs is a replication. This guide shows how to set up a network so that it can be run many times, how to control its random numbers with seeds, how to compare settings fairly, and how to collect and summarize the results. The words used here are explained in the Glossary . A function that builds the network A network can be simulated only once from the start. Calling simulate_sc_net again with the same sim_time simulates nothing more and gives a warning. So write a function that builds a fresh network, and call it for every run. Its arguments are the settings you want to vary and the seed of the run. import random import statistics import SupplyNetPy.Components as scm def build(s, seed): demand_rng = random.Random(f"demand {seed}") # random numbers of the customers lead_rng = random.Random(f"lead time {seed}") # random numbers of the lead times nodes = [{'ID': 'S1', 'name': 'Supplier', 'node_type': 'infinite_supplier'}, {'ID': 'R1', 'name': 'Shop', 'node_type': 'retailer', 'capacity': 300, 'initial_level': 150, 'inventory_holding_cost': 0.2, 'replenishment_policy': scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s': s, 'S': 300}, 'product_buy_price': 4, 'product_sell_price': 10}] links = [{'ID': 'L1', 'source': 'S1', 'sink': 'R1', 'cost': 20, 'lead_time': lambda: lead_rng.randint(1, 3)}] demands = [{'ID': 'd1', 'name': 'Customers', 'demand_node': 'R1', 'order_arrival_model': lambda: demand_rng.expovariate(1), 'order_quantity_model': lambda: demand_rng.randint(5, 15)}] return scm.create_sc_net(nodes, links, demands) def run(s, seed): sc = build(s, seed) scm.simulate_sc_net(sc, sim_time=365, logging=False) return sc Pass logging=False to simulate_sc_net . With logging on, every run prints its whole log and writes it to a file, which slows down a study of many runs and buries its output. Seeds Each run above draws its random numbers from its own random number generators, started from the seed. The same seed gives the same customers and the same lead times, so run(60, 1) gives the same profit every time it is called, and a result can always be repeated. The seeds here are strings such as "demand 1" , so the customers and the lead times of one run get different random numbers, and no run reuses the numbers of another. If the network has random disruptions, also call scm.set_seed(seed) before you build it. It seeds the random numbers the library itself uses for disruptions. Comparing settings fairly Run every setting with the same seeds. Then each setting faces exactly the same customers and lead times, and the differences in the results come from the settings themselves. This is called common random numbers. That is why the customers and the lead times have separate generators. If they shared one, the lead times of the replenishment orders would use up random numbers in a different order under each setting, and from then on the two settings would see different customers. rows = [] for s in (60, 120): for seed in range(30): sc = run(s, seed) shop = sc["nodes"]["R1"].stats rows.append({'s': s, 'seed': seed, 'profit': sc["profit"], 'lost_sales': shop.lost_sales[1], 'avg_inventory_level': shop.avg_inventory_level}) Each row holds the settings, the seed and the results you want to keep, from the network results ( sc["profit"] ) or from the statistics of a node. The Statistics and Results guide lists what there is. Averages and confidence intervals The average over the replications is the estimate, and its confidence interval shows how precise it is. for s in (60, 120): profits = [row['profit'] for row in rows if row['s'] == s] mean = statistics.mean(profits) half_width = 1.96 * statistics.stdev(profits) / len(profits) ** 0.5 print(f"s = {s}: profit {mean:.0f} ± {half_width:.0f}") This prints a profit of 10161 ± 651 for s 60 and 7696 ± 581 for s 120, as 95% confidence intervals. To narrow an interval, run more replications. Four times as many make it about half as wide. Because both settings used the same seeds, the difference can also be measured run by run. The profit with s 60 minus the profit with s 120, for the same seed, averages 2465 ± 159. That interval is much narrower than the two above, because the luck of each run, a busy year or a quiet one, is the same for both settings and cancels out. With pandas installed, pandas.DataFrame(rows) turns the rows into a table, and df.groupby('s')['profit'].agg(['mean', 'std']) gives the same averages. Run length and warm-up sim_time is the time at which the run stops, and events due at exactly that time do not happen. So sim_time=365 covers time 0 up to just before 365. Every run starts with its initial inventory levels, nothing in transit and no orders waiting. To leave this first stretch out of the results, run a warm-up before the measured period. sc = build(60, 1) net = scm.Network(sc) net.simulate(30, logging=False).reset_stats().simulate(395, logging=False) print(net.results["profit"]) # from 30 to 395 How a warm-up resets the statistics is explained in the Statistics and Results guide. Running replications in parallel Replications do not depend on each other, so they can run at the same time on several processor cores, with Python's concurrent.futures . from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor def profit(args): s, seed = args return s, seed, run(s, seed)["profit"] if __name__ == "__main__": with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool: results = list(pool.map(profit, [(s, seed) for s in (60, 120) for seed in range(30)])) Each run builds its own network inside its process, so a run gives the same result as when it runs alone. On Windows and macOS, each process starts Python afresh and imports your script. So put the functions at the top level of a script file, not in a notebook cell or inside another function, and start the pool under if __name__ == "__main__": as above. Starting the processes takes time, so this pays off only when the runs are long or many.

docs.text: Imagine a shop manager who wants to know whether to reorder when 60 units are left or when 120 are left. One simulated year gives an answer, but customers arrive at random, so another year could give a different one. To answer the question properly, the manager simulates many years with each setting, compares the averages, and checks how precise they are. Each of these runs is a replication. This guide shows how to set up a network so that it can be run many times, how to control its random numbers with seeds, how to compare settings fairly, and how to collect and summarize the results. The words used here are explained in the Glossary .

docs.text: A network can be simulated only once from the start. Calling simulate_sc_net again with the same sim_time simulates nothing more and gives a warning. So write a function that builds a fresh network, and call it for every run. Its arguments are the settings you want to vary and the seed of the run. import random import statistics import SupplyNetPy.Components as scm def build(s, seed): demand_rng = random.Random(f"demand {seed}") # random numbers of the customers lead_rng = random.Random(f"lead time {seed}") # random numbers of the lead times nodes = [{'ID': 'S1', 'name': 'Supplier', 'node_type': 'infinite_supplier'}, {'ID': 'R1', 'name': 'Shop', 'node_type': 'retailer', 'capacity': 300, 'initial_level': 150, 'inventory_holding_cost': 0.2, 'replenishment_policy': scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s': s, 'S': 300}, 'product_buy_price': 4, 'product_sell_price': 10}] links = [{'ID': 'L1', 'source': 'S1', 'sink': 'R1', 'cost': 20, 'lead_time': lambda: lead_rng.randint(1, 3)}] demands = [{'ID': 'd1', 'name': 'Customers', 'demand_node': 'R1', 'order_arrival_model': lambda: demand_rng.expovariate(1), 'order_quantity_model': lambda: demand_rng.randint(5, 15)}] return scm.create_sc_net(nodes, links, demands) def run(s, seed): sc = build(s, seed) scm.simulate_sc_net(sc, sim_time=365, logging=False) return sc Pass logging=False to simulate_sc_net . With logging on, every run prints its whole log and writes it to a file, which slows down a study of many runs and buries its output.

docs.text: Statistics and Results Imagine you have just simulated a year of a supply chain with one distributor and three retailers. Now come the questions. Did the network make a profit? Did the retailers serve their customers, or did they run short? Which retailer held too much inventory? And which supplier, or which link, kept the others waiting? SupplyNetPy answers these at three levels, the whole network, each node, and each link. This guide shows where each answer is found, how to read it, and how to leave the first part of a run out of the statistics with a warm-up. The words used here are explained in the Glossary . Results for the whole network simulate_sc_net adds the results for the whole network to the dictionary it is given. They are added up from every node, and include the total cost, the revenue and the profit, the orders placed and received, the shortage, the lost sales and the backorders. scm.simulate_sc_net(sc, sim_time=365) print(sc["profit"], sc["total_cost"], sc["shortage"]) With a Network , the same results are in net.results . What each result means is listed under simulate_sc_net in the API reference . Statistics of a node Every node keeps its own statistics in node.stats . Read them with node.stats.get_statistics() , or print a table of several nodes side by side with print_node_wise_performance . print(sc["nodes"]["R1"].stats.get_statistics()) # one node scm.print_node_wise_performance(sc["nodes"].values()) # every node, as a table rows = scm.get_node_wise_performance(sc["nodes"].values()) # every node, as data get_node_wise_performance returns the values as data, ready for a pandas DataFrame, and format_node_wise_performance returns the table as text. The statistics answer a few kinds of question. Counts of orders are given as [number of orders, units] . Question Statistics How many orders went in and out? demand_placed and fulfillment_received for the orders the site placed and what arrived, demand_received and demand_fulfilled for the orders placed with it and those it fulfilled Did the site serve its orders? shortage , backorder , lost_sales , waited , avg_waiting_time How much inventory did it hold? inventory_level at the end, avg_inventory_level , zero_inventory_share (the share of time it had no units), inventory_waste (expired units), dropped_qty (delivered units that did not fit) How did disruptions affect it? disruptions , disrupted_time , availability , blocked , disruption_lost_sales , explained in the Disruptions guide What did it cost and earn? inventory_carry_cost (the holding cost), inventory_spend_cost (what it paid for the units it received), transportation_cost , destroyed_value , then node_cost (all of them added up), revenue and profit A raw-material supplier also records what it mined and what mining cost, and a manufacturer what it made and what making it cost. Both costs are part of its node_cost . Three of these are easy to mix up. shortage counts the units a site was missing when an order arrived. It is a running total and is never reduced, even if the order is filled later. backorder is what the site owes right now, the orders still waiting for units. lost_sales counts the customer units the site never delivered, for example because the customer would not wait. So a customer who orders 20 units when the site has 15 adds 5 to shortage , whatever happens next. The rest depends on the customer. A customer who does not wait (the default) leaves without any units, so all 20 are lost sales. With consume_available , the customer takes the 15 units, and only the missing 5 are lost sales. A customer who waits (a customer demand with a tolerance ) puts the whole order of 20 in backorder until the units are there. If the wait runs past the tolerance, the customer gives up and the 20 units are lost sales. Averages and shares are worked out when they are read, from the totals. When there is nothing to divide by yet, for example avg_waiting_time before any order has been fulfilled, the value is None . The inventory values are also None for an infinite supplier and for a customer demand, which have no inventory to measure. A customer demand has statistics too. demand_placed and fulfillment_received show what its customers ordered and what reached them. Statistics of a link Imagine a retailer that buys from two distributors. Its node statistics say how much it ordered and received in total, but not how much came from each distributor, how long each one made it wait, or how often each link was disrupted. Every link keeps its own statistics for this, in link.stats . They count the replenishment orders the buyer placed over the link, what arrived, the shortage and backorders at the supplier, the waiting time (how long orders waited at the supplier before they were sent), the lead time, the costs, and the disruptions of the link. From these totals they work out averages such as the fill rate (the share of the units ordered that the supplier sent at once, without the order having to wait), the order cycle time (waiting time plus lead time) and the availability of the link. Read one link with link.stats.get_statistics() , or several at once with print_link_wise_performance(links) , which prints the same kind of table as print_node_wise_performance . For the view of one site, pass its links. node.suppliers holds the links the site orders over, and node.buyers holds the links its buyers order over. retailer = sc["nodes"]["R1"] scm.print_link_wise_performance(retailer.suppliers) # what R1 ordered, and from whom scm.print_link_wise_performance(sc["nodes"]["D1"].buyers) # who ordered from D1 rows = scm.get_link_wise_performance(sc["links"].values()) # every link, as data get_link_wise_performance returns the values as data, and format_link_wise_performance returns the table as text. The full example is in examples/py/link_statistics.py . Link statistics count replenishment orders only. Customers do not order over links, so customer demand is found in the statistics of each customer demand. The figures on the links of a site add up to the figures of the site itself, so the two can be checked against each other. One exception is blocked . An order that no supplier can take is never sent over any link, so it is counted only at the buyer. Two statistics describe how uneven the orders are, and they answer different questions. order_size_std is the standard deviation of the order sizes, and units_per_time_unit_std is the standard deviation of the units ordered in each time unit, where a time unit with no order counts as 0. A distributor that orders 60 units at time 3 and 60 units at time 7 has an order_size_std of 0, because every order is the same size, but a large units_per_time_unit_std , because its orders come in bursts. Compare units_per_time_unit_std along the supply chain to measure the bullwhip effect, the way orders become more uneven as they pass from the customers towards the raw-material suppliers. Warm-ups A run starts in an unusual state. Every site starts with its initial inventory level, nothing is in transit, and no orders are waiting. If you are interested in how the network behaves once it has settled, leave this first stretch out of the statistics with a warm-up. Run for the warm-up period, reset the statistics, and carry on running. scm.simulate_sc_net(sc, sim_time=30) # warm-up scm.reset_stats(sc) scm.simulate_sc_net(sc, sim_time=230) # the measured period reset_stats(sc) starts the statistics of every node, customer demand and link again in one call, and the results of the second simulate_sc_net cover only the measured period, from 30 to 230. With a Network , the same is net.simulate(30).reset_stats().simulate(230) . To reset only one node or one link, call node.stats.reset() or link.stats.reset() . A reset changes only the counting, not the simulation. The running totals go back to zero and the clock of each statistic starts at the moment of the reset, so the averages cover the measured period only. What describes the present is kept, such as the orders still waiting in backorder and the current inventory level, and so are the inventory, the orders in transit and any disruption still going on.

docs.text: Supplier Selection Imagine a retailer that can buy the same product from two distributors. Shipping from the first one is cheaper, but its orders take two days to arrive. The second one charges more for transport, and its orders arrive the next day. Each time the retailer orders, it has to pick one of them. In SupplyNetPy, the rule for this choice is called a supplier-selection policy. The replenishment policy decides when to order and how many units, and the supplier-selection policy decides which supplier receives the order. This guide shows how to choose a built in policy and its mode, how to choose suppliers at random, and how to write your own policy. The words used here are explained in the Glossary . Giving a site its policy A distributor or retailer that has more than one supplier takes two settings. supplier_selection_policy is the policy's class, and supplier_selection_mode is "fixed" or "dynamic" . As with replenishment policies, pass the class itself, without creating an object from it. retailer = {'ID': 'R1', 'name': 'Retailer1', 'node_type': 'retailer', 'capacity': 100, 'initial_level': 100, 'inventory_holding_cost': 0.2, 'replenishment_policy': scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s': 40, 'S': 100}, 'supplier_selection_policy': scm.SelectCheapest, 'supplier_selection_mode': 'dynamic', 'product_buy_price': 100, 'product_sell_price': 110} Without these settings, a site uses SelectFirst in fixed mode, so it orders from the supplier whose link was created first. A site with only one supplier does not need them. The built in policies Each policy chooses among the suppliers that can take an order right now. A supplier is skipped while its site, or the link to it, is disrupted. Policy Chooses Class First The supplier whose link was created first SelectFirst Available The first supplier whose inventory level can fill the whole order. If none can, the first supplier, and the order waits there until enough units arrive SelectAvailable Cheapest The supplier with the lowest transportation cost, the cost of the link to it SelectCheapest Fastest The supplier with the shortest lead time SelectFastest When lead times are random, SelectFastest draws one lead time from each link to compare them. The shipment then draws its own lead time, so the chosen supplier is the one that looked fastest at that moment, and it may still turn out slower. Fixed or dynamic The mode says how often the choice is made. In dynamic mode, the policy chooses again for every replenishment order. Use it when the best supplier can change during a run, for example with SelectAvailable , whose answer depends on the inventory levels at that moment, or with SelectFastest and random lead times. In fixed mode, the policy keeps the first supplier it chose and sends every later order there. This models a site with a regular supplier. While that supplier, or the link to it, is disrupted, the orders go to another supplier, chosen by the same rule. Once it recovers, the orders go back to it. In fixed mode the policy's rule decides only the first order and the orders placed during a disruption. So SelectAvailable in fixed mode looks at the inventory levels only once. Since fixed is the default of every built in policy except SelectProbabilistic , give supplier_selection_mode='dynamic' whenever you want the rule applied to every order. To see where the orders went, print the statistics of the site's links. Each row shows what the site ordered over one link and what arrived. scm.print_link_wise_performance(sc["nodes"]["R1"].suppliers) Choosing suppliers at random Imagine a retailer that spreads its orders over three distributors. About half of its orders go to D1, about 30% to D2 and the rest to D3, with no rule such as the cheapest supplier. Each order goes to one of them by chance, with these shares. SelectProbabilistic does this. Give it the probability of each supplier in supplier_selection_param , keyed by the ID of the supplier. retailer = {'ID': 'R1', 'name': 'Retailer1', 'node_type': 'retailer', 'capacity': 100, 'initial_level': 100, 'inventory_holding_cost': 0.2, 'replenishment_policy': scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s': 40, 'S': 100}, 'supplier_selection_policy': scm.SelectProbabilistic, 'supplier_selection_param': {'probabilities': {'D1': 0.5, 'D2': 0.3, 'D3': 0.2}, 'seed': 7}, 'product_buy_price': 100, 'product_sell_price': 110} The probabilities must sum to 1, and none can be negative. A supplier with probability 0 is never chosen. Every link to the site needs a probability, and every probability needs a link, so a mistyped ID is reported when the network is built, before the run. The policy makes a new choice for every order, so it always works in dynamic mode, and supplier_selection_mode is not needed. Over many orders, the shares come close to the probabilities. The statistics of the site's links show the real shares, as above. When you create the objects yourself, a site is created before its links. Give its probabilities once you know them. r1.selection_policy.set_probabilities({'D1': 0.5, 'D2': 0.3, 'D3': 0.2}) The links are checked against them at the site's next order. When a supplier is disrupted The probabilities are the shares while every supplier can take orders. The setting on_disruption says what happens when one cannot. With 'rescale' (the default), the order goes to one of the other suppliers, which keep their ratios. With 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 and D1 disrupted, D2 and D3 get 0.6 and 0.4 for that order. Once D1 recovers, the shares are 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 again. With 'block' , the choice is made as if no supplier were disrupted. If it falls on a disrupted supplier, the order is not placed, and it is counted as a blocked order at the site and on the link. The site orders again when a supplier or a link recovers, or when its inventory drops. 'supplier_selection_param': {'probabilities': {'D1': 0.5, 'D2': 0.3, 'D3': 0.2}, 'on_disruption': 'block'} If every supplier with a probability above 0 is disrupted, the order is blocked with either setting. So with disruptions, the shares at the end of a run differ from the probabilities. Say D1 is disrupted during 40% of the orders, and the others never are. With 'rescale' , D1 receives about 30% of the orders (0.5 × 0.6), and the site never goes without. With 'block' , D1 is still chosen for half of the orders, but receives only about 37.5% of the orders sent (0.3 out of 0.8), and the site goes without for the blocked orders. Random numbers The policy draws one random number for each order from its own random number generator, so its choices never change any other random numbers in the run, such as those of disruptions. Give a seed to repeat the same choices in every run. Two runs with the same seed see the same random numbers, so when you compare two sets of probabilities, only the orders whose number falls near a boundary go to a different supplier. These are common random numbers, explained in Running Experiments . Without a seed, the policy takes one from the site's random number generator, so scm.set_seed still makes the run repeatable. You can also give your own random.Random as rng . Manufacturers A manufacturer does not use a supplier-selection policy. For each raw material, it orders from the first raw-material supplier of that raw material that can take an order, in the order the links were created. While that supplier, or the link to it, is disrupted, it orders from the next one. A manufacturer given a supplier-selection policy, a mode or settings for the policy warns that they are not used. Writing your own policy When no built in policy fits, write your own as a subclass of SupplierSelectionPolicy . Suppose the retailer above should order from whichever distributor has the most units right now. class SelectMostStock(scm.SupplierSelectionPolicy): def select(self, order_quantity): candidates = self._active_suppliers() selected = max(candidates, key=lambda link: link.available_quantity()) return self._apply_mode(selected) Give it to a site like a built in policy. 'supplier_selection_policy': SelectMostStock, 'supplier_selection_mode': 'dynamic', A site reaches each supplier over a link, so the policy works with links. select is called with the number of units in the order and returns the link to the chosen supplier. Follow the same three steps as the built in policies. self._active_suppliers() returns the links in self.node.suppliers that can take an order right now, so disrupted suppliers and links are skipped. Choose one of them with your own rule. return self._apply_mode(selected) applies the fixed or dynamic mode, so your policy follows supplier_selection_mode like the built in ones. To compare suppliers, use what the link offers. link.available_quantity() gives the supplier's inventory level, so the policy does not need to reach past the link into the supplier's inventory. link.cost is the transportation cost, link.lead_time() draws a lead time, and link.source is the supplier itself. Policies with settings A policy can take settings, given to the site in supplier_selection_param , just as SelectProbabilistic takes its probabilities. Suppose the retailer should order from the cheapest distributor, but skip any distributor that has fewer than 20 units. class SelectCheapestInStock(scm.SupplierSelectionPolicy): _param_keys = ("min_units",) def select(self, order_quantity): min_units = (self.params or {}).get("min_units", 0) candidates = self._active_suppliers() stocked = [link for link in candidates if link.available_quantity() >= min_units] selected = min(stocked or candidates, key=lambda link: link.cost) return self._apply_mode(selected) The site gives the setting with the policy. 'supplier_selection_policy': SelectCheapestInStock, 'supplier_selection_mode': 'dynamic', 'supplier_selection_param': {'min_units': 20}, The policy finds its settings in self.params . When the site is given no settings, self.params is None , so the example reads from an empty dict instead and uses 0. When no distributor has 20 units, the policy takes the cheapest one anyway. _param_keys lists the settings the policy reads. The library warns about any other setting, because the policy would ignore it, so a typo such as 'min_unit' does not go unnoticed. Without _param_keys , no setting is checked. Some settings name suppliers, as the probabilities of SelectProbabilistic do. To check them against the site's links, override check_links(self) and raise a ValueError when a setting does not match. self.node.suppliers gives the links, and link.source.ID gives the ID of each supplier. create_sc_net calls check_links once every link exists, so a mistyped supplier ID is reported before the run. If you run a network without create_sc_net , call site.selection_policy.check_links() yourself once its links are created.
docs.title: Supplier Selection

docs.text: Imagine a retailer that can buy the same product from two distributors. Shipping from the first one is cheaper, but its orders take two days to arrive. The second one charges more for transport, and its orders arrive the next day. Each time the retailer orders, it has to pick one of them. In SupplyNetPy, the rule for this choice is called a supplier-selection policy. The replenishment policy decides when to order and how many units, and the supplier-selection policy decides which supplier receives the order. This guide shows how to choose a built in policy and its mode, how to choose suppliers at random, and how to write your own policy. The words used here are explained in the Glossary .
docs.title: Supplier Selection

docs.text: A distributor or retailer that has more than one supplier takes two settings. supplier_selection_policy is the policy's class, and supplier_selection_mode is "fixed" or "dynamic" . As with replenishment policies, pass the class itself, without creating an object from it. retailer = {'ID': 'R1', 'name': 'Retailer1', 'node_type': 'retailer', 'capacity': 100, 'initial_level': 100, 'inventory_holding_cost': 0.2, 'replenishment_policy': scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s': 40, 'S': 100}, 'supplier_selection_policy': scm.SelectCheapest, 'supplier_selection_mode': 'dynamic', 'product_buy_price': 100, 'product_sell_price': 110} Without these settings, a site uses SelectFirst in fixed mode, so it orders from the supplier whose link was created first. A site with only one supplier does not need them.
docs.title: Giving a site its policy

docs.text: Each policy chooses among the suppliers that can take an order right now. A supplier is skipped while its site, or the link to it, is disrupted. Policy Chooses Class First The supplier whose link was created first SelectFirst Available The first supplier whose inventory level can fill the whole order. If none can, the first supplier, and the order waits there until enough units arrive SelectAvailable Cheapest The supplier with the lowest transportation cost, the cost of the link to it SelectCheapest Fastest The supplier with the shortest lead time SelectFastest When lead times are random, SelectFastest draws one lead time from each link to compare them. The shipment then draws its own lead time, so the chosen supplier is the one that looked fastest at that moment, and it may still turn out slower.
docs.title: The built in policies

docs.text: The mode says how often the choice is made. In dynamic mode, the policy chooses again for every replenishment order. Use it when the best supplier can change during a run, for example with SelectAvailable , whose answer depends on the inventory levels at that moment, or with SelectFastest and random lead times. In fixed mode, the policy keeps the first supplier it chose and sends every later order there. This models a site with a regular supplier. While that supplier, or the link to it, is disrupted, the orders go to another supplier, chosen by the same rule. Once it recovers, the orders go back to it. In fixed mode the policy's rule decides only the first order and the orders placed during a disruption. So SelectAvailable in fixed mode looks at the inventory levels only once. Since fixed is the default of every built in policy except SelectProbabilistic , give supplier_selection_mode='dynamic' whenever you want the rule applied to every order. To see where the orders went, print the statistics of the site's links. Each row shows what the site ordered over one link and what arrived. scm.print_link_wise_performance(sc["nodes"]["R1"].suppliers)
docs.title: Fixed or dynamic

docs.text: Imagine a retailer that spreads its orders over three distributors. About half of its orders go to D1, about 30% to D2 and the rest to D3, with no rule such as the cheapest supplier. Each order goes to one of them by chance, with these shares. SelectProbabilistic does this. Give it the probability of each supplier in supplier_selection_param , keyed by the ID of the supplier. retailer = {'ID': 'R1', 'name': 'Retailer1', 'node_type': 'retailer', 'capacity': 100, 'initial_level': 100, 'inventory_holding_cost': 0.2, 'replenishment_policy': scm.SSReplenishment, 'policy_param': {'s': 40, 'S': 100}, 'supplier_selection_policy': scm.SelectProbabilistic, 'supplier_selection_param': {'probabilities': {'D1': 0.5, 'D2': 0.3, 'D3': 0.2}, 'seed': 7}, 'product_buy_price': 100, 'product_sell_price': 110} The probabilities must sum to 1, and none can be negative. A supplier with probability 0 is never chosen. Every link to the site needs a probability, and every probability needs a link, so a mistyped ID is reported when the network is built, before the run. The policy makes a new choice for every order, so it always works in dynamic mode, and supplier_selection_mode is not needed. Over many orders, the shares come close to the probabilities. The statistics of the site's links show the real shares, as above.
